Draw TeX, diagrams, charts and comparisons in the phone's transcript, as the Mac does

A reply's $…$, \(…\), $$…$$ and \[…\] are found before the Markdown parser sees them, with the
desktop's guards, so a price stays a price and cmark never eats a subscript. ```mermaid,
```realm-chart and ```realm-compare are read to the desktop's contract, and a body that does not
parse stays its code with the reason in its head.

TeX and diagrams are drawn by KaTeX and Mermaid (the desktop's pinned releases, vendored by
scripts/blocks-vendor.mjs) in one web view kept behind the app, and photographed once per block and
face. Charts are Swift Charts on the Mac's series palette, and a comparison is a grid with its pick
on a raised band, or a card per option where its columns do not fit.

Answer permissions and reply from Realm Mobile's notifications

A permission push offers Allow, Allow always and Deny, worded as the desktop
card words them, and a finished or failed turn offers Reply. Each answers over
the encrypted channel with session.answer or session.send, opening a short
channel under a background task when the app is suspended or not running, and
posts a notification saying why when the Mac cannot be reached. Allow, Allow
always and Reply need the phone unlocked.

The Mac adds two optional fields to the sealed push, category and request, so
the relay is unchanged. Delivered permission notifications are taken away once
Home shows their session no longer needs you.

Make a teammate's Computer tab say what it is doing on this Mac

The tab named a machine and three tools, then listed every session in one flat
list, so it never said what was running, what Stop would stop, or what any
session produced. It is now a report read from the top: a head in plain words
("2 sessions working · 1 needs you", what its sessions hold open, what today
came to) with a Stop that names what it stops; Now, with the session that
needs you first and an Answer button; Done by day, each row ending in the PR it
opened or merged, the release it shipped, or Failed with the reason; and On
this Mac, the terminals, devices and browser tabs its sessions hold, with Open
and Stop. Wide, Done gets a column of its own.

Outcomes come only from what a session's log recorded: the gh pr create,
gh pr merge and gh release create commands it ran and what GitHub printed
back, and the last error of a session that ended in error. The server reads
them for the computer's list alone.

Name an unpinned mobile session by the default its CLI marks

The mobile API names a session's model through the shared modelLabel, so a
Codex session with no model now reads as the model Codex's own list marks
default (GPT-6 Astra in the fixture), as the Mac's chip does, instead of
Realm's static guess. The fixture and the tests that held the guess move with it.

Run a sub-agent on the model its parent runs, and name it that way

A session with no model pinned runs its CLI's default, and a child started
with no model keeps that null, so it runs the same default. Every label for
it, though, read Realm's fixed guess (Fable 5.1): the agent_start and
agent_run report, the delegation line and Agents tab, the joined-teammate
note and the session's Context row. They now name the default the CLI's own
model list marks, the way team_list does since #249, and fall back to the
guess only where the list says nothing.

agent_review and browser_agent_run started their child on the harness
default even when the caller had pinned a model on the same harness. They
now take the caller's model there, as agent_run's children do.

Test that a sub-agent with no model is named and run as its parent's model

A child of a session with no model pinned runs the CLI's default, and the
report, the delegation line and the joined-teammate note should name that
default as the CLI reports it rather than Realm's fixed guess. A reviewer
and a browser agent on the caller's harness should run the caller's model.
Name the teammates' at-work set apart from the view's helper

Wait for the task's settle before hearing the read's broadcasts
Hear only the read's own broadcasts in the teammate unread test

Mark a row unread once its sub-agents finish, and clear it on select

A lead that ended its turn while sub-agents still ran wore the unread mark,
and a teammate row stayed marked after its chat was read: the server moved
the read mark and told nobody. The mark now waits for every sub-agent under
a session, and a moved read mark is broadcast as session.seen, re-reading
the teammates and the phone's home.

Working is a spinner and done is a check, both in the quiet ink, and an unread teammate says so by its bold name rather than a blue dot.

Keep the streamed part of a reply across a reload

A reply's text lives only in its deltas until its assistant_text is stored, so a
window reloaded mid-turn (or a phone opening the session) read a log with none of
it and started the reply at whatever delta came next. The server now keeps each
session's reply so far, sessions.streaming returns it with the seq it covers, and
every delta carries where it joins that text, so the read and the deltas around it
meet with nothing missing and nothing doubled.

Release 2.8.0

Name the space's own folder by its folder in the Move sheet, and say under Runs on where the session is

From a worktree, the sheet offered the space's folder as This checkout, which read as where the
session already was. Every checkout is now named by its folder, as the desktop's Move sheet names it,
and Runs on draws the session's own checkout the way Move to draws the others.

Bring two app tests up to Home's quiet line and the empty Review

A Home row has shown its state or what it is about, not both, since d4e1ffba; the row test still
looked for the model on a waiting row. Review went with the first Teams in 2da93eb6, and the server's
fixture stopped writing review.decide; RealmKit's test followed in ff81facc but the app's did not.

List sub-agents one line each, grouped failed first, with the report a press away

The Sub-agents sheet stacked a title, the model, the state, the time and three lines of report for
every agent, and every title repeated its teammate's "captain - ". It read like a log.

Each agent is now one line: its state's mark, what it was asked and how long it ran. The sheet groups
them under Failed, Needs you, Working, Done and Stopped, and drops the "<handle> - " every title
shares. A row still opens the agent's session; its chevron unfolds the report, the note and the model
in place. The session info sheet's Sub-agents section uses the same row, in the same order without
the group heads.

Show one space's team and sessions in the column, with one signal for each state

Under the space's name the column now lists, in order: Needs you from every space and profile,
the pinned teammates as a row of icons with the Lead first, the space's team as one flat list with
an age on each row, and a Sessions caption over the five sessions that moved last, with "Show all"
opening every session by time.

A teammate has no disclosure any more. The sessions it started are on its own page, not nested
under it in the sidebar. The person's groups are the only nesting left, and a group can be renamed
from its caption's menu. Pin and Unpin are on a teammate's menu.

Every row speaks one set of signals. Bold means unread, a spinner in the age's slot means working,
and the amber dot, the only dot left, means it needs you, a failed turn included. A row's tooltip
says the same thing in words. The green and blue dots are gone. The Team and Sessions captions no
longer fold, so their remembered folds go too.

Put the profile's spaces on the rail, and the profile on the rail's avatar

The column shows one space at a time now. Each space of the profile on screen is a tile on the
rail under the destinations, lit while the column shows it, with the count of what waits on you
there at its shoulder; the + under them makes a new space. A right-click on a tile, or the "···"
on the column's title, offers the space's settings, Rename and Delete, and the rest of what the
old section menu had.

The column's head is the space's name as a plain title. Switching profile moved to the avatar at
the rail's foot, which wears the amber dot while another profile has something waiting. The
section heads, their fold and the New space row at the column's foot are gone.

Put the Team on the phone: each teammate's row on Home, its chat headed by it, its messages in transcripts, and its Edit sheet

Home lists the profile's teammates under Team, each with its icon drawn as the Mac draws it, the Lead's star, its state as a dot and a word, and what it is working on; a long team shows its Lead and its busy ones and the rest on the Team page. A space's page heads with its Team. A teammate's chat is headed by the teammate and its replies are its own; a message an agent sends a teammate is a line with the teammate's icon and where the ask stands, and another teammate's word stands under its sender. The Edit sheet changes a teammate's name, brief, icon, model, permission and Lead. A chat the Team lists is not listed again as a session.
Read teammates, a transcript's messages to them, and an edit to one in RealmKit

Tell a phone what each teammate is doing, who a transcript's messages went to, and take its edits

teammates.list now carries each teammate's icon, its state and since when, whether its chat is unread, the task it is working on (or the newest it started) and what it runs on. A team_message row names the teammate it went to, resolved as the server resolves `to`, with the words as the teammate reads them; a teammate's message in a chat names its sender. teammate.update saves the Edit sheet through teammates.update, and a teammate changing says home.changed. Every field is optional, so an older Mac or phone reads the other as before.

Let a phone list each space's teammates and open a teammate's chat

An archived teammate's chat is refused as FORBIDDEN. A Mac older than these calls answers METHOD_NOT_FOUND and a phone offers no teammates, so neither side needs the other to be new.

Share photos, videos, files, links and text into Realm from any app on iOS

Realm is in the share sheet. It sends what was shared to one of the sessions Home last listed, or to a new session with an agent in a space. Realm then opens on that session with the files and words in its composer, ready to send.

Give the phone an inbox for what other apps share into Realm

The share extension copies each file in from the URL the other app gives, so a film is never read into its memory, and writes the share's manifest last. The app only takes a share once its manifest is there, and moves its files into the outbox instead of reading them. The inbox also keeps what the extension can offer: the sessions, spaces and agents the app last heard from the Mac.

the built app: typing in a long session took a median 176 ms per keystroke (worst 544 ms), and a
reply streaming in while scrolling held 18 frames for 2.9 s of every 6, the worst 467 ms.

Typing re-rendered the whole transcript, three ways at once:
- the session pane read the draft, so every keystroke re-rendered the pane — the composer now reads
  its own draft (DraftedComposer);
- setDraft handed back new chip/mention/link arrays on every edit even when nothing in them changed,
  and the pane subscribes to three — it now keeps the old list when the contents are the same;
- Markdown keyed its parse on the identity of an inline path handler, so every message re-parsed and
  re-sanitised whenever the pane rendered — it keys on whether a handler exists.
And the composer sized itself by collapsing the real field to 0 and reading it back, which relaid the
pane's whole column twice a keystroke; it now reads an unseen, contained sizer and writes the height
only when it changes.

A long transcript now draws its newest ~400 blocks (Transcript's window). Earlier turns load as the
reader scrolls up to them (or from "Show earlier messages"), the window holds still while the reader
is reading, a saved prompt opened from the Library is drawn before it is jumped to, and the scroll
memory puts a reader back into the same window. Keys stay the whole transcript's, so drawing further
back remounts nothing, and history drawn further back does not play the entrance new messages get.
The session summary no longer re-folds the whole transcript on every event for the bar's yes/no, and
the touched-files set stops re-normalising every path the session ever named.

After, on the same session: 5,375 nodes on the page instead of 69,326; typing 24 ms median (a short
session measures 16 ms in the same harness), worst 32 ms; plain scrolling with no long frames; and a
reply streaming in while scrolling holds 2-3 frames for ~0.25 s in 6 s.

keeps the plain step blink (two frames a second) and only the eased animations — smooth, phase,
expand, pulse — give way to it, which is what Low power is for. Reduce motion still holds it still.

clip sliced by UTF-16 unit, so a cut at an emoji kept its first half:
text no tokenizer or strict decoder takes. A training run on recorded
Instagram and TikTok screens refused its whole training set for 125 such
rows — the shadow's questions clip each option's label to 48. clip now
backs off a whole character; the recorder clips with it; and every row a
run writes has any lone surrogate from elsewhere — an app's own label, a

Give Realm a Mac menu bar, and bring the window back where it was left

The menu bar was Electron's default: no Settings…, no File menu, no Help, and
Reload and Developer Tools for every user — ⌘R reloaded the whole app out from
under whatever was running in it. Now it reads like a Mac app's. Settings… sits
under the app's name on ⌘,, then File, Edit, View, Go, Window (which macOS
completes with the window list) and Help (which macOS gives a search field).
Reload and Developer Tools are under View ▸ Developer in development builds only.

Every app row is a command from the keybinding catalog, and the shortcut it
shows is what the person's own keybindings resolve that command to, so a
rebinding in Settings ▸ Keys is a rebinding in the menu bar. The renderer
reports the rules whenever they load or change; a click sends the command back
and runs through the same runner the keystroke does. Settings is a catalog
command now too, `settings.open` on ⌘, — new defaults are merged into existing
keymaps, so it reaches everyone without overriding a binding.

The keystroke never goes through the menu. A menu accelerator fires before the
page sees the key, and on macOS `registerAccelerator: false` does not stop it,
so a shortcut in the menu would walk past the `when` clauses that keep ⌘B bold
in a rich field. Main asks, per keystroke, whether the person's rules bind the
chord, and if they do the page gets it — in a browser pane as well, which keeps
its own ⌘B. Copy, paste, undo, quit and hide stay the menu's. The keystroke
parser moved into contracts so both sides read a key as the same chord.

was. A place on a display that has since gone is replaced by the same size,
centred on the main display, rather than opening where no pointer can reach.

Nearly every one of those lines runs beside a change of surface that already
carries the boundary, so the line only has to sharpen it. The two that are the

Make the window behave like a Mac app, not a page in one

The difference people feel between a Swift app and this one was not one thing
but a dozen small web idioms, each of which a Mac user notices without being
able to name. This takes them out one by one, and measures each in the real
renderer (native-feel-live.mjs) rather than in the stylesheet.

Clicking. A button no longer shrinks when pressed — that is a touch idiom, where
a finger hides the control — it darkens on the mouse-down frame, one rung past
hover. And the press TRACKS the pointer the way an NSButton does: drag off a held
button and it lets go at once, drag back and it lights again. Chromium cannot
say that in CSS (it drops `:active` for good when a held pointer leaves), so
press-tracking.ts marks it up. Hover and press arrive instantly; only a hover's
release fades, and a row chosen from a list changes instantly both ways. The
hand cursor is gone from every control and kept for links. Chrome no longer
selects on a drag or a double-click; fields and code still do.

Menus are the system's. `Menu` hands its rows to an OS menu through main —
material, type-to-select, icons as template images, shortcuts as accelerators,
and the only surface that can open over a browser pane — and draws its own only
where there is no bridge (tests, and live scripts that set REALM_HTML_MENUS). A
right-click in text now gets what a Cocoa text view gives it, which Electron

Carry the test runner Realm installs on an iPhone to read and drive it

A real iPhone has no simctl and no serve-sim: the one sanctioned way to
read another app's element tree on it, and to touch it, is an XCUITest
running on the phone. This is that test, trimmed from Maestro's iOS
runner (Apache-2.0; LICENSE and NOTICE say what was taken and what was
changed). It never finishes: it serves the screen, the foreground app's
tree, and tap, swipe, text, key and button input over HTTP until Realm
stops the xcodebuild that runs it.

It is built without fetching anything — Maestro's HTTP server package is
replaced by a page of Network.framework — and listens on the phone's
loopback only, so nothing on the phone's Wi-Fi can drive it. It never
answers a system alert on its own, and does not expose the side button:
a phone the runner locked is one only its owner can unlock again.

Let an agent's answer fade in as it streams, instead of stamping on a chunk at a time

you scroll until it becomes the product. Realm's version is built from its own
geometry. The mark has six faces, and it turns out to be drawn on an equilateral

returned to the cells they were always drawn on.

boundary — each one something the shipped app does, with its limit stated. On

Put the landing page's hero in a dimension of its own

Tembo's page makes one move well: it names where agents should work, then puts
the product in that place — a sky, for a cloud. Realm's word for the place is a
realm, so the hero now says "Give your agents a world to work in" and shows the
workspace through a portal in one.

The portal is drawn by a single WebGPU field fixed behind the whole page rather
than a canvas per section: one device and one frame loop however long the page
gets. It works in the DOM's own coordinates, so the product image's rect goes
into a uniform unchanged each frame and the light stays on that element's edge
at every breakpoint and zoom. Around it, frames recede in log space — which is
what perspective does to evenly spaced planes — twisting as they go into a slow
vortex and flowing inward, toward the image. The pointer bends the corridor and
lights what it bends; a click sends a ring through it. Neither touches the rim,
which belongs to an element that does not move.

Captures are RGBA — the window they photograph is translucent — so every capture
frame now carries the page colour behind it. Without that the field would move
under their sidebars.

A frame loop answers to none of the stylesheet's motion controls, so this
re-implements them: reduced motion holds one frame and redraws only when the
page moves, a hidden tab stops the loop outright, and no WebGPU leaves the page
as it was with a CSS glow on the portal. The backing store is clamped to the
device's largest texture, which a wide enough window would otherwise pass.

Find a model's fast-mode answer under its context-window variant

The CLI lists some models only as a variant: Opus 5.5 appears as `default` and `opus[1m]`, both
resolving to `claude-opus-5-5[1m]`. A session that picked plain `claude-opus-5-5` matched no entry
exactly, so its fast-mode support was never stated and its Speed control never appeared — every
Opus 5.5 session started by name, 44 handshakes in the last day alone, had its answer dropped.

The lookup now falls back to the id without its bracketed suffix. The CLI serves fast mode on the
plain id (checked against the real CLI's initialize response: `fast_mode_state: "on"`), and an entry
naming the exact id still outranks a variant of it. Only a bracketed suffix counts as a variant; a
different model that shares a prefix does not.

Offer fast mode before the first message, and stop blaming the switch for old turns

The Speed switch only appeared once the session's own harness had said its model could run fast
mode — in the `init` that arrives after the first prompt. So the one prompt it could never be on
for was the first, and the user saw it appear only after sending.

That answer is now remembered past the session that heard it. The server files each `init`'s
answer in a settings row (`models.fastSupport`), keyed by agent and the model the session ASKED
for — the row's model, not the id the harness resolved it to, because a session that has not
started knows only what it will ask for; the harness default gets its own entry. A new session on
the same model is offered the switch from its first message, and its own `init` overrides the
remembered answer the moment it has one. A model no session has run yet has no entry and keeps
waiting for its harness: remembered, never guessed. The renderer re-reads the row whenever any
session's harness states an answer, since the session that wants it is never the one that heard.

The note under the switch stopped misreading a report. Switched on after a turn that ran without
it, that turn's usage still said "off" with the harness's reason for a request nobody made, and the
picker announced that fast mode could not run. Usage now says which turns asked; a report on a
turn that did not ask means the switch is untried, and the note says it takes effect next turn,
without the warning tone.

Say on Codex's usage too which turn asked for the Fast tier

Codex's report of the tier is the thread's own echo, and it lags the switch by one `turn/start`.
Flipped on after a turn that ran off, the picker read that turn's "off" as a refusal of the switch.
Each usage report now carries `fastModeRequested` from the turn it describes, as Claude's does.

The fake server's approval turn can now report usage (`USAGE`), so a test can park a turn, flip
the switch while it waits, and see the report still describe the request it ran under.

Start a session fast when it was switched on first, and say which turns asked

Fast mode switched on before a session's first message never reached the harness. The adapter
handed `query` a top-level `fastMode`, and the SDK's `Options` has no such key — `fastMode` is a
`Settings` key — so it was dropped without a word. Under the SDK the CLI gates fast mode on the
flag settings layer saying `fastMode: true`, and without it every turn reported
`sdk_opt_in_required`. The start option now rides in `settings`, which the SDK passes to the CLI as
`--settings`, the flag layer the gate reads.

Nothing would have caught the old line at compile time: a spread is never checked for excess keys,
and `Settings` itself ends in a catch-all `[k: string]: unknown`, so even `satisfies Settings` passes
a misspelling. The key is checked against the keys `Settings` DECLARES instead.

The test that should have caught it asserted the wrong key. Its fake `query` accepts anything, so it
agreed with the bug. It now asserts `settings`, and a type test holds the other half to the SDK's
real shape: an SDK that grows a top-level `fastMode` fails the typecheck there.

Each turn's usage now also carries `fastModeRequested` — whether THAT turn asked for fast mode. A
switch flipped mid-turn is about the next turn, but the report the current turn ends with describes
the old request; without the stamp the picker cannot tell a refusal of the switch from a report on
a turn that never asked, and it said fast mode could not run.

model` and the session quietly runs something else. The pinned 0.3.258 knows
`claude-opus-5` and not `claude-opus-5-5`; 0.3.281 knows both. So the floor moves
in BOTH apps/server and packages/adapters — the server's copy is the one a
packaged app actually spawns.

That rule was written down in three comments and enforced by none of them, which
is exactly how `claude-fable-5-1` shipped against a floor that could not route it
and fell back silently. It is a test now: every curated id is checked against the
binary that will be asked to run it, and the two floors are checked against each
other, because bumping adapters alone passes every other check and still ships
the old binary.

The scan streams the 210 MB binary and stops once every id is found; it takes
about a tenth of a second. It fails rather than skips when the SDK resolves and
its platform binary does not — a check that quietly stops running is how the rule

Show the product at the top of the README, on a ground it can keep

It now leads with the mark, the sentence the site leads with, and one capture of

open this file most often came for `pnpm dev`.

Frame each capture on the part of it the claim is about

Every scene is shot at the whole 1440x900 window, and most of them spend half of
that on the dimmed sidebar and the empty canvas either side of the subject. Shown
entire in a page column the subject arrived at about 60% of its own size, so the
page carried a picture of the product rather than a readable one — the schedules
scene is two rows in the top third of a frame whose lower half is empty, and the
activity scene's subject is the sidebar list, a strip an eighth of the frame wide.

A claim now names the region it is evidence for and the frame goes there. The
capture files are untouched, because `/features` reads the same ones and the full
frame is still the honest artifact; this is a crop at render, which is what
design.md asks for — one large legible product view and a few purposeful crops.
The picker in the agents scene gains its bottom back, which the old frame cut.

The narrow frame keeps the same region rather than zooming past it. Going deeper
there was the first thing tried and it sliced the plan block down its left edge,
which is precisely the focal relationship a narrow screen is meant to keep; the
4/3 frame gives back in height what it loses in scale. A focal point closer to an
edge than half a frame is held back to the edge, so the activity list can be the
subject without dragging the page's own background in beside it.

Write the 1.4.0 and 1.4.1 releases into the site's changelog

The changelog stopped at v1.3.0 while the download button, which resolves the
latest release at render, had been offering v1.4.1 for a day — so the page
advertised a version it did not list.

v1.4.0 is here as well as v1.4.1, because withdrawing a release is not the same
as it never having existed: its tag was public, and the entry carries a note
saying the build could not start and pointing at the release that shipped its
work. Both mirror `CHANGELOG.md` rather than telling the same story twice, and
the italics the root file uses become bold, which is one of the two inline spans
`Prose` renders.

Give the caret the controls VS Code has, as far as Chromium allows one

The app had exactly one cursor setting — whether a TERMINAL's blinks — and its
own contract explained the gap: the prompter's caret is the platform's, and
Chromium cannot be told to hold it still until `caret-animation` lands (139; this
app ships on 138). What that note left out is that the gap is not one hole, it is
three, and two of them were reachable all along.

A terminal's cursor gets a SHAPE: block, bar, underline — the three xterm draws
and the three every emulator offers. Its own control rather than a mode of the
blink, because a bar that holds still and a block that pulses are both pairs
people ask for, and one list of four makes half of them unreachable.

The CODE editor's caret gets its own blink switch. CodeMirror draws that caret
rather than the platform, so unlike the prompter's it can be told — and it is a
separate setting from the terminal's, the same split VS Code makes between
`editor.cursorBlinking` and `terminal.integrated.cursorBlinking`. The two are in
different places doing different jobs.

Both reach what is already open. `drawSelection` takes its rate at construction,
so the caret sits in a compartment and is reconfigured live, which is the
argument the terminal hub already makes for the blink: a preference that only
reached the next file opened is one somebody flips, sees nothing, and gives up on.

The prompter's caret stays out, and the editor switch's own copy says so — the
sentence belongs where a reader would otherwise go looking for the control that
is missing. Lifting it needs Electron 38 (Chromium 140), which is a bump, not a
setting.

Come back to where the reader was in a render and in a guide `scroll-memory` covered the source view, the rich editor and the code editor. The three surfaces it did not cover are the ones with no text to fall back on: a Quick Look render IS the document, and a guide is where someone reads for an hour. A Quick Look render is an in an ordinary scroller, so the hook attaches to it and nothing else is needed. A guide is a cross-origin frame, and the hook works by touching an element there is no way to touch. So the position rides the bridge the guide already has: the runtime posts its own offset as the reader moves, the pane keeps it, and hands it back on the next ready. The runtime re-applies it while the page is still growing — KaTeX and images both land after ready — and stops the moment it takes or the reader moves themselves, which is the same discipline the hook runs. A PDF still cannot. Chromium renders it in a nested viewer that runs no script of ours and sits behind an origin the pane cannot read, so there is nothing to ask and nothing to tell. Saying so is better than a setting that silently does nothing for the format people would test it with first. The spreadsheet is out for a duller reason: `.sheet-grid` is not the scroller — the grid scrolls inside itself — so a ref there would keep a number nobody reads.

Let a right-click on either arrow show the trail behind it

The gesture every browser has, and the one control this pane could not have:
`BrowserPane` bans dropdowns outright because a `WebContentsView` composites over
every piece of renderer DOM inside its rectangle, so a popover anchored to the
Back button would open behind the page it is about.

An OS menu is not renderer DOM. Main builds it from `navigationHistory` and pops
it as a window above the app, which is how Safari and Chrome do the same thing —
the no-overlay invariant is not bent, it is simply not what this surface is.

Building it in main also keeps the trail there. It is `webContents` state, and
broadcasting the entry list to the renderer on every navigation, to render a menu
nobody has opened, would be a message per page load for a list most people never
ask for. The renderer sends the button's corner, because only it knows where the
button is.

Twelve rows, titles cut to 64 characters. A `<title>` is routinely a sentence and
occasionally a paragraph, and the menu is a list of places rather than a reading
surface; a 300-entry trail is a scroll, not a menu.

Measure the leading through the cascade, where the only real answer is

The stylesheet now says `calc(1.6 + var(--lh-shift))` and a unit test can assert
that string, which is a statement about the file rather than about the text. What
matters is the used value, and jsdom computes no cascade at all.

So the live check grows a probe wearing the transcript's own class and reads
`getComputedStyle().lineHeight` in px, before and after the slider moves: 15px
prose at 1.6 is 24px, and at +30 it is 28.5px. If the registration were missing
or the property did not inherit, both readings would be the UA's default and
identical — which is exactly the failure a string assertion cannot see.

Let the reader set the leading, without flattening what each surface chose

There was no line-height control at all, and 99 hard-coded ratios behind it.
Prose is 1.6, markdown 1.55, a code block 1.65 — those are a judgement about
each surface, and a control that set one number would collapse them and lose the
reason a code block breathes more than a paragraph.

So it is an offset, the argument `--fw-shift` already makes for weight. One
slider writes `--lh-shift` as a ratio and each surface adds it to its own:
messages, markdown, fenced code, the prompter's trio and a rich document. Code
panes, terminals and diffs keep theirs — their line box is a grid the gutter is
measured against.

Registered with `@property`, for the same reason `--zoom` is: unregistered and
unset, `calc(1.6 + var(--lh-shift))` is invalid at computed-value time and the
whole declaration is dropped, so a renderer with no preload bridge would lay its
prose out on the UA's default.

The readout names the ratio prose lands on rather than the stored offset. "+10"
is a number about the control; 1.70 is a number about the text, and the text is
what you are looking at while you drag it.

`parseFontPref` takes it field by field like the rest, so a `ui.fonts` row
stored before this existed reads back as the default instead of putting NaN in
a `calc()`. The composer's mirror, textarea and hint carry one expression
between them — the test that pins their metrics together now pins the calc.

Put the profile's spaces in the rail, where the rest of its navigation is

The spaces were a chip strip between the head and the body — a third band whose
whole job was navigation, sitting over the title like decoration on it. The rail
two inches below already held every other place this page can send you.

Two lists in one rail: the page's sections, then the profile's spaces under
their own heading. Buttons rather than radios for the spaces, because a section
is a choice of what this page shows and a space is somewhere to go — one wearing
the tabs' `role=radio` would promise the rail keeps it lit after you leave.

`.page-rail-list` is stated ABOVE the narrow container query on purpose. Written
below it, the base `flex-direction: column` would beat the query's `row` — a
container query carries no extra specificity — and the horizontal strip would
come apart into two short stacks side by side. That is the same trap the chip
strip's own gutter rule documented, and the test that pins the order is what
caught me falling into it.

Add the live check the five sidebar and splits commits are answerable to

Every claim in this stack is about something jsdom cannot see: a strip that only
exists past two splits, an inset measured from where a tab's text actually lands,
a control that is `opacity: 0` until `:hover`, and two chords.

It earned its keep on the first run. The strip called itself Splits while the
tabs in it were named "Group 2" and "Group 3" — `nextGroupName` had been missed,
and no unit test could have caught it because none renders a name it generated.

The reaper kills by PORT rather than by pid. The server is a second Electron
process spawned by the one we start, so killing the parent leaves it holding
REALM_PORT, and the next run refuses to start on a port nothing is using any
more — which is what the first two runs of this script did.

Put a trash on the sidebar rows that had no way out but a right-click

Sessions have the shelf: a conversation you are done with gets put away. Every
other kind has no answer for what archiving would mean — a destination page is
one per space, a diff is a view of a checkout, a terminal is a pty — so those
rows carried one control and one only, and ending the thing meant discovering a
context menu.

The trash takes the shelf's place for the kinds that have no shelf, in the same
22px box, revealed by the same hover and the same :focus-visible. Two-step like
everywhere else, and it reads the switch from the previous commit, so a user who
turned the asking off is not asked here either.

Armed state is held by row id rather than a boolean: these rows share one
component, and a flag would arm every trash in the sidebar on one click. Danger
colour only on hover and while armed — a column of red trash cans at rest would
read as a list of problems rather than a list of things.

"Pane group" is the data structure's name, and it leaked all the way to the
toolbar. What a person makes when they split a pane is a split; the bar above
the panes, the sidebar's button, the palette's row and the ⌘⇧[ / ⌘⇧] commands
all now say so. The type, the store actions and the command ids keep their
names — those are the code's own vocabulary and renaming them is a different
edit with no user-visible half.

The strip was cramped against the window edge: 34px tall with 10/12px of inset
and 5/12px tabs, which put a tab's text within a few pixels of the traffic
lights on one side and the pane below it on the other. 38px, 14/16px inset,
6/14px tabs. The 2px gap between tabs is untouched — the insert marker is
positioned into that exact gap, and widening it would leave the marker sitting
against a tab rather than in the space it names.

⌘⇧G makes one. `paneGroup.new` was in the command catalog with no default
binding, so the strip's + was the only way to add a split while ⌘⇧[ and ⌘⇧]

"Really delete?" is the right default and the wrong tax. A person clearing out a
day of scratch terminals answers it twenty times without reading it once, and a
guard nobody reads is not a guard — it is a keystroke.

Settings ▸ App ▸ Deleting turns it off. On unless the user has said otherwise,
and read with `!== false` rather than `=== true`, so an unset key and a missing

Scope is the two-step on an ITEM and on a schedule — the four places that
actually say "Really delete?". It does not reach the confirms that are not
deletes: removing a split keeps its panes and says so in its own wording, and
discarding a quick chat throws away a draft. Nor the destructive dialogs that
name their object and offer an explicit Cancel, which are a different pattern
answering a different question.

Give Quick Chat a chord, since the sidebar row was the only way in

Every other way to start something has one — ⌘N a session, ⌘T a terminal — and
the fastest thing in the app was the one you had to reach for the mouse to open.
⌘⇧N pairs it with ⌘N, which is the relationship the two already have.

Open, not toggle: closing a quick chat deletes its session, so a second press of
a command named for opening would throw away the conversation the first press
started. `openQuickChat` already no-ops when one is up, which is the behaviour
the sidebar button has always had under the same name.

Call the sidebar's catch-all section Sessions, because that is what is in it

"Space" named the container rather than the contents, and it sat directly under
"Open" — a heading that names what its rows ARE. A reader scanning the two saw a
category and a place, and the place is already named twice above it: once in the
space header, once in the strip.

Give an unlocked friend pack the whole vocabulary, not a share of it

The pack's names were the reason to unlock anything, and mixing them into the
house verbs meant a group typed its word and then watched three runs in four say
"Percolating" — the generic app with a rare surprise in it, rather than theirs.

An unlocked pack replaces the house verbs entirely, including the nameless egg
lines that were the switch's stand-in for names nobody had. They come back when
the pack is forgotten.

Let the Agents page be a room and a wall, not only a list

Three views over the same agents, because "what is everything doing" and "what
did that one just say" are different questions and a list only answers the
second. The wall is tiles — one per agent, state on its face. The office is the
room `@realm/pixel-office` describes, with a figure per agent in a seat, and a
prompter that redraws it from a sentence.

Ordering comes from `session-activity`, which is also what the sidebar's new
"Sort spaces by activity" switch reads. It replaces the strip's drag order with
a computed one; turning it off restores the order you left, because dragging was
never touched, only not read from.

The fan-out sheet is the other half: one brief, N agents, from the sheet the
rest of the app already opens things in.

design.md gains the rule the office canvas cost us — a `requestAnimationFrame`
loop answers to neither the reduced-motion reset nor the `data-quiet` pause, so
it runs under a preference that silenced everything else and burns a core in a
window nobody is watching. Read both in JS and stop the loop; a canvas holds its
last frame for free. It also gains the label rule the Schedules page cost us two
commits back.

Show a picker's scrollbar while it scrolls, and not the rest of the time

The prompter's pickers kept a track on screen permanently: a grey bar beside a
list of six models that says nothing, because a list that short is obviously not
scrolled. Hiding it outright is worse — then a list that IS long gives no sign
there is more.

`useAutoHideScrollbar` is the macOS behaviour rather than a timer someone tuned:
the bar appears on scroll and withdraws after it stops, so the affordance shows
up exactly when it is information.

Stop the download handler deciding which file types are worth having

There was a file-type allowlist — documents, archives, images, audio, video —
and it refused everything else, including through the user's own Save button.
It was the wrong boundary. The web serves `.7z`, `.parquet`, `.ipynb`, a
firmware `.bin`, a font, a file with no extension at all, and a list that has
to be extended every time someone downloads a normal thing is a list that is
wrong by default.

The boundary that matters is the grant, not the extension: default-deny is the
resting state, and `download_blocked` is what an agent sees when it stays that
way — no live grant, or one already expired or spent.

Let a schedule name a single moment, not only a recurrence

Everything on the clock had to be written as cron, so "in two weeks, open the
PR" became a year field — a one-shot wearing a recurring expression's clothes,
which the page then showed as armed forever because nothing told it the firing
was the last one.

`once:<epoch ms>` is the second spelling, and `nextFireOf` is the single gate in
front of both. Absolute milliseconds rather than local wall-clock text, which is
the opposite of the choice cron makes one section up and deliberately so: "every
day at 9" has to survive a DST change, while "the 30th at 1pm" is an instant
somebody already picked and has no reason to be ambiguous. Digits only —
`once:1e12` and `once:0x10` are refused rather than coerced, because this field
decides when unattended work runs.

A schedule with nothing left to fire is a state the model already had
(`nextRunAt === null`, still enabled), so the page reads that as Completed
rather than needing a new column.

`realm-schedule` also reaches sessions now: a conversation can put work on the
clock without going to the Schedules page.

app.ts additionally carries the probe wiring from the previous commit and a
parked fake session used by the Agents wall two commits on — the authoring
sessions interleaved this file.

Tell a signed-out session what to do about it, instead of the raw failure

A turn that fails because the CLI is signed out reads exactly like a turn that
failed for any other reason: a red block with whatever the adapter said. The
user is left to guess that the remedy is a command, and which one.

`failover.ts` gains `authFix`, the one case where Realm can name a specific
thing to do — and it only names it after re-probing the CLI, because the
credentials file cannot say "signed out" on macOS and a remedy offered on a
guess is worse than no remedy. `probe.ts` asks `claude auth status --json`,
which is the only source that can answer false.

The fix travels to the transcript on the existing error event rather than a new
one, so every error row already written still parses. `CommandCopy` is the
control it renders with — a command Realm shows rather than runs, with the one
affordance that helps.

Give Realm a pixel office, and a model that can draw into it

The Agents page has only ever been a list, and a list is the one shape that
cannot answer "what is everything doing right now" at a glance. An office can:
a room with seats, furniture and a figure per agent, where position and posture
carry the state the list spends a column on.

This is the room itself and nothing that renders it. `@realm/pixel-office` owns
the vocabulary — tiles, furniture, seating — and the validator, so the rules for
what a legal office is live in one place rather than in whichever surface drew
one last. `generatePixelWorld` and `generatePixelSprite` are the two ways a
world arrives: a whole room from a description, or one sprite to put in it.

Assets are vendored rather than fetched; VENDOR.md records where each came from
and under what licence.

parameter of `release()` and not in scope in a module-level function. Reaching "booted" would have

Writing past Node's event loop is what makes a synchronous wait legitimate.

and fails on the reintroduced fault with the SyntaxError attached.

— which Node refuses at load: "Named export 'Terminal' not found". The app would have started, spawned
its server, and had it die immediately.

Every gate was green. The suite passed because vitest resolves that import through its own transform;
`tsc` passed because the types are fine; `pnpm build` passed because compiling a bundle does not run
it. The first execution of that code was going to be on a user's machine.

Two changes. `noExternal` bundles it, so esbuild resolves the name at BUILD time where a failure is a
build error. And `pnpm release` now boots the packaged server on a scratch REALM_HOME and requires it
to report ready, before the commit and the tag exist — the whole class of fault, not just this
instance: any top-level import that resolves when compiled and explodes when loaded.

The smoke step is injected like `exec` and `log` so the scratch-repo tests stub it, and one test
drives a failing boot to prove the release stops with no commit and no tag behind it.
release: v1.4.0

Be the authenticator a passkey needs, because Electron ships the API without one

Signing in to GitHub in a browser pane reported "partial passkey support",
and pressing the passkey button raised no Touch ID prompt at all — it sat
there and then failed.

Measured on Electron 37 before anything was written: `PublicKeyCredential`
is present and `isConditionalMediationAvailable()` answers true, but
`isUserVerifyingPlatformAuthenticatorAvailable()` answers FALSE. That exact
combination is what a site reads as partial support. Nothing prompted
because there was no authenticator behind the API: Chromium's macOS Touch ID
authenticator is gated behind a delegate Chrome implements and Electron does
not, and the hybrid transport needs the QR sheet that lives in Chrome's UI
layer.

Neither missing half can be supplied from here, and one of them never will
be. Driving the macOS system passkey sheet — the one that offers iCloud
Keychain — needs `com.apple.developer.web-browser.public-key-credential`, an
entitlement Apple issues to browser vendors. So the passkeys already on this
Mac stay out of reach, a site the user already has a passkey on needs a
second one registered here, and `PASSKEY_STORAGE_NOTE` says so in the words
Settings shows rather than leaving someone to work it out at a sign-in.

What Realm can do is be the authenticator. Chromium's virtual authenticator
is not a test double bolted on from outside: it is a real CTAP2
implementation inside the same FIDO stack, doing real P-256 signatures over
real authenticator data, and a relying party cannot tell its assertions from
a security key's. One goes into every pane; the private keys are sealed in
the same Keychain-anchored store the saved sign-ins already live in, under a
fifth domain (`passkey`) folded into the keyring the way `machine` and
`eggs` were — a missing domain is a key to mint, never a corrupt keyring to
discard, or an update would silently destroy every enrolled sign-in.

Four measured facts shaped the design, and three are not what the CDP
documentation suggests:

  - A virtual authenticator installs on a view that has loaded NOTHING,
    which is what makes the platform-authenticator answer true on the first
    paint of the first page — when a sign-in page decides what to offer.
    `Page`/`Runtime` do not: on a document-less view `Runtime.addBinding`
    never returns, so the pane loads `about:blank` first.
  - Presence cannot be granted after the fact. Flipping presence simulation
    on mid-flight does nothing — the request waits out the page's own
    timeout and fails. So the shim BLOCKS before dispatch rather than
    reporting after, and Touch ID happens first.
  - A withheld request is a request that waits and then refuses. That is
    every pane's resting state, and it is what stops an agent driving a pane
    from using a passkey unattended: no key loaded, no presence to simulate,
    and neither available without a fingerprint.
  - A pending conditional-mediation get POISONS the next modal one with
    `OperationError` — and a conditional get is what a sign-in page fires on
    load. Realm has no autofill surface to offer it to, so those are held
    unresolved and never dispatched, which is both what a conditional get
    does with nothing to show and the only way the button beside it works.

The rp id is derived from the pane's own URL, never from the `rp.id` the
page put in the options object, because two decisions are made before
Chromium ever sees the request: whether to raise a prompt, and which private
keys to unseal. `passkeyRpIdForPageUrl` is the passkey half of the gate
`normalizeOrigin` is for passwords, and deliberately a different rule — a
subdomain may use its parent's passkey, which is what WebAuthn scoping is
for, while the suffix must start at a label boundary or `notgithub.com`
walks straight through.

A refused request is otherwise invisible — the page gets `NotAllowedError`
and renders its own shrug — so the pane says which of four quite different
problems it is, because each needs something different from the user.
Settings lists what Realm holds and is the only way to forget one, with no
Add button: a passkey exists because a site asked and the user answered
Touch ID, so there is nothing to type and nothing an agent can call to mint
one. Removing one there deletes Realm's copy and says plainly that the site
still lists it.

Between requests a pane holds no key material at all: keys go in for the one
approved request, presence goes off first on the way out, and the
authenticator is cleared — including on the branch where the request blew up
after the page was released, which is the branch that most needs it.

`apps/desktop/scripts/passkeys-live.cjs` runs the real thing under the real
Electron binary: github.com/login now reports the platform authenticator
available with the shim in place, a real registration lands a key in the
vault, a FRESH pane with an empty authenticator asserts with it (same
credential id, real signature — only possible via the vault), the counter is
written back, and with the fingerprint refused it fails `NotAllowedError`
holding nothing. Emptying the vault and retrying in the pane that just
registered fails too, which is how "holds no key material" is asked in a way
that cannot be fooled.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Merge branch 'feature/self-drive' into integration/v0.6: Realm uses itself

Let Realm use itself: a readable terminal, a sign-in it can finish, and its own interface

Let a reader quote one passage of an answer instead of describing it

Selecting text in the transcript did nothing. A reader who wanted to ask
about one sentence of a forty-line answer had to describe which sentence,
and "the bit about the catch-up window" is both slower to write and less
exact than the sentence itself.

Select a passage now and a bar opens over it. Quote appends it to the
prompter as a blockquote, focuses the textarea and parks the caret on the
line below, so the next thing typed is the question about the passage.

The markdown is exact because markdown allows no latitude here: a
blockquote needs a blank line in front of it or the paragraph above
swallows it, and a blank line INSIDE one ends it — so an interior empty
line gets a bare `>` rather than being left empty. Without that a
two-paragraph passage renders as two quotations with the reader's own prose
apparently between them.

Copy is the other button, and it is there because it is the other thing
anyone does with selected text: a bar that opened over a selection and
refused the obvious half would read as having hijacked the gesture rather
than served it. What is deliberately absent is a button that SENDS. The
question is the reader's to write, and a control that guessed it would be
answering something nobody asked.

Four refusals, each for its own reason:

  - Whitespace only. A click that drags two pixels is a click, and a bar
    that opens on it opens when the reader was only putting the caret
    somewhere.
  - Crossing two messages. The offer is "quote THIS"; a selection running
    from an answer into the next user message has no single passage behind
    it, and quoting the pair hands the agent its own words attributed to
    nobody.
  - A message still being written. Text that is still arriving moves under
    the selection, and MessageActions withholds itself from a streaming
    message for exactly this reason.
  - Anything that is not prose. Tool cards, permission cards and plans are
    structured records, and a quote of their rendered text is a quote of
    the interface rather than of anything the agent said.

The bar is mounted OUTSIDE the scroller, which is load-bearing rather than
incidental: `.transcript` carries the edge dissolve, and a mask applies to
everything its element paints. That costs a scroll listener — the bar is
positioned against `.transcript-wrap`, which does not move — and buys a
control the mask cannot reach.

That claim was wrong in its first draft, and is now measured. The comments
said the bar would fade at the TOP edge; that band is 40px and the bar
flips BELOW a passage that high, so it never sits deep in it. The hazard is
the bottom band at 68px, which swallows most of a 32px bar. The live check
re-parents the bar into the scroller at identical coordinates and reads the
brightest pixel of its label fall from 243 to 194.

The quote crosses the pane as a pulse (`{ text, n }`) rather than a string.
The same passage quoted twice is two requests, and a value-equal prop
delivers only the first. It lands in the Composer rather than being written
to the store by whoever handled the click, so the insertion ends where
every other insertion there ends — in `pendingSel`, the one path that
focuses the textarea and places the caret. A store write alone leaves the
quote sitting in a prompter the reader still has to click into.

The tests are split three ways because jsdom forces it: a Range there
reports every rect as zero, so a suite driving a real selection would
assert against a bar at the origin and pass whatever the placement
returned. The arithmetic is tested as pure numbers, the behaviour (which
listener it opens on, the mousedown guard, the absent-callback rule) in
jsdom, and the geometry in the Electron window.

Two things only the window could catch:

  - The bar was placed off-screen when the passage had been scrolled out of
    view (top: -412). Today that is invisible by accident; the first change
    that clamps coordinates into view would start parking a bar at the pane
    edge pointing at a passage nobody can see. It stands down instead. The
    fix needed a second guard — an unmeasured wrapper is all zeros and every
    selection fails an overlap test against it, so "no layout yet" was
    reading as "off screen".
  - `:last-of-type` is the last element of its type among siblings, not the
    last match, so the bottom-edge reading had been selecting whatever block
    happened to be last in the column.

`Range.prototype.getBoundingClientRect` is stubbed in the renderer's test
setup: jsdom implements Range but not its geometry, so the component threw
there rather than reading a zero. It is guarded on `Range` existing at all,
because that file also runs for the main-process suites, which declare the
node environment and have no DOM globals whatsoever.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Stop the browser panes announcing themselves as Electron

A pane sent `… Chrome/138.0.7204.251 Electron/37.10.3 Safari/537.36`, and
there was no user agent override anywhere in the app — that string is
Chromium's default, straight out. Two things in it are wrong, in the
specific sense that no browser any site has been tested against sends them.

`Electron/37.10.3` is the loud one. Sites do read it: some serve a degraded
page, some refuse, and all of it is invisible from this side because the
page simply behaves differently and nobody can see why. What is left once
it comes off is true — Chromium, on macOS, at the version we ship.

The build number is the quiet one. Chrome froze the minor/build/patch at
zero in its own UA years ago, so a real Chrome 138 sends `138.0.0.0`.
Sending `138.0.7204.251` marks the client as not-a-browser about as
clearly as the Electron token does, and for no benefit at all.

What this deliberately does NOT do is claim a newer Chrome than the engine
is. It would silence an out-of-date interstitial today and buy that by
telling a site it may use features this renderer does not have — which
surfaces as a blank panel three clicks into a flow and cannot be diagnosed
from the page. Being out of date gets fixed by not being out of date.

So this does not quiet the Brightspace dialog: D2L reads the Chrome major
and the major is still, honestly, 138. That one is the Electron bump's to
fix. This is the part worth doing either way, and the part that keeps
working afterwards.

Both the derivation and the wiring were measured rather than assumed:

  - `session.setUserAgent` reaches views created AFTER the call and leaves
    existing ones on the old string (Electron 37, observed). So the session
    covers what has no view — workers, the partition's own fetches — and
    the factory covers the view in hand. One function feeds both, so they
    cannot drift, and it is idempotent so applying it twice cannot compound.
  - With both in place a real page's document request, its subresource
    requests and `navigator.userAgent` all come back clean.

The limit, also measured, because a half-fix presented as a whole one is
worse than none: `navigator.userAgentData.brands` still reports `Chromium`
rather than `Google Chrome`, and overriding the UA string does not change
it — Electron exposes no API for the client-hint metadata. A site that
sniffs client hints still sees Chromium. The string is what the
overwhelming majority of sniffers read, and it is the half we can reach.

The version is read off the session rather than hardcoded, so it tracks
whatever Chromium the app ships without anyone remembering to update it —
the failure mode a constant has is claiming an engine that no longer exists.

Give "Sort spaces by activity" a switch, so the setting is reachable from the app

The preference was real, persisted and honoured by the strip, and nothing in the interface could turn
it on — SpaceStrip's own comment pointed at a Settings section that did not exist.

It gets a Sidebar section rather than a row under Appearance: a sort order is not a matter of looks,
and the comment already named the section. One row for now. The sidebar's other preference — invert
swipe — stays in the strip's own header menu, where it sits on the gesture it changes; moving it here
to make the section look fuller would take a control away from the thing it acts on.

The hint says what the switch COSTS, not only what it does. Dragging stops working while it is on,
and a switch that disabled a gesture without saying so would read as the gesture breaking.

Also fixes the comment that sent people here: it quoted a label ("Sort by activity") that is not the
one on screen, and a misquoted label is a small lie that survives a search for it.

Pin the stamp the sort key depends on, which nothing was testing

The committed spec covers spaceActivity exactly, and covers nothing that keeps its input current.
Deleting the stamp from applySessionStatus left all 643 tests in the sidebar and store green while
"sort by activity" quietly stopped following activity.

Two tests: a status CHANGE reorders the strip, and a repeat of the same status does not — the second
is the half that says why the guard is `prev !== status` rather than unconditional.

Write the store half SpaceStrip has been importing, so the branch builds again

SpaceStrip.tsx and space-strip.test.tsx are committed and import `spaceActivity`, `sessionUpdatedAt`
and `setSidebarActivityOrder`; store.ts exported none of them. The branch has not typechecked or
built since, and seven tests have been failing on it.

Written to the committed tests rather than copied from anywhere: they specify the sort key exactly —
the newest session in the space and never the sum, Infinity for one holding a question, zero for a
space whose sessions are elsewhere.

`spaceActivity` iterates `sessionSpace`, not `sessionStatus` as its neighbour `spaceBadge` does. The
badge's question IS about status; this one's is not, and a session with a timestamp that nothing has
broadcast about yet is ordinary — iterating statuses would score its space at zero.

One thing the tests do not pin, added because the feature is visibly broken without it:
`applySessionStatus` stamps `sessionUpdatedAt`. That path patches status locally rather than
refetching, so without it `updatedAt` sits at whatever the last list said and "sort by activity"
only re-sorts on a refetch. Stamped on a real change only — a repeat of the same status is a
broadcast, not movement.

Let an agent put a file into a page, without the panel it cannot dismiss

Driving a browser pane, an agent could read, click, type and scroll, and
every route to attaching a file dead-ended. Typing a path into an
<input type="file"> does nothing. Clicking "Choose files" opens a native
NSOpenPanel — which nothing in the toolset can drive, and which is MODAL,
so the pane is wedged until a human dismisses it by hand: the agent cannot
even undo its own click. Dropzones had no tool at all. The task that found
this was a Devpost gallery and a demo video on YouTube, and it stopped
dead three different ways.

Driving the panel was the one option refused outright. It needs
Accessibility/UI scripting (`System Events`' `UI elements enabled` is false
on this machine), and asking someone to hand over machine-wide automation
so an agent can work a file picker is the wrong trade for what it buys.

So Realm never opens the panel. `browser_upload({ browserId, ref, paths })`
takes any of three refs and does not ask the caller to know which:

  - The <input type=file> itself, or the hidden one a visible label stands
    for — `DOM.setFileInputFiles`, no click and no chooser. This is how
    nearly every styled uploader is built and it is the happy path. The
    label search takes a `for=`, a containing <label>, or an element
    holding EXACTLY one file input; two is ambiguous and falls through
    rather than attaching a gallery's photos to the avatar field.
  - A button that opens a picker from script — interception armed FIRST,
    then the click. The ordering is the whole safety property, and
    `Page.fileChooserOpened` then names the very node the page meant to
    fill, which is the only way to learn its accept= at all.
  - A dropzone — a real DataTransfer of real Files and the three events one
    listens for, chosen on the element's own listeners rather than on the
    words "drag and drop" in its markup. Last, and capped at 25 MB: it is
    the only route where the bytes travel through the page.

The wedge is now prevented rather than recovered from. EVERY agent click or
key arms interception for a short window, because any click can be the one
that opens a picker, so an agent can no longer put a native panel on screen
at all. The window is short on purpose — interception belongs to the page,
and a pane left armed is one where the user's own "Choose files" button
silently does nothing. `browser_dismiss_dialog` cancels what was caught, by
telling the page nothing was picked. It says so plainly when there is
nothing to cancel: a panel opened outside Realm's control is beyond CDP's
reach, and claiming otherwise would be the more useless answer.

What bounds an upload, all of it decided BEFORE the card is raised, because
a card's job is to describe a decision and not to be the only thing behind
one:

  - Keys and secrets are REFUSED, not prompted — ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, keychains,
    *.pem, .env, bare key names. Per file, after realpath, so a friendly
    name inside the space folder pointing at a private key is refused by its
    real name; and against the path as WRITTEN too, so `~/.ssh/id_rsa` reads
    as a refusal rather than as a spelling to correct.
  - The space folder is the default root. Outside is allowed but VISIBLE:
    the full resolved path goes on the card, quoted, and the card now draws
    the file list instead of leaving it in the JSON disclosure — "Allow" on
    a set of files nobody has seen is not consent.
  - All-or-nothing per call. The user answered a question about a set;
    silently uploading four of five answers a question they were not asked.
  - accept= and multiple are enforced against the live node, so a wrong file
    fails here with a reason instead of being dropped silently by the site.
    A refusal attaches nothing and hands the chooser BACK — otherwise the
    node is known to nobody and the page waits for a file that can never
    arrive.

And it is answerable afterwards without a screenshot: the result reports the
names read off `input.files`, and a snapshot renders an attached file input's
names the way it renders a textbox's value. `value` is nullable, because "I
could not read it back" and "the page cleared it" are different facts and
collapsing them would report a landed upload as a failed one.

`browser_upload` cannot go inside `browser_batch`, for the reason
`browser_fill_credential` cannot: a batch is one prompt for many steps, and
this one's prompt IS the files and the site. `browser_dismiss_dialog` can —
it carries no payload and names no destination.

Give the space a switch for whether Realm may press Approve itself

The setting existed and defaulted off; nothing could turn it on but writing the key by hand, which
made the automatic half of the sign-in flow unreachable from the app.

It lives on the space page's Connections tab because it is a per-space decision and that tab is the
one surface already mounted for a single space — an app-level page would have to grow a space picker
to ask a question this one already knows the answer to. Read on mount rather than at boot for the
same reason: cached globally, it would be a value true only for whichever space was looked at last.

Null until the read lands, and nothing rendered meanwhile. A switch drawn OFF while its real value is
still in flight is a claim about a permission, and one that flips under the pointer a moment later.

The copy says what OFF means as well as what ON does. A label describing only the on state leaves a
reader unsure the feature works without it — it does; the terminal and the consent page arrive either
way, and the switch decides only who presses the button.

Put a Sign in button on the card that has been printing a command at people

InstallCard's header comment said a signed-out agent could only ever be offered the command to copy,
"because logging in is a browser flow or an API key, not a command Realm can run to completion on
someone's behalf". That stopped being true the moment Realm had a terminal that talks back and a
pane to put the consent page in.

The button is offered for a signed-OUT agent with a login command and nothing else. `missing` has no
credentials to fix — it has no CLI — and spawning a terminal to run a command that is not installed
would hand the user a "command not found" they would read as the sign-in failing.

The note under it says where Realm stops, because the browser tools refuse that click and a card
that started the errand without saying who finishes it would be making a promise the rest of the
system then breaks.

Answer a sign-in on the terminal, not on the outcome, so a button can start one

SignInFlow.start waited up to forty-five seconds for the CLI to print its URL. That is right for a
tool call, which wants the whole outcome and can block for it, and wrong for a button: the terminal
pane is on screen the instant it is spawned and the user is already watching the command run, so a
click that sat unacknowledged until the CLI finished would be reporting, very late, something they
had been looking at the whole time.

So `start` returns once the shell is running with the command typed, and hands back the rest as
`settled`. The tool awaits both halves; `signin.start` awaits only the first and lets the consent
pane arrive the way every other pane does, through the item broadcast.

`settled` cannot reject. A caller that ignores it must not be able to produce an unhandled rejection,
and a caller that awaits it is owed an outcome rather than a throw — a sign-in whose URL never came
is a real result with a screen attached.

Drop a read-only tool set that classified nothing

The browser provider keeps one because browser_batch consults it to decide which steps need gating.
There is no terminal_batch, so this copy was defined, re-exported, and read by no one — a table that
looks authoritative about which tools are safe while having no bearing on whether any of them gate.
What decides that here is which handler calls broker.gate.

Stop telling the user Realm's own tools are on by default, now that three of them are not

The hint said "On by default" flatly. That was already untrue of realm-computer and realm-vm, and
realm-app makes three. It names the property they share instead of listing them — reaching outside a
pane Realm made — so it stays true as the list grows, which is the same reason the rows themselves
are built from whatever the gateway reports rather than from a table here.

Let Realm read and press its own interface, and refuse the two buttons that would let it approve itself

A browser pane is a WebContentsView driven over webContents.debugger; Realm's window is a
BrowserWindow with the same debugger on it. buildSnapshot, performAct and markAct never knew which
they were pointed at — they take a CdpSend — so this is a binding, not a port, and everything that
path has learned stays true: refs against live geometry, the occlusion check, the agent cursor at the
point the input went to.

The refusal is the reason this is shippable. An agent that can click Realm's buttons can click
Realm's own permission dialog, approving the request it is blocked on; no permission model survives
that, because every approval in Realm ends up as a button in that window. The permission card and
the bypassPermissions confirmation carry data-no-agent, and main refuses any ref inside one — read
from the live DOM at act time, because a snapshot taken before a card appeared is a fact about a
different screen. A ref that will not resolve refuses too: "the check errored" is not a reason to
press Approve.

Marked in the DOM rather than matched on labels, because a label gets reworded and shared with
buttons that grant nothing, while the attribute is a claim the component makes in the file where
whoever changes it will see it. no-agent-surfaces.test.ts is the list, written down so removing one
is visible.

Off until a space asks, joining realm-computer and realm-vm. The rule that would have made it
default-on — everything acting inside Realm ships on — is the rule this is the exception to:
everything else reaches a pane Realm made, and this reaches the window the user is reading.

The window-scoped DriveFrame added earlier is gone: those acts go through markAct too, into this very
document, so the injected frame already lands around the whole app with the cursor beside it. Two
ways to draw one thing is one too many.

Sign an agent CLI in, instead of handing the user a command to go and run

InstallCard states the position this replaces, in its own header comment: "A signed-out agent is
always the second case, because logging in is a browser flow or an API key, not a command Realm can
run to completion on someone's behalf." That was true of a command Realm could only spawn and read.
It stops being true once there is a terminal that talks back and a pane to put the consent page in.

signin_start opens a terminal, runs the CLI's own login command, reads the URL off the rendered
screen — whole, across the wrap — opens it in a pane, and hands the agent both ids. It does not press
Authorize; unless the space enabled it, the browser tools now refuse that click and the tool result
says so, because an agent that has to discover a refusal has spent a turn learning what a sentence
could have told it.

The command comes from AGENT_CLI_COMMANDS and never from the caller. That is the whole basis of the
ticket: the URL was printed by a program Realm chose to run, not produced by anything an agent said.
A caller-supplied command would turn the flow into a laundering step for any URL.

The consent URL is preferred over the first URL on screen — every one of these CLIs prints a docs or
status link in its banner first, so taking the first match would open documentation and wait for an
approval that was never coming.

Also: the provider-list test asked about one provider's switch by array index, which made each line
a second, accidental assertion about registration order. Asked by name now; order stays pinned by
the whole-array comparisons above, which is where that claim belongs.

Ask where the pane IS before acting, because the consent guard never covered the click

guards.ts refuses agent navigation to a consent URL in every mode, on the grounds that "a click on
Authorize grants a durable capability no per-action permission prompt can express". It guards
browser_open and browser_navigate, and its own comment admits it cannot see "a same-site link the
agent CLICKS (click targets come from the page, not from tool args — browser_act has no URL to
test)".

That admission is larger than it reads: the act the guard exists to prevent is pressing the button,
and any pane that reached a consent screen by a redirect, a click, or the user's own address bar
could be acted on freely, in every mode including bypassPermissions. browser_act now fetches the
pane's URL — describe already runs there for the permission card's title — and refuses.

SignInTickets is what can say yes, and it is a ticket rather than a mode because what makes an
automated sign-in defensible is provenance: this exact URL was read off a terminal Realm started,
running a login command out of AGENT_CLI_COMMANDS, seconds ago. A space-wide switch would be a
standing grant to authorize anything on any origin for as long as it stayed on.

So the switch decides whether tickets are minted and the ticket decides whether one act is allowed.
Off by default: Realm still opens the terminal, types the command and puts the consent page in front
of you, and the last click is yours.

Assert each frame scope on its own body, because joined they covered for each other

Mutating the pane ring to 3px left the test green: the assertion ran against both scopes' bodies
concatenated, and a `toContain` over a joined haystack is satisfied by whichever half still agrees.
The window rule was untouched, so it answered for the pane rule — which is precisely the drift the
describe exists to catch.

Draw "an agent is controlling this" on Realm's own panes, from the table the injected one reads

The mark already exists around a browser and a simulator, injected into the page over CDP because a
WebContentsView composites above all DOM and nothing the renderer paints beside one can reach it. A
terminal pane is ordinary DOM in this window, so it needs the other implementation — the one
agent-cursor.ts described before either half existed: "two surfaces, two transports, one appearance
— so the appearance is a number table both read, and styles.test.ts asserts the parity".

That table could not live in src/main: the desktop app compiles main and renderer as separate
composite projects, so a renderer file importing it is a TypeScript error rather than a decision.
It is AGENT_FRAME in contracts now, and the injected frame's own ring and glow read from it instead
of spelling literals — the two faces of one signal cannot drift any more.

What is NOT copied is the geometry. Inside a page the pane's edge is somewhere else entirely; here
it is right there, and styles.css already says what a flush glow does beside a neighbour — "in a
four-way split a flush ring would run straight into its neighbour's and the two would look like one
target". So a pane-scoped frame insets and takes the pane's corner, as the drop highlight does.

Nor are the literals: the injected CSS lands in a foreign page where no Realm token exists, so it
