Make the space swipe a spring the fingers hand off to, and catchable at any point

The gesture was already 1:1 with the fingers. What it did the moment they
lifted was a CSS transition — a fixed curve over a fixed duration, started
from rest — and three things follow from that which no amount of tuning
the curve fixes. A page thrown hard and a page nudged over the line landed
at the same speed, which is the seam between a gesture and its animation.
The slide could not be caught: grabbing a page mid-flight fought the
transition and jumped. And a reversal was a cut rather than a re-aim.

So the endgame is a spring now (`state/spring.ts`), in the two numbers
Apple hands designers rather than the three physics hands engineers:
damping and response. It always animates from where the thing IS, it
carries velocity, and it has no duration to run out — so an interrupt is
just a new target, and the release velocity is handed straight to it.

Both springs here are critically damped, and the bounce Apple gives a
thrown sheet is deliberately refused: this is a PAGER. Overshoot on a
sheet shows more of the sheet; overshoot on a page that fills the column
shows the edge of the page after the one you asked for. A throw gets the
velocity handoff and a shorter response instead — it arrives sooner
because it was thrown harder, not because it bounces.

Two of the three physics constants were also wrong in kind rather than in
degree. Rubber-banding was a flat 0.35 multiplier, which is not resistance
— the page just becomes heavy and keeps going, so the end of the track
never announces itself; it is Apple's progressive curve now, giving 55% to
the first pixels and asymptotically less after. And the flick projection
was a linear 70ms lookahead, where the thing being modelled is exponential
decay: `project()` is the function from Designing Fluid Interfaces, at the
snappier 0.99 rate a 240px surface wants rather than a screen's 0.998.
Velocity is clamped to 8px/ms, because two deltas that arrive in the same
millisecond divide by the 1ms floor and report a throw no hand could make.

Folded in from #46 (hudsonaikins), whose report was the other half of this:
a lone space no longer moves at all, and a drag has to be 6px and half
again more horizontal than vertical before anything follows it. A diagonal
flick down a long list used to drift the column sideways on its way past.

transform every frame: 67 animated frames converging from 254px, landing
exactly on the page, no CSS transition ever set, never overshooting, a hard
throw landing 50ms sooner than a gentle one, and a page grabbed mid-flight
continuing from where it was rather than snapping back.

A length in `px` shrinks in exact proportion when the page zooms, so a
column sized in px keeps the same share of the window at every zoom level.
Zooming out to fit more of the work on screen therefore bought nothing
back from the prompter: it got smaller exactly as fast as everything
around it, and stayed as dominant as it was at 100%.

`--prompter-w` multiplies by the zoom now — clamp(480px, 720px × zoom,
720px). At 80% the column is 576 CSS pixels rather than 720, which is 461
on screen where a plain px column would still be drawing 576. Zooming IN
is unchanged, because the ceiling is today's number and the dock's own
`100% - 48px` already owns the case where the pane is narrower than the
column. The floor is a reading measure rather than a taste: 480px of 15px
text is about 55 characters, the bottom of the band design.md asks for.

The factor cannot be derived in the renderer — `devicePixelRatio` is the
display's scale times the zoom, and a 2× display at 100% reports what a 1×
display at 200% does — so it comes from `webFrame.getZoomFactor()` through
the preload. Chromium fires no event for a zoom change, but it always
changes the viewport, so `resize` is the signal and re-reading a
synchronous getter there costs nothing. `--zoom` is registered with an
initial value of 1: unregistered and unset, the calc is invalid at
computed-value time and takes the column's width with it, so a renderer
with no bridge would have no prompter column at all.

The transcript follows, because the two are one rail. The reading column
and the box you type into have shared an edge since the refresh, and
letting only one of them move would break that at exactly the zoom levels
where the window is busiest.

zooms the window the way the View menu does (`webContents.setZoomFactor`,
from the wrapper — CDP has no page-zoom command) and measures the dock at
both levels. Every link in that chain is outside the suite.

Refuse to run against a server this app did not ship, and prove the daemon end to end

`decideLaunch` has known since Phase 2 that a daemon running a different bundle is a
handoff; this decides what to do about one.

**The gate ships whole, and is always correct.** Stopping a daemon and starting the
new one loses nothing a restart would not have lost anyway — sessions resume from
their provider ids, runs are requeued, terminals come back with their scrollback. The
one thing it costs is a turn that happens to be mid-flight, which is exactly why the
user is asked when there is one and not asked when there is not. A daemon that will
not answer `daemon.info` counts as busy: a dialog somebody dismisses costs a click,
and a silent stop costs a turn. *Keep working* is offered only when the wire is one
this app can drive, because carrying on with a socket we cannot use is not a choice.

The banner stopped telling one lie. "Connection lost — reconnecting…" is honest about
a dropped socket and false about a server that has crashed five times in two minutes,
and the two are indistinguishable from the renderer's side — only main can tell them
apart, so it says which, and the words live in a pure function that can be read
without a window. That also closes the supervisor's loose end from Phase 3: its states
had a channel out of main and nothing listening on the other side.

Behind `daemon.handoffMode = "drain"`, and marked experimental, the overlap. The
load-bearing rule is not refusing new work — it is refusing to START a cold adapter
handle for a session that has not got one. An already-exec'd child keeps its inode and
is fine; a NEW agent would exec a path `install-local.mjs` has deleted. Quiescence is
held for ten seconds rather than sampled, because a session that just settled may be
about to run a queued message and a daemon that closed in that gap would take the
queue with it.

`install-local.mjs` needed both halves the plan called for. It counted the daemon in
`runningPids` — same Electron binary, different argument — so `app:update` would have
asked the app to quit, then waited fifteen seconds for a server nobody asked to leave
and refused to install. And it now KEEPS the previous bundle, sweeping unreferenced
ones at the start of the next install: a daemon still executing out of the old bundle
execs every agent from a path inside it.

**Two live checks, and they earned their keep immediately.** The lifecycle one kills
the app outright — ⌘Q now means "put the UI away", so an ordinary quit would prove
nothing — and then asserts over the socket that the daemon still serves, that a
session advances with no Realm running at all, that the next launch adopts rather than
replaces, and that a cursored terminal read is the tail of the whole buffer.

It found a real bug in the launcher: the fifteen-second wait budget bounded the whole
orchestration rather than one wait, so stopping the old daemon spent it and the
replacement was never given time to boot. Every handoff on a machine where the old
server took a moment to exit would have failed to start anything. Each action now
restarts the clock. No test over an injected clock could have caught it — the fake
handoff returns instantly.

Two of my own assertions were wrong rather than the code, and both are now stated as

Say so when an agent could not continue the conversation above it

passed it back as `resume` on the next send. What it has never said is whether that
worked — and a resume that silently starts a fresh thread under an old transcript is
the one lie worth removing here: every message stays on screen, looking for all the
world like context the agent has, and the agent has none of it.

So `init` now carries `resumeRequested` and `resumeOutcome`, and a session that HELD
an id and came back without one gets a `context_reset` seam. It joins `handoff` and

from all three is the same sentence — what is above this line is not what is below
it — and drawing that three slightly different ways would be a distinction that
means nothing.

longer in `~/.codex`, and that rejection killed the boot. Since Realm hands back the
same id on every send, one refusal made the session permanently unstartable: every
attempt failed identically, with nothing anywhere to say why. It now falls back to
`thread/start`, which is not merely the other call — it is the one that carries
`developerInstructions`, so the memory channel comes back with it. A resume that
merely TIMES OUT is deliberately not a refusal: the app-server said nothing at all,
and a second bounded call would spend another whole boot budget on the same silence,
so `withTimeout` now marks its rejections and only a real refusal falls back.

ACP already computed all three outcomes and told only a log line, which is the one
place the user cannot see. It reports them now.

Claude's claim is the narrow one. The SDK forks to a new session id on resume rather
than continuing the old one, so "the request was accepted" is the strongest thing
that is true for it, and `continued` is defined to mean exactly that and no more.

`AGENT_SESSION_RESUME` states which of the three situations each agent is in:
`native` (the adapter always asks), `advertised` (ACP, where resume exists only if
`initialize` said `loadSession` — a per-binary, per-run fact this table has no
business restating), `none` (measured absent). `minVersion` is null for every kind,
and that is a finding rather than a placeholder: Realm has measured no version
boundary for any agent, and a number invented here would be a claim its owner never
made.

Failover needs no special case — it clears the token BEFORE the restart, so there is
no id to have been refused and `handoff` is the only seam that speaks there.

Give terminal output a cursor, so reattaching to a shell is not the same as losing it

`terminal.data` has always been a fire-and-forget broadcast with no cursor: bytes
that arrived while nobody was listening were simply gone. That was survivable only
because the server died with the app, so "nobody listening" meant "nothing running".
With a daemon it is the ordinary case — every reattach is output that arrived with
no client — and a socket that drops for two seconds loses whatever the shell said in
those two seconds, permanently.

So `terminal.data` now carries a run id and a sequence number, and the client holds
a cursor. It is the app's only true delta stream and the reason this is needed at
all: every other event carries whole current state, which is why a refetch repairs
them, and terminal output is the one thing a client cannot ask for again unless
somebody kept it.

**A cursor whose run id differs is treated as absent.** That single rule covers three
situations that would otherwise each need their own branch in the renderer — the
server restarted, the pty exited and respawned, and this client has never seen this
terminal — and in all three the right answer is the same: the previous screen, then
everything since.

Scrollback on disk is opt-in and off by default, because what it keeps is whatever
your shell printed: a token a CLI echoed, a `.env` you catted. Turning it off purges,
because a switch that leaves yesterday's output on disk is not an off switch. What
the switch does NOT gate is the in-memory buffer, which is always on — it holds bytes
that were broadcast to every client anyway, and gating it would break reconnect
catch-up to protect nothing new.

Two details in the replay are load-bearing. `\x1b[?1049l\x1b[0m` between the history
block and the new shell: a tail captured while vim or htop held the alternate screen
would otherwise strand the restored pane in an alt buffer, and every byte the new
shell printed would land where nobody is looking. That is the one way a raw-tail
replay can break a pane, and it closes for three bytes and a test. And `restoreAll`
now spawns at the size the output was printed at rather than a hardcoded 80×24,
because a replayed 120-column screen above a fresh 80-column shell is a ragged seam
nobody would blame on the pty's default.

The replay must not read as live, so the pane bar carries a state word on the
`MachineMeta` precedent — `Replayed` while the old screen is all there is, `Not
running` when there is no pty, and nothing at all the moment the new shell speaks.

A raw tail rather than a headless emulator, deliberately: `@xterm/headless` with a
serialize addon would give a cleaner screen at the price of a second terminal parser
on the hot path for every byte of every pty. `history.data` is opaque to the client,
so that swap changes no contract and no renderer code if it is ever wanted.

`decideLaunch` is the whole decision, as a pure function, because every branch of it
is a way the app can fail to start. It takes all three facts about the running
daemon, because each one lies on its own: a pid is reused, a port is answered by
somebody else, and only `system.info` returning the SAME bootId the state file
records says "this is the daemon that wrote this file". The outcomes are adopt,
spawn, hand off, or wait — and `wait` earns its place, because a daemon that is

another one meanwhile is the two-daemons bug. `ensureDaemon` spawns at most once
per launch for the same reason: a spawn that has not written its state file yet
reads as "nothing there" on the next pass.

`detached: true` is load-bearing twice. A child in our process group takes the ⌃C
typed in the terminal that ran `pnpm dev`, and takes SIGHUP when that terminal
closes — either would kill the thing this feature exists to keep alive. Since
stdout is now a log file rather than a pipe, there is no ready line to wait on, and
the daemon we spawned becomes ready the same way one we adopted does: the state
file appears and the port answers. One readiness path instead of two.

event to hang it on, so the signal is the bridge, which already redials every two
seconds. The rule is the point: respawn only when the socket is down AND the
recorded pid is gone. A disconnect while the pid is alive is a busy or flapping
socket, and respawning there is how you get two daemons over one `realm.db` — the
one failure here that is data-shaped rather than crash-shaped.

Daemon mode is packaged-only by default, because an orphaned daemon in development
is a daemon running yesterday's build until somebody notices. `REALM_DAEMON` opts
either way; `packaged-smoke.cjs` takes the `0` so it stops leaking one per run. The

Everything here is groundwork for a server that outlives the app, and each piece
answers a question the current shape never had to ask.

A daemon cannot announce its port on stdout. A pipe is a parent-child channel, and
the app that launches next has no parent to read from — the daemon's own next write
after that parent exits takes EPIPE. So the port, and everything else a second
launch needs, goes into `<home>/daemon.json`: written by rename at 0600, validated
on every read, and absent rather than throwing for every kind of broken file. The
shape lives in `@realm/contracts` because two packages read it, which is exactly
what a contract is.

Mutual exclusion is on the HOME, not the port. What two servers would corrupt is
one `realm.db` — two live-session maps, two schedulers claiming the same rows, two
processes racing the migration runner. `daemon.lock` is taken with `wx` before
`createApp`, so the loser has not yet opened the database, and it exits with
ALREADY_RUNNING rather than an error, because a second launch adopting a running
daemon is the ordinary case and not a failure. Electron gets a single-instance lock
too, so we rarely get there at all.

WebSocket dial is not subject to CORS, so before this any page in any browser could
open `ws://127.0.0.1:<port>` and call `sessions.create`. That was survivable only
because the port was ephemeral and died with the app; a daemon holds one for days.

and the renderer's browser `WebSocket` can set — and is read from the 0600 file, so
a web page cannot learn it. Origin is the second lock, for a token that leaked into
a log: the allowlist is measured rather than assumed, since a packaged window is a
`file://` document and Chromium stamps `Origin: file://` on its handshake. Refusing
every Origin, as first sketched, would have locked out Realm's own window.

A token is not optional, so the renderer, main's bridge and all seventeen live
checks that dial the socket land in the same commit.

`hotkeys.ts` writes that down for ⌘W. So no amount of grabbing the keyboard can
deliver them, and the pane must not pretend otherwise. Sending them deliberately
is what every remote-desktop client does.

latin-1 historically and extended only where both ends speak the pseudo-encoding,
so it cannot pretend to be transparent — and automatic Mac→guest sync would
silently push whatever is on somebody's clipboard into a machine that may be
running anything. Read goes through main rather than `navigator.clipboard`, which
is gated on a user-gesture heuristic a menu selection cannot reliably satisfy.

clipboard, and a renderer that could would be one mistake from doing it silently.

Actual size is the only mode where `image-rendering: pixelated` is honest.

Those needed a seam — a pane kind contributing rows to the ⋯ menu — and it is a

rows read live store state, and a table indexed by kind calls hooks
conditionally. Every kind's hook runs for every pane in a fixed order and the
kind decides only which result is used. `PanelBar` stays kind-agnostic, which is
its whole point.

JSON-RPC socket would put megabytes a second alongside session events, and the
real cost of a stream is not the capture — it is an SCStream with an output
delegate on its own queue, a didStopWithError path for display reconfiguration
and mid-stream permission revocation, filter re-creation whenever the window set
changes, and a long-lived helper with a lifecycle in main. The existing one-shot
needs none of it. Each frame is scheduled after the previous settles rather than
on an interval, or a slow capture queues behind itself forever.

one app's WINDOWS, never the desktop, which is honest at any number of displays.

granted, at which point the route disappears rather than offering a picker whose

Fetch a guest's image, verified twice, and boot it

W5's other half: the catalog, the image store, and QEMU wired into the service.

The catalog is PINNED IN THE REPO, and the reason is the checksum: one fetched
over the same channel as the image verifies nothing at all, since whoever could
substitute the image could substitute the hash beside it. Pinning makes the
release the trust anchor — something the user already decided to trust. A network
refresh may only EXTEND the list and loses every id collision to the entry here,
so a wrong feed can add something nobody had and can never change what shipped.

Every `sha256` in it is deliberately EMPTY in this release, and an entry with no
hash is offered as an import rather than a download. Publishing a hash nobody
verified would be worse than publishing none: it would look like a guarantee.
Windows and macOS are a NOTE rather than entries — an ARM64 Windows ISO has no
stable direct link and needs virtio driver media loaded during setup, and an
entry that downloaded something and then could not install it is worse than not
offering it.

Downloads verify TWICE, and the two passes cover different bytes. The streaming
hash covers what this run wrote and fails a fresh download early. The from-disk
re-hash is the only pass that covers bytes a PREVIOUS attempt wrote — which is
the whole point of resuming, and the only way a half-download corrupted before
the process restarted is ever caught.

The named trap has a test: a server that ignores `Range` answers 200 with the
whole body, and appending that to a partial file produces a corrupt image of
exactly the right length. Silent, and invisible to an implementation that skips
verification because it "already downloaded this". Rename happens only after
verifying, because the reverse leaves a bad image under a name `has()` reports as
present and every later start uses it without asking again.

An imported file is probed with `qemu-img info` and refused unless it is qcow2 or
raw with NO backing chain — the extension is never trusted. A backing chain is a
reference to a file Realm did not copy and cannot keep: the machine works until
that file moves, then fails with an error about a path nobody remembers choosing.

`driverFor` picks QMP for a guest Realm booted and RFB for everything else, and
QMP is the better channel where it exists: a unix socket with filesystem
permissions, and it works with NO VIEWER CONNECTED — the pane's socket may be
closed and `screendump` still produces a frame.

Display numbers start at 40 rather than 0, and are PROBED rather than counted. A
number this process has not handed out is not the same as a free port: 5900 is
what a Mac's own Screen Sharing uses and the next few are where a hand-started
x11vnc lands, so a guest could otherwise boot onto somebody else's screen.

A crash keeps the row, which is where this departs from `TerminalService.onExit`.
A dead pty has no state worth keeping; a dead VM still owns a disk image and a
configuration the user chose, and "start it again" is the whole recovery.

Reach a cloud sandbox: four transports, and the shape each provider hands out

"Connect a machine by address" was one transport — raw TCP — and no hosted
sandbox is reachable that way. Each of the four this was checked against exposes
something different, and the differences are the work:

  E2B Desktop runs x11vnc on 5900 and novnc_proxy on 6080, published at
  https://<port>-<sandboxId>.<domain>/vnc.html. Modal's tunnels()[port] gives a
  .tls_socket — a host and port with TLS in front and nothing in the shape to say
  so. Namespace offers an HTTP ingress, or a TCP one by TLS passthrough with a
  client certificate. Vercel Sandbox gives an exposed port a public HTTPS domain.

So: `tcp`, `tls`, `ws`, `wss`, behind one byte-channel interface, because the RFB
handshake is a byte protocol and does not care how the bytes arrived. Each is
tested against a real server of its own kind — a TLS server under a certificate
minted per run rather than a fixture with an expiry date, and a websockify stand-in
that is a WebSocket piping binary frames to a TCP socket, which is what E2B's
novnc_proxy actually is.

The WebSocket transport can also send HEADERS, and that is not a detail. A
sandbox behind an authenticating ingress — Namespace's `x-nsc-ingress-auth` is
the documented case — needs a bearer on the upgrade, and **a browser cannot set a
header on a WebSocket at all**. There is no version of this that works from the
renderer, whatever else the relay is for. Sealed in the same keyring the password
is, under its own column, because it authenticates to the proxy in front of the
machine rather than to the machine.

`parseMachineAddress` takes whatever a person actually pastes and SHOWS what it
resolved to, in the units it will be dialled in. Two traps it exists for: an E2B
stream URL points at `vnc.html`, which is noVNC's own web app — following it
hands the RFB client a lump of HTML and produces "not an RFB version line", true
and unactionable — so Realm dials websockify beside it; and a Modal tunnel dialled
as plaintext writes an RFB version line into a TLS handshake and gets silence.

Realm calls nobody's API. No SDK dependency, no provider token in the keyring, no
four release cadences to chase — what a person has after running their own tooling
is a URL or a host and port, and that is what this takes. The routes are the four
SHAPES someone arrives with rather than one row per vendor, because a vendor list
goes stale the week somebody launches a fifth.

Two notes carry a limit rather than a reassurance, and deliberately: Vercel's docs
say nothing about WebSocket upgrade through an exposed port, and Namespace's TCP
ingress wants a client certificate Realm cannot present. An honest "this may not
work, here is why" beats a confident connect that dead-ends.

Three things measured that the safe-looking answer got wrong. `ws` takes
subprotocols as its second ARGUMENT — an `options.protocol` is silently nothing,
so the first version offered none while claiming to; offering `binary` turns out
to be free, since older websockify requires it and permissive servers reply with
no subprotocol at all, which `ws` accepts rather than failing as RFC 6455 allows.
And SNI must be omitted for an IP literal: RFC 6066 forbids it, and Node warns
today and says it will ignore it later.

the no-overlap invariant lives in the schema instead of the allocator's care.

The password never leaves the server. `MachinesStore` maps a row to a `Machine`
carrying `hasPassword: boolean` and no field a secret could occupy — a `Machine`
travels to every connected client — and the sealed box is reachable only through
a method a caller has to name.

Realm performs the RFB handshake itself, in `rfb-handshake.ts`, as a pure
function of (state, bytes): TCP delivers bytes rather than messages, and every
hand-rolled protocol client's bugs are in the partial reads, so the tests feed
the same conversation one byte at a time and demand the same answer. None is
preferred over VNC auth where both are offered, so a server that will take us
without a password is never handed one; ClientInit always asks to SHARE, because
a 0 there disconnects every other viewer and doing that to somebody's own session
on their own Mac is the one thing this must not do. Apple's Diffie-Hellman types
are refused BY NAME rather than hung on — that configuration is what macOS
Screen Sharing offers when it wants an account password instead of a VNC one, and
naming it is what lets the pane say which setting to change.

Two things measured rather than assumed. `des-ecb` does not exist in the Node
this suite runs on — OpenSSL 3 moved single DES to the legacy provider — while it
does exist in the Electron the app ships, which is the worst possible shape for a
bug: green in the app, red only in the tests. Three-key EDE with K1=K2=K3 is
single DES by construction, is in the default provider everywhere, and is
byte-identical to BoringSSL's `des-ecb` on the same inputs. The known-answer
vectors are pinned from BoringSSL so neither that nor the spec's bit-reversed key
schedule can be "simplified" away silently.

And the `agents-page` icon has been missing for as long as the page has existed.
`Icon` falls back to `icons.folder` for a name it does not hold, so the page wore
a folder in the sidebar and in its own pane bar and nobody filed it — a folder on
a page reads as deliberate. `icon-kinds.test.ts` turns that whole class of
failure, silent and invisible to types, into a red suite.

anywhere.

Let the user watch the agent drive the page

An agent's browsing left a status dot, an inline ticker and a ring that flashed
for 900ms. You could read that a click happened; you could not see it happen.

The ring stays and keeps its job — it says "this element", it is quad-shaped,
and it is the only honest mark for `type` and `key`, which dispatch no mouse
event at all. Beside it now: a cursor that says "this point" and carries the
press, and a frame around the page that says the screen is being controlled.
`scroll` gets the cursor and nothing else, because a wheel event goes to a point
and there is no element to outline. `type` and `key` get no cursor, because a
pointer at a field no mouse touched is the one outright false thing this could
draw. `fillCredential` still gets nothing at all.

The mark SWAPS position rather than travelling. All three mouse events fire at
the same point, so a tweened arc would depict a journey that never happened —
and a hover menu the drawn path crossed would not open, which is the drawing and
the page visibly disagreeing. `--dur-swap`, not `--dur-move`, so the tokens do
not carry the lie either. Nothing is drawn at any intermediate point, and
nothing moves while nothing is happening.

The attribute the marks are tagged with takes a value, and the value is
load-bearing: the sweeps narrow to rings while the snapshot filter stays
presence-based, or every act would delete the cursor it was placing and every
`browser_batch` snapshot would blink it away.

Also fixes a live defect the ring had on its own: it was hard-coded `#4c8dff`
while the picker beside it already read the user's own `--rl-accent`. The
renderer pushes the accent to main on every theme apply — one value per window,
because that is what an accent is — and all four in-page marks wear it.

Disappearance has three owners, and the first is the page: a dwell watchdog on
the same 1500ms deadline the menu-bar driving indicator uses, reset on every
placement, so a dead bridge or a crashed host cannot leave a pointer stuck on
someone's page. `agent-cursor.test.ts` holds the two numbers equal.

Reduced motion is the page's own media query rather than a `matchMedia` read, so
it re-evaluates when the preference changes mid-drive and cannot be inverted by
one edit. Under it the mark jumps — which is literally the event stream — the
press becomes an opacity flash, and the frame's ring stays painted while only
its glow stops moving: the rule the in-flight ping already writes down.

`agent-cursor-live.cjs` is the evidence, and it had to find its own: measured
here, `BrowserWindow.capturePage` composites no child `WebContentsView` — a
window entirely covered by a bright green page captures as pure white — so it
reads the view's own capture, which is the view's rect by construction. Two
mutants run against it: the hard-coded blue leaves no accent pixel anywhere, and
a dropped watchdog leaves 9878.

Keep a native browser view inside its own bounds

A WebContentsView composites above the window's DOM unconditionally, and
`toViewBounds` rounded x and width independently — so a pane whose left edge
sat at 1054.344 gave a view starting at 1054, a third of a pixel outside its

Authored by a concurrent Codex session in this worktree; committed here so the release does not
carry it as an uncommitted change.

Write down the design judgment the UI work keeps rediscovering

design.md carries the judgment — what Realm's interface is for, how it decides between density
and calm, what the priority order is when requirements conflict. AGENTS.md points at it and
draws the line the two files have to keep: literal values stay in the tokens, styles and
components that own them, and this file does not become a second stylesheet. When review
feedback reveals a reusable principle it goes here; when it reveals a repeatable mechanical
failure it goes into a test near the implementation.

Also ignores .playwright-cli/, which is scratch output from live checks.

Rebuild the site around what Realm does, not how to configure it

The site was a landing page and eight hand-written docs pages, and the docs were the half that
went stale first: they described panes, skills and the gateway at a level of detail that has to
be re-edited every release, and nobody who had not already installed Realm was reading them.

They go. What replaces them is the two things a visitor actually wants: a features page that
shows the app — a carousel over real product screenshots, not a mock — and a changelog, so
"what changed" is answerable without opening GitHub. The download button asks GitHub for the
current release instead of pinning a URL here, because the disk image is named for its version
and there is no fixed path to the newest one; a rate limit or a release with no dmg falls back
to the releases page, which is always true.

The header, footer and nav collapse into one SiteHeader, the WGSL background becomes the same
liquid-glass treatment the app uses, and the icons pick up the new mark.

A new app icon, drawn rather than rendered

The old icon was a WGSL shader rasterized by vgpu: a gradient field that read as a smudge at
32px, could not be edited without editing a fragment shader, and had no form left at all in the
menu bar. The dock is where an icon is judged, and it was losing there.

This is a mark instead — two interlocking bays that read as one solid, on the app's own near
black. app-icon.svg is the canonical source and render.mjs takes it through qlmanage and
iconutil to every native size, so the 16pt and the 1024pt come off the same geometry.
stage-pack.mjs already copies resources/icon.icns to where electron-builder's mac.icon points,
so the app, the dmg and the site's app-icon.png all move together.

candidates/ keeps the studies this was chosen against, WGSL because that is what they were
drawn in; render-candidates.mjs and render-dock.mjs sheet them at dock sizes, which is how the
smudge was diagnosed. The three variants/ renders of the old shader go — nothing produces them
any more.

A menu item can carry an icon. The slot is reserved by every item as soon as one asks for it,
so labels stay on one left edge — a menu where three rows start at x and one starts at x+20

off this machine rather than shipped as artwork: the mark belongs to Apple, and the copy on the

path would let a renderer point the extractor at any file on disk.

A file preview decides between filling its frame and sitting in it, so a 32px icon stops being
upscaled to the width of a pane and a page still reaches the edges. The space list takes an

Rename armed an editor on the tab strip AND one in the sidebar for the same group, so both
surfaces mounted an autoFocus input, the second stole focus from the first, the first's blur

The idle summary sat above the composer, which meant it covered the thing you type into at

next turn started — so what a turn produced was unreadable a minute after it existed.

It becomes an ordinary message in the transcript instead: written where the turn ended,

Pick a control inside a simulator streamed into a pane

serve-sim mirrors an Apple Simulator into an ordinary web page, so the whole device screen is
one canvas: every control on it is pixels, and elementFromPoint can only ever return the
surface. Picking anything inside the phone produced a chip that described the video frame.

What the device does publish is its accessibility tree, beside the stream at /ax, and
device-ax.ts resolves a click point against it. The chip's DOM half still describes the

them. Nothing here talks to a simulator; it talks to one HTTP endpoint and does arithmetic, so
the geometry is testable without a Mac or a booted device.

A background Agent/Task call returns within a second — "Async agent launched successfully" —

Everything fails closed: an unrecognized message is nothing at all, and the dock falls back to

nothing about them. A tool description is read once a tool is already being considered, which

A Library that holds the files, not just the skills

Every file any session wrote or was given, across every space, in one
browser. Grouped by day, because the question is almost always "the
thing from this afternoon" and a flat list sorted by date answers it
only after you have counted rows. Tiles rather than a table: a name and
where it came from are the two facts that matter, and a table would
spend its width on columns nobody scans.

The load is the interesting part. The per-session summary already
answers this for one session by folding that session's whole event log
in the renderer, and that does not scale — the fold needs every block of
every transcript in memory, so a home with two hundred sessions would
read a few hundred megabytes of tool output to draw a file list. So the
files are indexed: `artifacts`, one row per file, written at the one
choke point every persisted event passes through, with history
backfilled once on the resumable-cursor pattern the search index already
uses. Reads are a keyset range scan, never OFFSET — the index grows at
the head, and an offset page over a growing list repeats and skips rows
under the user while they scroll it.

Not a partial index on `session_events` (the v21/v22 trick) because the
predicate is not on a column: "a tool_call whose payload names a Write"
lives inside `payload_json`, and an index on `type = 'tool_call'` would
cover the most common row in the table to filter almost all of it back
out in JS. Materialising is what makes the read a range scan.

One extraction, shared by the append-time writer and the backfill, so an
index built by either cannot disagree with the other; the row id is
`<session>:<seq>:<path>`, which makes every insert an upsert and lets
the two overlap safely on the events either side of the cursor. A write
is indexed on the CALL rather than on a non-error result: pairing them
would mean a stateful indexer, and the failure it avoids — a file listed
that a failed Write never created — is one the browser discovers the
moment it tries to open it.

The session's title is joined at read time, so renaming a session
relabels its files instead of leaving them under a name it used to have.
And the two fixed reaches are named once now and imported: they appear
on two axes (the scope-group headings, and this browser's filter), and
scope-groups.test.ts was right that two literals is two places to drift.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Finish the turn somewhere else

A turn that dies because the agent hit its usage limit is not a turn
that failed. It is a turn that has not finished. Two answers, and the
whole design is in knowing which one a failure deserves:

Retry — same agent, same provider conversation, after a short backoff.
Nothing is lost, so this is right for a dropped socket or an overloaded
upstream. On by default: it finishes the turn on the agent you picked.

Handover — the next agent in the space's chain, same session, same
worktree, conversation carried across as written text. Off by default,
because moving work between agents changes who is billed for it, and
that is a decision to make once rather than one Realm makes silently at
the worst possible moment.

`classifyFailure` is the judgement both rest on, and it is deliberately
conservative. Missing a usage limit costs a stopped turn you restart by
hand. Inventing one spends quota on a loop that cannot succeed, or moves
your session because a test the agent ran printed the word "quota". So
the table is phrases, not keywords, and everything it does not claim is
fatal.

A handover may rewrite `agentKind` where `sessions.setAgent` refuses to,
and it is coherent for the same reason a fork is: the provider
conversation is not moved, it is carried as text. `providerSessionId`,
`model` and `effort` are cleared; a seam goes on the transcript naming
the agent, the reason and the destination. That seam supersedes the
error it recovered from — both events persist, but printing "hit its
usage limit" as a red alert directly above "hit its usage limit,
continuing on Codex" tells the reader twice, and the first telling says
the turn failed when it did not.

Forks get the same option by hand: fork onto a different agent. The
transcript travels as text either way, so continuing on Codex costs
nothing a same-agent fork does not.

Also, unrelated: a fenced code block wears the composer's curve now,
ringless, with no rule under its head — a ring around a large radius is
the one thing that makes the radius read as a mistake.

`apps/desktop/scripts/failover-live.mjs` drives all of it in a real
window: the worklet actually paints the block's corner, the seam's
sentence sits on its rule, and a scripted usage limit really does hand a
live session over.

Scheduled tasks: a clock in front of the runs

A schedule is a goal, a cron expression and a switch. When it fires it calls
`runs.create` and stops there — attempts, restart recovery, the human gate and
the refusal of `bypassPermissions` are all the run layer's, already built and
already tested, and a scheduler that executed things itself would be a second,
worse answer to every one of them.

The cron parser is 5-field, local-time, and implements the day-of-month /
day-of-week OR rule rather than simplifying it to an AND. Next-fire steps a
`Date` a minute at a time instead of doing arithmetic, so the hour that repeats
in autumn and the one that does not exist in spring are the calendar's problem
and not a correction. An expression that will never fire is refused at create,
because for unattended work an invisible failure can go unnoticed for weeks.

Inverting the dark grain from white specks to black passed every contrast
assertion, because on a dark face darkening the ground only ever raises the
ratio. It would also have made the lift pointless: the lift banks a margin by
pushing the ground away from the ink so the speckles can spend it coming back,
and two layers pointing the same way just carry the ground further from the
palette. That direction was stated in a comment and is now measured.

Also folds the field into one custom property instead of writing the gradient

what it actually holds is the ground's lightness to within .02.

Three of its claims cannot be reached from the CSSOM. Relative colour syntax
either parses or the whole declaration is discarded and the feature silently
vanishes with every string assertion still passing. Grain is a variance and
nothing else. And "still under reduced motion" is a statement about two frames,
so the check is that a pair a second apart is identical under the preference
and different without it — an animation slowed rather than stopped fails that.

Pixels are read off a planted copy of the first-run card rather than the card
itself: the real one is a form from its heading down and has no ground left to
measure. Its mutant is the class, removed and restored against the same frame.

The first numbers were chosen to be obviously safe and the result was a no-op:
on GitHub Light the field was not visible at all, which is a decoration that
costs a stylesheet and returns nothing.

Contrast is computed from luminance alone, so chroma is free and the lightness
is the only thing that has to stay still. Pinning the lightness to the ground's
own band and then pushing chroma as far as the gamut allows gives four times
the colour on a light face and twice on a dark one, at no cost to any tier.

That leaves the palette as the binding constraint rather than the floor: past
about .02 of OKLCH lightness the ground stops reading as the user's canvas with
something on it, so the wash now has to hold that line too, and does. The lift
goes to .07 for the same reason the alphas moved — it is what banks the grain's
budget, and at .05 the sheet was clearing its floor by .007 rather than .027.

Pin which surfaces are decorated, and which are deliberately not

The restraint is the point, so it needs a test: a confirm sheet asserting it is
still plain is the one that fails if the wash ever spreads by default. The rest
holds the pieces the CSS cannot see — that the pages get the field without the
texture their ground cannot afford, that two surfaces open together are two
different pictures, and that a re-render does not redraw one under the reader.

Prove the wash keeps every ink tier above its floor on all 17 faces

A background that looks right on Realm dark can put text under the floor on
GitHub Light, and there are seventeen faces to be wrong on. This paints the
decoration over each face's real ground and reads the ratio back, at every hue
offset the shipped randomiser can land on.

The numbers come out of tokens.css and out of grain.ts rather than being
restated here, down to reading the speckles' ceiling from the feColorMatrix in
the texture itself, so the proof cannot go on describing a stylesheet that has
moved.

srgb() and srgbLuminance() are new because compositing happens in gamma-encoded
sRGB while luminance() reads the linear channels: blending on the linear ones
and taking the luminance of the result describes a pixel that is never drawn.

Settings, Notifications and the first-run card are surfaces a person sits on
rather than passes through, and they are flat panels of one colour. Each now
carries a soft field of its palette's accent, and the first-run card carries a
film of grain over it.

Which layers a surface gets is decided by its ground, not by taste. The colour
field is pinned to a lightness inside the ground's own band, so it moves hue
without moving luminance and costs no contrast anywhere. Grain is a luminance
excursion and has to be paid for, so it goes only where a lift can bank the
budget first: that works on a --surface ground and not on --canvas, where the
derivation has left --ink-3 sitting exactly on its floor. The pages therefore
take the field alone.

Painted as background layers on the surfaces themselves. A background cannot
leave its own element, so this can never become the overlay-over-a-native-view
problem no-overlay.ts exists to solve, and the sheet's field cannot scroll out
from under the sheet's own content.

Anchor the decorative wash to the theme's own accent

A background that picks its colour freely will eventually pick one the app
already uses to mean something: --red is a failure, --green is a finished run.
Offsetting from the theme's accent inside a 40-degree arc keeps the field
inside the palette the user chose and out of reach of the semantic hues, on
every face.

Seeded once per launch and keyed by surface, so two surfaces open together are
not the same picture and neither one reshuffles under a re-render. Lightness
and chroma are deliberately not part of the draw; they carry the contrast
guarantee and are pinned where it can be checked.

Give the under-strip the card's ring and as much of its rounding as it can hold

The strip that carries the device and workspace chips had no ring at all and a
12px corner against the card's 36, so it read as a tab stuck under a card
rather than as the bottom of one object. It now takes the same --card-ring at
the same hairline width, and the same --r-squircle rung.

Rounding cannot match exactly and the reason is geometric, not a preference:
both the worklet and the browser clamp a corner to half its box, so on the old
42px box --r-squircle drew at 21 however it was written. Padding goes symmetric
at 12px, which costs 6px of height and buys a 24px corner. Closing the last 12px
would need a 72px strip — three times the height of the two chips it holds — so
the gap stays.

This also explains a measurement that looked like a regression earlier: the live
check reads the radius from the CSS value, so a clamped corner reports a low
fill fraction against a corner square larger than the curve it is measuring.

Let the space strip's fill dissolve into the material behind it

The strip sits on the macOS vibrancy, and a flat --rl-active fill behind the
active space read as a plate stuck onto the material rather than part of it. A
hard rounded-rect edge is the one thing the blur underneath cannot soften, so
the fill is a radial wash with no boundary instead — strongest under the glyph,
gone by the edge of the box. Scanning across it now ramps 24 → 48 → 24 where it
used to step.

The wash rides ::before rather than the element because a background-image does
not interpolate and .strip-space is in the §6 hover-transition list, so putting
it on the element would have cost the cross-fade. `isolation` is what makes
z-index: -1 mean "behind the glyph" instead of "behind the sidebar": with no
stacking context here the wash falls through the strip entirely.

The profile square beside it had the same flat fill against the same material.

Cast the prompter's lift from its curve, not from its box

A box-shadow is drawn from the border box, and the squircle surfaces set
border-radius: 0 because their curve is painted rather than declared — so the
lift landed as a square behind a rounded card. Scanning across the left edge
near the corner found it as a detached dark band six pixels out from where the
curve actually starts, at ground luminance either side of it.

It was there before the radius grew; at 20px the band was a sliver, and the
comment defending the arrangement said the lift was "blurred far wider than the
two curves diverge", which stopped being true when the radius reached 36.

drop-shadow traces rendered alpha, which is the worklet's path. Neither lift
layer has a spread, so the two forms are otherwise equal.

It rides a content-free ::before rather than the card itself, for two reasons
both found by measuring. A filter on the card promotes it to its own layer and
the worklet then stops repainting when --sq-ring changes, so focus stopped
brightening the edge — 38.96 → 42.43 became 37.75 → 37.50. And a negative-z
child paints above its parent's background, so at inset 0 this layer's fill
covered the ring the card draws for itself; two pixels of inset clears the 1px
focus ring and is invisible under a 2–6px blur.

The live check proved its own mutant was dead here: it removed the lift by
setting boxShadow to none, which no longer carries it, so it would have passed
without testing anything. It suppresses the filter now.

Say the suggested prompt the way a person would

The hints read like a brief rather than a sentence. "Take a skeptical pass
over the pane groups work: find the edge case this diff is most likely to
miss" is three clauses and two pieces of jargon to say "review my changes",
and it landed in a prompter the user was about to type in — so it had to be
read, parsed and then deleted.

Every hint is now one plain clause. The logic that chooses between them is
untouched: same branches, same order of specificity, same session facts. Only
the words changed.

The chip prompts got the same treatment. They fill an empty composer the user
is about to edit, so a starter arriving pre-loaded with qualifiers costs a
read and a delete before they can type.

The tests that pinned the old wording now pin the new; none was removed.

Put the whole renderer on the icon ladder, not just the sidebar

The five rungs are documented on Icon but were policed in one directory, so
GroupBar was written at 13 throughout and nothing noticed. A ladder that only
governs the folder it was born in is a house style rather than a rule, and 68
call sites outside the sidebar had drifted to 15, 13, 11, 10 and 9.

Each moves to the rung whose role it actually plays: a button's verb or a
field's leading glyph to control, a glyph that varies with its row to row, and
anything inside a box of 22px or less — or leading text at 12.5px — to inline.
GroupBar's tab glyph is the same on every tab, so it identifies nothing and is
control furniture like the + beside it.

Two sites keep an off-ladder size because no rung fits: the todo dot is 13px
across, and the video's poster button is 52px with a glyph that is its verb
rather than its subject. Both say so at the call site, where the next reader
stands, and the scan accepts an off-ladder size only where that sentence
exists. It also matches Icon and SpaceIcon alone — Spinner takes a size prop
too and is not on this ladder.

Give every test's scratch directory an owner that removes it

The suite reached for mkdtemp at 151 call sites and removed almost none of
them: one full run left 974 realm- directories in $TMPDIR, and the pile on
this machine had grown to 93 GB. Past that point parallel vitest workers fail
their scratch writes and the run reports the resulting ENOSPC as ordinary test
failures, which is a whole run's worth of misleading red. The same disk
pressure is why fork.test.ts, the document watcher and the checkpoint
retention tests flake under load and pass in isolation.

tempDir hangs removal on an afterAll registered when the helper module is
imported. vitest evaluates that once per test file, so a file removes exactly
its own directories, and it still removes them when a test throws. A
structural test holds the line the type system cannot: no test file may call
mkdtemp itself. Production code and the hand-run live scripts keep theirs —
they create scratch outside any vitest lifecycle and already unwind it on
their own exit paths.

Say which check actually catches a shifted contrast centre

The test claiming it survived its own mutant. Comparing deriveVars at the default
against deriveVars with no argument cannot detect the scale being centred
somewhere other than the default, because both sides move together — and naming
that mutant over a test that does not kill it is worse than not testing it, since
it reads as covered.

What it does catch is a drifted default ARGUMENT, which is a real mutant and its
own bug. It says that now, and points at the check with teeth for the other one:
the tokens.css ramp guardrail, where the default derivation is held against the
palette it was measured from and a shifted centre stops reproducing it.

Stop the barrel advertising an API nothing imports

packages/ui/src/index.ts says it carries only what is consumed outside the
package, and eleven of the names added on this branch were not: the document and
seed types, the role lists the parsers walk, the font var list and its weight
table, and resolveMode, which lost its last caller when the palette menu started
setting the face on screen. They stay exported from their own modules, where the
package's own suites import them directly.

Also folds two copies of "the seed this face is really wearing" into one helper —
the override fields and the preview were computing it separately — and rewrites
two comments that narrated how the branch got here instead of stating what holds.

Point the transparency check at the readout it means

Renaming the slider row's classes so the contrast control could share them left
two readouts answering to one selector, and this script was reading the contrast
number while asserting about transparency. It reads its own slider's row now.

While there: the switch and the amount are one number, so the script says so.
Dragging the amount to nothing turns the switch off and makes the amount inert,
and switching it back on restores a translucent ground — three facts that would
each look fine on their own if the switch had a stored boolean of its own, and
would contradict each other on screen.

Measure the new controls against the compositor, not against the CSSOM

The palette walk had to be turned inside out: the menu now sets the face on
screen and offers only palettes that have it, so picking a palette and then a
mode would apply Monokai to whichever face was showing and then ask it for a
light one. Mode outer, palette inner — and a palette with no such face is now
asserted to be ABSENT from that face's menu, which is the other half of the split
and the half no per-face check can see.

Six new checks for the things vitest cannot reach:

Each face keeps its own palette across a mode flip. A shared slot would show the
same palette both times and every per-face check would still pass, because each
of them only ever looks at one face.

An override repaints the whole ladder. This is the claim the CSSOM cannot make
either way: writing three raw values past the derivation resolves identically
until you look at what the pane is actually painted with.

The contrast control opens and closes the ramp on real pixels, moves nothing but
the ramp, and stays above its floors at both ends of its range.

The fonts reach real elements — font-family as the browser resolved it, not a
string comparison on a token — and the weight ladder stays four rungs, measured
on a laid-out element because getPropertyValue hands back the calc() unresolved.

The Settings previews paint more than one face at once, and the code preview is
coloured by the syntax roles rather than by the page.

Two of these needed the harness fixed rather than the app: a hex field commits on
focusout, not blur, so the synthetic FocusEvent had been setting values and
committing nothing.

Ring a palette card's swatches in that palette's own ink

Screenshotting all seventeen faces turned up a dot that is not there. A card is
painted in the theme it names, and every light palette's surface is within a step
of its page — so the swatch standing for the card ground vanished into the card
on Realm, One, GitHub and Rosé Pine Dawn, leaving three dots where there are four.

Nothing asserted could have caught it: the swatch was the right colour, on the
right ground, at the contrast the derivation promised. It was just invisible.

The hairline comes from the theme's own hint ink, so it is visible on any ground
that theme can produce. A fixed black or white ring would have been the invisible
one on half the set, which is the same bug with the sign flipped.

Vendor Catppuccin, GitHub and Rosé Pine, at their published values

Six more faces, every hue the value its upstream ships, corrected only by the
lift the vendored palettes already go through. Three of them needed a note about
what "published" means, because the obvious file is not what renders:

GitHub's values are read off the shipped theme JSON rather than off
@primer/primitives — colors.js overrides the foreground and the accent at build
time, so the primitives are not what the editor draws. Its light seed is
canvas.subtle rather than the editor's #ffffff, and that one is the ladder's
doing rather than taste: a light surface step climbs from the page, and off pure
white there is nowhere to climb, so every card would land back on the page.
canvas.subtle is GitHub's own chrome ground, which is what --page is.

Rosé Pine Dawn's text is #575279. The palette.json in that repo says #464261; it
arrived in a commit titled "temp: add json, toml, yaml", disagrees with the
TypeScript source and with the shipped theme, and is not what anything renders.

Catppuccin states only one syntax role globally — comments — because its port
assigns the rest per language. The seven hues are Catppuccin's and the mapping
from hue to role is Realm's, said so where it is written rather than presented as
vendored.

All six clear every floor on their upstreams' own values; nothing here was
hand-brightened to get there.

Show the window a choice produces, next to the choice

Every control on this page named a thing and showed nothing of it. A palette is
the one preference where the words are the least useful part: "Gruvbox" tells
someone who has not seen Gruvbox nothing at all.

So the mode row is three cards each painting a miniature window, and each palette
row carries a diff in the palette it names. Both are built from the same
derivation the app applies, and both paint from custom properties set inline on
their own element — the token blocks in tokens.css hang off data-mode at :root
and cannot be flipped per subtree, so a preview built on them could only ever
have shown the mode already on screen.

The code preview carries highlight.js's own class names, which styles.css already
maps onto the ten --syn-* roles. That is what makes it a preview of the transcript
rather than a picture with its own colour table beside one. It follows the
overrides and the contrast control too, because a preview of something other than
what the window will do is worse than no preview.

System shows both faces, clipped side by side. Choosing it cannot promise which
one you will get, and the card does not pretend to either.

Carry a theme between two Realms as the twelve values it is made of

The document is a seed and a face, because that is the only thing in this system
that is stated rather than derived. The ladder, the ink ramp, the tints, the
tooltip chip and the corrected hues all come back out of deriveVars from those
twelve, so a document carrying the derived palette instead would be ninety
numbers that go stale the moment a ramp constant moves — and would arrive as raw
colours the contrast floors never got to look at. Through the same machinery a
vendored palette goes through is the whole point of having the machinery.

A full seed, not a partial one. An override is an edit to a palette that is
already there; an import is a theme. Requiring all twelve means a blob is either
a theme or it is refused, never half of one silently merged over whatever the
user happened to have selected.

Refusals say what is wrong with the thing that was pasted — which colours are
missing, that it is a dark theme in the light row, that the format is from a
newer build — because "invalid theme" sends someone back to a JSON blob with no
idea which of ninety characters to look at. Nothing is applied until it parses,
and the seed is rebuilt field by field rather than cast, so nothing else the
document carries reaches the derivation.

Copy emits the face as edited rather than the palette's own seeds: someone who
spent a while moving three colours should not hand a colleague the theme they
started from.

Make the sidebar's translucency a switch and an amount over one number

The pane offered a percentage where the thing people want to say is usually just
"yes" or "no". Adding a separate switch would have meant two controls that can
disagree — a switch claiming "on" over a ground the slider has at fully opaque,
each contradicting the other on the same row.

So the switch is a VIEW of the number rather than a second one. Fully opaque is
what off means, because covering the material completely is the same as not
having asked for it: the switch reads whether the ground is below the maximum and
writes either the maximum or the default, and the amount is inert while it is
off. Dragging the amount to nothing turns the switch off, which is the same fact
said the other way round.

Offer the faces the app can actually deliver, and reach open terminals with them

Two families per role rather than every font on the machine. Enumerating those
needs a main-process hop, and the list it returns is mostly faces this layout
cannot use: Realm's chrome is set against a four-step weight ladder and tabular
figures, and a display face picked out of four hundred loses both silently. What
is on offer is what the app ships — guaranteed present, guaranteed to have those
axes — plus a genuine system stack for someone who would rather Realm looked like
the rest of their machine. Each bundled stack keeps the system one behind it, so
a face that fails to load lands where "System default" would have.

Weight is offered for the UI face only, and that asymmetry is a fact about the
stylesheet rather than a judgement: every mono surface sets its font with the
`font:` shorthand, which resets font-weight by definition, so reaching them would
mean editing fifty-odd rules in a shared file or hiding a weight inside a family
name. The UI face has no such problem, and the control is an OFFSET on the weight
ladder rather than an absolute weight — 450 and 500 would otherwise land on the
same number, losing the difference between a label and its value in the course of
making both heavier.

The terminal used to carry a hardcoded mono stack that happened to equal the
default, so the one surface that is nothing but code would have been the one that
ignored the code font. It reads the token now, and the hub pushes a change into
terminals that are already open — xterm reads its font once, at construction, and
a setting that only applies to the next terminal is a setting you try, see
nothing from, and give up on. Each opened terminal is re-fit, because the cell
size is measured off the face.

Let the reader set how far the ink ramp spreads

The one thing in a palette that is a matter of eyes rather than of design is how
far the secondary and hint tiers fall below primary text. The hues are the
palette's identity and the surface ladder is its structure — a slider that moved
either would be a repaint wearing the word "contrast" — but the ramp's two
exponents are a preference, and nothing downstream of them is a claim about
anybody's taste.

So the control is a multiplier on those exponents, 0-100 with 60 the shipped
ramp, and it cannot make anything illegible at any setting. That is structural
rather than arithmetic: inkStep already floors every tier at WCAG before it
walks, so the bottom of the range is where the floors start binding rather than
where the ramp keeps sinking. The top is bounded too, because a ramp collapsed
into one flat tier destroys the hierarchy contrast exists to draw.

Walking to a floor turned out not to be enough on its own. css() writes three
decimals of lightness, which is finer than a display resolves and coarser than a
WCAG floor, so a tier stopped the instant it reached 3.00:1 could be written at
2.9987 — Gruvbox dark's secondary tier at the bottom of this range is exactly
that case. Both walks now measure the value they will emit.

Let a palette's ground, ink and accent be moved, through the derivation

A colour picked in Settings has to be worth as much as a vendored one, which
means it cannot be a raw value written past the machinery: a moved background
that did not bring the surface ladder with it leaves the cards, the tooltip and
the chart ground floating on a page they were never derived from, and every
contrast floor still passes because they are measured against the old surface.

So an override is a PARTIAL SEED, merged before derivation. The ladder, the ink
ramp, the tints and the lift correction all follow it exactly as they follow One
Dark's. A partial seed rather than three fields because a copied theme has to
carry the same document — the picker edits three of the twelve, an import may
state all of them, one type and one merge.

Where a colour cannot reach its floor the page names it instead of moving it.
The ground and the ink are the two seeds nothing corrects — a palette's identity
is its paper and its text, and lifting them silently would hand back a theme the
user did not pick — so contrastMisses measures the derived palette and says which
role landed where. Hues keep the ordinary correction inside the lift budget, and
are reported only when the budget runs out.

Overrides arrive from a user-editable settings row and hexToOklch throws on
anything that is not a colour, so they are validated field by field on the way
in; an unvalidated "blue" is a white window at boot with no page left to undo it.

Choose the palette for light and the palette for dark separately

One selection for both faces forces one of them to be a compromise: the palette
that suits a lit room is rarely the one that suits a dark one, and the mode
preference already says WHEN to switch without saying what to switch to.

A slot per face, each offered only the palettes that have that face. That
dissolves the conflict a single selection had to resolve by pinning: a dark-only
palette used to hold the window dark at noon, overruling the other axis from
inside this one. Now it simply is not on offer in the light row, and the mode is
the preference and nothing else. A slot that names a palette without that face —
hand-edited, or migrated — falls back to Realm, whose face is the static CSS and
so is the one that cannot be missing.

The single stored name is read once more, as the fallback for both slots, so a
home written by the previous build keeps its palette on whichever faces it has.

Give Realm's own palette a seed, so it can be moved like any other

The picker already carried four of Realm's colours as literals because it cannot
read them off a document that is wearing some other theme. A per-theme colour
override needs the same thing and more of it: a user who moves Realm's accent has
asked for a palette, and there has to be a ground under it to derive one from.

State all twelve instead of the four, as the hex the stylesheet's own ramp
guardrail already recovers from tokens.css, and pin them there value for value.
Realm's ThemeDef still states no seeds, so an untouched default writes nothing
and stays byte-for-byte the static CSS.

Say each of these things once, and only where it is a constraint

A read-through of the diff turned up the usual residue. A doc header that
argued for its own design rather than stating it, a test comment dated against
the shape the markup used to have, a handler type exported with no caller
outside its own module, a media-file builder with video and audio branches no
test ever asks for, and an assertion waiting on something it had already
checked on the line above.

Prove the two things jsdom cannot see about these surfaces

Both changes turn on facts about compositing, and jsdom has neither layout nor
a compositor. The attachment check gains the half it could not cover before:
that a lightbox opened from a tile inside the prompter actually paints over
the card it came out of — it is portalled to <body> precisely to escape the
pane's stacking context, and whether that works is a question only a real
screenshot answers. It also probes that `attachment:open` is registered in the
built main bundle, on a path that cannot exist so the gate refuses it and
nothing is launched. The PDF's own click is deliberately not exercised: it
would leave Preview open on whoever ran the script, and it cannot be stubbed
around because contextBridge freezes `window.realm`, so an assignment over the
method silently does nothing and the real call goes through regardless.

The drop highlight gets a check of its own, measuring the same property
prompter-fade-live measures for the same reason: a blurring layer inside this
pane that outranked the prompter is a bug this app has already shipped once.
Sharpness rather than a pixel hash, because adding a backdrop-filter flips the
text above it from subpixel to grayscale antialiasing and the bytes differ
even when nothing is wrong. The mutant — the glow forced above the dock —
collapses the card to 0.607 of its energy; layered correctly the ratio is
1.0000, so the measurement discriminates and the threshold is not fitted to
the result.

The tile's shape assertion needed the same repair its jsdom twin did: it read
the tile's direct children, and the hidden filename now rides inside the open
button, so it had stopped looking at anything.

Take a dropped file anywhere on the session pane

The prompter was the only thing that accepted a file. Once a conversation has
started that card is a strip along the bottom of the pane, and dragging a
screenshot onto a strip is a chore with nothing to recommend it — the pane is
what the file is for, so the pane is what should take it.

The pane's target closes over its own session id, so a four-way split lands
each file in the pane it was dropped on rather than in whichever session
happened to be focused. Both targets now share one hook, because the part
worth having exactly one copy of is the depth counting: a drag across a child
fires leave-then-enter, so the state has to be a count, and once two targets
are nested the inner one has to take the drag off the outer on all four events
rather than only on the drop. Claiming only the drop leaves the outer target
counting a leave whose enter it never saw — it goes negative and stays lit for
the rest of the drag. So the prompter claims, exactly one of the two is ever
lit, and a file dropped on the card is attached once.

`carriesFiles` moves in beside `isRealmPaneDrag`, which is where it belonged:
it is the same vocabulary, and the two are exhaustive and disjoint. A session
or a pane dragged between groups sets neither `Files` nor a dropEffect here
and passes through untouched, which is what keeps PaneHost's drop edges and
the browser pane's dragstart bounds sync working.

The affordance is an inner glow — a ring at the pane's edge falling away
inward — rather than a flat overlay, and it sits on layer 1, under the
prompter's dock. That is deliberate: a blurring band that outranked the card
is precisely the bug prompter-fade-live.mjs exists to catch, and the glow
passing under the prompter is the same thing the transcript already does. The
mask rides the blurring layer, never its parent, or the blur would have an
empty backdrop to work on. Reduced motion takes the fade-in (the blanket rule
reaches a real element, which is why the glow is one and not a pseudo);
reduced transparency takes the blur and leaves the ring, since a preference
about translucency should not remove the affordance itself.

Let a tile open the file it is a picture of

An attachment tile showed you the file and then refused to be clicked. In the
prompter the only control on it was the remove button; in a sent message the
tile opened a lightbox, but only when the file happened to be media, so half
the row was inert and the two halves of the app disagreed about what a tile
even is.

Opening now lives on the tile itself rather than on either caller, which is
what makes the pending chip and the sent chip the same thing. What "open"
means is decided by what the file is: an image, a video or an audio file goes
to the lightbox the transcript already uses, and everything else goes to the
app the user reads that type in. There is no element that could render a PDF
or a spreadsheet, and a viewer that showed a broken image for the other half
of the row would be worse than the tile that did nothing.

That second path needs a bridge call, and it is deliberately not `media:open`.
That gate answers about paths harvested from an agent's prose and has to stay
narrow enough that only inert, decodable formats get through. This one is
asked about a file the user picked or dropped themselves, so it admits every
document type Realm's mime table names — and the table being the gate is the
point: `open` RUNS a .app or a .command instead of showing it, and no bundle
extension is in the table. Both sides ask `isOpenablePath`, so a tile never
offers an open main will turn down.

Open and Remove are siblings in the markup, never nested. A button inside a
button is invalid, and the alternative — one handler untangling its own event
target — is the version that eventually deletes a file the user meant to look
at. Escape leaves the lightbox and focus returns to the tile it came out of.

Name GPT-6 Astra in the notes the picker writes itself

Codex serves this model live — `AGENT_MODELS.codex` is deliberately empty
because the catalog is enumerated from the CLI's `model/list`, so nothing here
makes it appear or disappear. What is missing is the one line Realm writes
rather than fetches: MODEL_NOTES overrides the catalog blurb, and without an
entry Astra would show OpenRouter's paragraph where every model beside it shows
a sentence.

Astra Pro is the same model with `reasoning.mode: pro`, which is a real choice a
user makes and a real difference in price, so it gets its own line rather than
inheriting Astra's.

Sol's note said "OpenAI's flagship", which Astra now is.

Keys verified against both spellings the wire uses: Codex's `displayName` is
"GPT-6-Astra" and the catalog's vendor-stripped name is "GPT-6 Astra", and
canonicalModelKey collapses both to `6-astra-gpt`.

Test the budget that ships, not one the tests dialled down

The retained limit was a constructor option no caller ever passed, and an
isRetained accessor nothing outside the tests read. Both existed to make the
eviction tests smaller. Removing them costs a few lines of setup and buys
tests that exercise the policy users actually get.

Also pins down that a browser being driven keeps its dot across a space
switch: browserDriving is keyed by browser, not by space, and selectSpace
resetting it would silently lose the one signal that says work is happening
somewhere the user cannot see.

Prove against the real binary that the page survives the switch

Every unit test here can only show which methods the pane calls. The claim
that matters is about a renderer process — that it is still alive, still
ticking, still drivable, and still holding the same document — and nothing in
jsdom can distinguish that from a view that quietly reloaded.

So the check reads back state that only exists at runtime: a global, a typed
form value, a scroll offset and a click count, all set before the retain and
all still there after the re-adopt. A reload would zero every one of them.

Recorded on Electron 37.10.3: a hidden view ticks a 50ms interval 22 times a
second and reports itself visible to the page (throttled it is ~1Hz and
"hidden"), CDP mouse input still lands on it, a screen sample over its rect
shows the DOM underneath rather than the page, and retaining a fourth view
destroys the least recently retained one.

Keep a browser the agent is working in out of the eviction queue

hasView is already true for a retained view, so tools reach a browser whose
space is off screen without any change. What was missing is the other
direction: the off-screen budget had no idea the agent was there, and would
happily evict the browser holding a half-finished task the moment the user
visited a fourth space.

Every op now marks its view in use — ahead of the attachment cache, because a
long task attaches once and then acts for minutes. Ops against a view that is
genuinely gone are refused first, so "in use" never names something that is not.

Move the decision to close a browser from the pane to the user

The pane's unmount was the only thing that ever destroyed a view, which made
"the user switched space" and "the user closed this browser" the same event.
They are not, and the pane is the wrong place to tell them apart: it cannot
see why it is going away.

So the pane now releases — main hides the view and keeps it running — and the
store destroys, from closeFromLayout. That covers every way a browser really
gets closed (the panel bar's x, the sidebar row, cmd-W, archive, delete),
including the branch that closes a pane sitting in a group other than the one
on screen, where the view is already hidden and alive.

The macrotask deferral stays and keeps its old job: a StrictMode double-mount
or a leaf reparented by a split must not make the view blink through a hide.
Its name no longer says destroy, because it no longer destroys.

Let a browser view outlive the pane that was showing it

A pane unmounting has never meant the user closed anything: switching space
or pane group swaps the whole rendered tree, and BrowserPane's cleanup was
destroying the WebContentsView with it — losing the page, its history, its
scroll position and any work in flight.

Background throttling goes off for the same reason retention exists. Measured

Pin the linger a new act has to cancel

Mutation-testing the indicator found this one uncovered: dropping the

which is the one direction of this signal that is a lie.

The display is now the one the windows are on, by largest intersection.
