the included windows, so the width and height taken from it asked for a
display-sized image with the app composited into a corner — the opposite of
what the comment beside it claimed. The crop is now asked for explicitly.

Verified against Calculator: a 21965-byte JPEG measuring 230x408, which is
that window's accessibility frame exactly.

Refuse a forbidden app by name before looking it up

Resolution ran first, so asking to snapshot a forbidden app that was not
running answered "com.apple.Terminal is not running" instead of "never
driveable". Two things wrong with that: the refusal doubled as a probe for
which apps are up, and the rule rested on resolution having succeeded, which
is not where a hard block belongs.

It also made the live check's by-name refusal vacuous in the way its own
comment warned about — it passed only on a machine that happened to be
running the app, and went red here the moment Terminal was closed.

A pid or a frontmost target still cannot be judged before resolution and
keeps the check after it.

Show the apps a space has allowed, and let the user take them back

The card now writes a grant that outlives the session, so it has to say so:
on a computer-use card "Allow always" becomes "Always allow in this space",
because plain "always" next to "Allow" reads as "for now" and a user
answering about an application on their own Mac is owed the scope they are
granting. Only the label changes — the same three decisions reach the server,
where a fourth would have to be understood by every adapter that can receive
one.

The list itself lives in the space's Connections tab, beside the browser
origins, since both are lists of what agents in this space may reach outside
it. It is review-and-remove with no add field: an entry is a bundle id,
which nobody knows by heart and which fails silently when mistyped — the
card is where an app should be added, with macOS supplying the identity.

The store keeps the server's answer rather than the argument, because the
server drops what it will not honour; storing the request would leave a user
believing they had granted something that is not in effect.

Let a space remember which apps an agent may drive

The per-app card was the only bound on computer use, and it lived and died
with the session — so the same TextEdit was approved again in every new
session, forever. Answering "always" now writes the app to a list the space
keeps, and the card is asked once per app instead of once per app per
session.

Per space, because that is where the feature is switched on: realm-computer
is the one provider that stays off until a space enables it, and a list
scoped wider than its own switch would let a space that was just given
computer use inherit approvals made somewhere else. Global would make
approving TextEdit once license every space that will ever exist.

The broker keeps owning modes and prompting and learns nothing about bundle
ids: `preapproved` says the caller already holds a standing grant, and
`onAlwaysAllow` hands the answer back to whoever knows where to put it. It
sits in the same place a session grant does, so it satisfies a
promptUnderBypass gate the same way — and so plan and ask still refuse, since
a list says which apps are eligible, never that a read-only session may act.

The forbidden list outranks it at every door: the provider refuses before the
allowlist is read, so a forbidden app never reaches a card whose "always"
would write it down; and the store refuses to hold one on add, on replace,
and on read, because the settings row is user-editable JSON and a value that
was never written through it can still be read through it.

Revoking needs the live half too — a session that already answered "always"
holds its own grant and would keep driving an app after it was taken off the
list, so dropping an entry drops that grant with it.

Say in the menu bar when an agent is driving the Mac

The browser pane's driving dot has a window to live in. Computer use has
none, and worse: the helper refuses to click unless the target application
comes frontmost, so at the instant an act lands Realm is by definition not
the active app and may be behind everything. A dot in the sidebar would be
the one indicator guaranteed to be off screen whenever it fired.

So the signal goes in the menu bar, which is visible whichever app is in
front, and is where macOS puts its own screen recording and location
indicators. A floating window was the alternative and is worse than useless:
an overlay above the target is the case the helper's occlusion filter cannot
see, and one owned by Realm would sit over the point about to be clicked.
Nothing here animates, so reduced motion has nothing to take away.

Main raises it, because the server's half ends before any input is posted —
lighting it around the permission card would say the Mac was being driven
while the user was still deciding whether it may be. It is counted rather
than flagged so two sessions acting at once do not take it down early, it
lingers so a run of short acts reads as one showing instead of a flicker
that shifts every other menu-bar item, and it is lowered in a `finally` so a
helper that dies mid-act cannot leave it claiming the Mac is still driven.

Give the app list's exclusions a subject that is actually running

`listApps` filters the forbidden set before it returns, so every check that
read "no forbidden app is in the list" was empty by construction: it went
green whether the filter worked, whether the filter was missing, and whether
the list came back empty. The same held for "Realm never lists itself", which
looked for "realm" in a run whose host is Electron — the ancestry walk that
does that exclusion was never exercised.

LaunchServices is now asked separately for what is up, so each absence has a
subject that is demonstrably running; a machine with no forbidden app up is
reported as a skip instead of as proof; the list is checked against that same
inventory so an empty list cannot pass for a filtered one; and the host of the
check itself is the subject that exercises the ancestry exclusion.

`every` holds of an empty array, so the two scans that relied on it now name
what they expect rather than scanning for the absence of something.

Measure where a page's parts actually land, in the app rather than in jsdom

Alignment is the one property the suite cannot hold an opinion about: jsdom has
no layout, so `max-width` and `margin-inline: auto` are two declarations that
parse and nothing more. This boots the built app on a scratch home and reads the
real rects for every page shape at seven pane widths — the bare column, the
column beside a rail, the notifications split and the Tasks lens — either side
of both responsive thresholds.

It also settles the scrollbar question the same way, by sampling the composited
pixels down a scroller's gutter rather than by reading the stylesheet back: a
painted track and a transparent one produce identical CSS to a file test.

Centre a page's column in its pane instead of parking it at the left edge

A page pane is routinely twice as wide as the column it holds, and every one
of them — Settings, Notifications, Library, Connections, Profile, Space — was
laying that column out from the left edge and leaving the rest of the pane
empty. They all share `.page`, so centring one and not its siblings would have
been a worse inconsistency than either choice applied everywhere.

The head, the rail and the content are centred as ONE block rather than
independently: centring the content alone strands the title at the pane's edge
introducing a form in the middle, and centring it in the space beside the rail
puts the rail outside the thing it belongs to. The cap is whatever that page's
own parts add up to, so the pages that hold more are not squeezed into the
reading measure — the notifications split keeps room for both its columns, and
the Tasks lens keeps the width its opt-out was for. Below the cap nothing moves,
which leaves the narrow-pane pass untouched.

The profile page's chip strip joins the other bands, which also gives it the
24px gutter it had been missing: it was the one thing on any page starting at
the pane's very edge.

Let the chip-kind test narrow, and stop the live hover racing itself

`isChipKind` now reads as the type guard it always was, which drops the
assertion `chipSpans` needed to build a span out of a run it had just checked.

The live hover check moved the pointer to a position it was already at, so the
move it depended on could go undelivered and the chip would read as unlit while
being perfectly lit. It now steps off the run first and waits for the state
rather than for a fixed delay.

Say under the pointer that a chip is a thing to click

A chip that a click takes whole should look like one before the click. Every
usual way of saying so is closed here: a border and padding are metrics the
mirror may not have, and a cursor over a hit area needs a hit area, which a
layer with no pointer events does not have. What is left inside the paint
budget is the tint the chip already wears, one step up.

Hover is also the only chip gesture that cannot be answered in offsets — there
is no selection to read — so it is the one place the composer asks the mirror
for real geometry, by asking the runs themselves for their boxes. That is
cheaper and far more predictable than a caret-from-point API, and it needs
nothing else to change. Typing clears it: the pointer has not moved but every
chip after the caret has, so the offset it was over no longer means what it did.

The stylesheet guardrail now matches any rule that reaches a `.ch-*` run rather
than only the bare class, so a state variant is held to the same paint-only
budget as the run it decorates.

`chip-hover-live.mjs` covers what jsdom cannot: that a real click on the painted
pill selects the token — the pill is drawn by the mirror while the offset comes
from the textarea's own metrics, and the two agreeing is the mirror's whole
premise — and that lighting a chip moves no glyph. Both are paired with a
runtime mutant so a passing measurement cannot be vacuous.

Let a chip be one thing to the caret, without moving a glyph

A chip is paint, so the caret walks through it a character at a time and a
click drops into the middle of a token that means nothing in halves. The fix
does not need the mirror's geometry: the browser has already resolved a click
to a character offset by the time `click` fires, and `selectionStart` is that
answer in the same coordinates the chip runs are in. Everything here is
arithmetic on those offsets, so it is testable without a pixel.

`chipSpans` reads the chips off the segments the mirror actually painted rather
than re-scanning the draft. That is the load-bearing choice: a token that lost
an overlap — `@mac` inside backticks — is not on screen as a pill, and a
gesture that took it anyway would act on a promise the screen never made. It
also fixes that case for the existing atomic backspace, which used to eat a
backticked token whole.

Which gesture each kind of chip gets is decided per gesture, not globally. A
click is AIMED: nobody clicks the third character of `@mac` on the way to
somewhere else, so a click takes either kind whole — interior only, because the
trailing edge is how a hand gets from `@mac` to `@mac-cli`. Arrow-stepping and
the atomic delete are the opposite: the caret arrives in a mention constantly
just by moving, so those stay element-only, where nineteen presses to cross
`@[button "Sign in"]` is the caret pretending a token is a sentence.

Delete joins Backspace so the token is atomic from both sides.

The strip that carries the device and workspace chips had no ring at all and a
12px corner against the card's 36, so it read as a tab stuck under a card
rather than as the bottom of one object. It now takes the same --card-ring at
the same hairline width, and the same --r-squircle rung.

Rounding cannot match exactly and the reason is geometric, not a preference:
both the worklet and the browser clamp a corner to half its box, so on the old

at 12px, which costs 6px of height and buys a 24px corner. Closing the last 12px
would need a 72px strip — three times the height of the two chips it holds — so
the gap stays.

This also explains a measurement that looked like a regression earlier: the live
check reads the radius from the CSS value, so a clamped corner reports a low
fill fraction against a corner square larger than the curve it is measuring.

Let the space strip's fill dissolve into the material behind it

The strip sits on the macOS vibrancy, and a flat --rl-active fill behind the
active space read as a plate stuck onto the material rather than part of it. A
hard rounded-rect edge is the one thing the blur underneath cannot soften, so
the fill is a radial wash with no boundary instead — strongest under the glyph,
gone by the edge of the box. Scanning across it now ramps 24 → 48 → 24 where it
used to step.

The wash rides ::before rather than the element because a background-image does
not interpolate and .strip-space is in the §6 hover-transition list, so putting
it on the element would have cost the cross-fade. `isolation` is what makes
z-index: -1 mean "behind the glyph" instead of "behind the sidebar": with no
stacking context here the wash falls through the strip entirely.

The profile square beside it had the same flat fill against the same material.

A box-shadow is drawn from the border box, and the squircle surfaces set
border-radius: 0 because their curve is painted rather than declared — so the
lift landed as a square behind a rounded card. Scanning across the left edge
near the corner found it as a detached dark band six pixels out from where the
curve actually starts, at ground luminance either side of it.

It was there before the radius grew; at 20px the band was a sliver, and the
comment defending the arrangement said the lift was "blurred far wider than the
two curves diverge", which stopped being true when the radius reached 36.

drop-shadow traces rendered alpha, which is the worklet's path. Neither lift
layer has a spread, so the two forms are otherwise equal.

It rides a content-free ::before rather than the card itself, for two reasons
both found by measuring. A filter on the card promotes it to its own layer and
the worklet then stops repainting when --sq-ring changes, so focus stopped

child paints above its parent's background, so at inset 0 this layer's fill
covered the ring the card draws for itself; two pixels of inset clears the 1px
focus ring and is invisible under a 2–6px blur.

The live check proved its own mutant was dead here: it removed the lift by
setting boxShadow to none, which no longer carries it, so it would have passed
without testing anything. It suppresses the filter now.

The floating cards wrote `calc(var(--r-float) + 4px)` six times over. The

The under-strip does not follow it. Only about 26px of that strip shows below

its height; a corner cannot be rounder than half its box, and at 36px the curve

rather than as its bottom edge.

than assuming it: the prompter's corner fills 0.904 of its corner square where a

Import the fence from where it lives, and stop saying things twice

`browsers/guards` had become a pass-through for two functions it no longer
owns, on a file whose subject is OAuth consent detection. Its six callers now
import from contracts directly, and the header there stops claiming the
renderer fences anything — it does not; `elementContext` composes the block and
runs server-side. What put the fence in contracts is that `elementContext` is a
contract both processes link.

Three new declarations had been wedged between an existing doc comment and the
thing it documents — the downloads block in the preload, the SessionService
header, and the browser notice's rule. Each is back with its subject.

The bubble-versus-composer chip argument was stated in three places and the
picker promise's lifetime in four. One statement each, at the boundary that
needs it. The picker button also drops `data-active` for the `aria-pressed` it

Stop a picked element's own name from hanging or speaking

Three faults, all reachable from a page choosing what to call its controls.

A label clipped to the maximum could not be disambiguated: appending ` 2` and
re-clipping returns the same string, so the second pick of a long-named control
looped forever — synchronously, on the click path, in the renderer. The suffix
now has room made for it and the loop is bounded by the number of chips a
message may carry at all.

A page that names its button `hi @mac` put a live mention token inside the
user's draft. The send-time scan recognised it, the server resolved it, and the
turn went out prefixed `/realm:mac` — with nothing visible to the user, whose
composer paints the whole token as a single chip. Labels now lose their `@` the
same way they lose their brackets, and a mention falling inside an element token
is dropped from the chip scan, which also restores the partition `chipRuns`
promises: overlapping runs were printing characters twice.

`url` was outside the fence on the claim that a page cannot author it. Only its
origin is true — `pushState` writes the path and query, `document.title` writes
the title. The full URL joins the markup under the fence and the index line
states the origin, which is the part a webContents cannot be moved off.

A pick main refuses outright (the debugger will not attach when DevTools already
has it) rejected across the IPC with nothing to catch it, leaving the toolbar
button lit over a view that was not picking.

Refuse the ninth picked element in the composer, not on the wire

MAX_ELEMENT_CHIPS was enforced only by the send schema, so a draft that grew one
chip too many looked fine while it was being written and then bounced on send —
leaving the user holding a message they could not post and no way to tell which
pick had done it. The pane now says so at the moment of the pick.

Say which session the picked element went to

"Added it to the prompter" answers nothing when two sessions are open, and the
pane the chip lands in is by definition not the one the user is looking at.

Remove the picker live check's scratch dir on the timeout path too

A run that hung is exactly the run nobody comes back to clean up after.

Put the picker's claims about Chrome in front of a real Chrome

Everything the Overlay comment asserts is a claim about Chromium that no unit
test against fake CDP payloads can settle, and one of them turned out to be
load-bearing in a way worth proving: Chrome does NOT leave inspect mode after
emitting `inspectNodeRequested`, so the second click is swallowed too, and a
picker that skips the disarm keeps eating the user's clicks.

The check also settles that the picking click never reaches the page — the
anchor's own handler does not run and the page does not navigate — which was
the whole reason for choosing Overlay over an injected listener, and that AX
names the element `button "Sign in"` where the tag alone would have said `a`.

It cost one real finding: inspect mode inspects the node it is hovering, so a
press with no mouse move before it falls straight through. A hand always moves
first; a script has to be told to.

Say what actually keeps an element chip in one piece

Its rank never decides anything — no other span can begin at `@[`, so a chip is
never in a tie, and what protects it from a URL inside its label is that it
starts first.

Give the prompter's chips a shape, and a chip's backspace

The mirror could already colour a mention; what it could not do was make one
look like an object you could pick up. Padding, a border and a smaller face are
all metric changes, and the caret under this layer belongs to the textarea, so
none of them were available. `box-shadow` with a spread and no offset is: it
paints a pill outside the run's box while the box still occupies exactly the
glyphs' width, so the two layers stay character-for-character aligned. Element
chips get the same treatment and their own tint.

The rule that makes this safe is now enforced against the stylesheet instead of
trusted to review — a `.ch-*` rule may only declare colour, background, radius,
shadow and underline, and anything else fails.

Backspace at an element chip's trailing edge deletes the whole token. Element
chips only: `@[button "Sign in"]` is syntax nobody types through, and half of it
is neither a chip nor anything an agent can use, whereas `@mac` is a chip a hand
passes THROUGH on its way to `@mac-cli` — an atomic backspace there would eat
four characters at the one moment the user is mid-word.

Pin that a switched-off skill's mention is not a chip in the bubble

Nothing noticed the bubble recognising the whole space library rather than the
enabled, valid half the composer paints.

Draw a sent message's chips as chips

The user bubble rendered `{b.text}` as one raw text child, so a message that
showed a coloured `@mac` in the composer arrived in the transcript as flat grey
prose. The chips were a property of typing rather than of the message, which is
backwards: the bubble is the record, and the record should say what was named.

This is the one surface where a chip can be shaped like one. The composer's
chips are paint over a textarea whose caret they must not move, so they get a
background and nothing else; nothing in a bubble shares a box with a caret, so
here they are real pills with padding and a border.

The runs between chips stay plain text rather than becoming markdown.
`chipRuns` partitions rather than rewrites, so every character the user sent is
still on screen in order — a mention keeps its `@`, and only an element chip's
brackets are dropped, being delimiters rather than content.

Mentions are recognised against the LIVE library, by the same scan the composer
runs. A skill deleted since the message was sent stops reading as a chip and
goes back to being the `@name` the user typed, which is also what the agent was
told, because the server could not resolve it either.

Read the dispatched draft's elements straight off the sidecar

The re-derive there could never change the answer: the text is this draft
trimmed, and setDraft has already kept the sidecar in step with it. sendMessage
still re-derives, because its text is the prompter's and may have moved on.

Cover the dispatched draft's picked elements

`dispatchDraft` re-derives and clears the element sidecar exactly as
`sendMessage` does, and nothing noticed when either half was removed.

Pin that a chip-free send omits the elements key rather than sending it empty

live-api.ts is one line per method and the store tests see only the fake, so
nothing until now would have noticed `elements: []` going out on every message
in the app.

Send a picked element to the prompter as a chip

The picker had nowhere to put what it found. It now lands in a session's
composer as a chip: a short `@[button "Sign in"]` token in the draft text,
with the element itself kept in a sidecar beside it. The sidecar is
`draftMentions`' twin and follows its one rule — an entry lives exactly as
long as its token survives in the text — so deleting the chip forgets what it
named, and a draft that was edited down to nothing sends nothing extra.

The token had to be text because the draft is a string end to end and the
composer's caret belongs to a textarea. `@` because the composer already
teaches that sigil; brackets because a label carrying spaces and quotes will
not fit `@id`'s charset. It costs no precedence rule: `[` is not an id
character, so the mention scan's candidate after `@` is empty and the token is
skipped whole.

What the agent receives is the user's text with a fenced block appended,
composed server-side in `resolveMentions` alongside the `@`-stripping it
already does — the transcript keeps what the user typed, chips and all, and
the page's account of itself never enters it. `elements` is optional on the
wire and the prompter omits the key outright when a draft has no chips, so a
message that never touched a browser pane puts exactly the bytes on the wire
that it always has.

The fence moves to contracts because two processes now need it, and a
delimiter whose whole job is to be unguessable should not exist twice.

Which composer receives the pick is decided structurally: by the time a pick
resolves the focused leaf is the browser's, so there is no "current composer"
to ask. A pick that lands nowhere says so — the user's only evidence it worked
is a chip appearing in a pane they may not be looking at.

Let the user point at an element inside a browser pane

The browsed page is a native WebContentsView compositing over the renderer,
so React never sees a click inside its rectangle and there is no preload to
carry one out. The only channel that can say where the user pointed is CDP,
and Chrome already ships the mechanism: `Overlay.setInspectMode`, which is
what DevTools' own inspect button drives.

Overlay beats an injected click listener on every point that matters here.
Chrome consumes the picking click, so aiming at a link does not navigate and
aiming at a submit button does not submit; the hit test is the browser's own,
so shadow roots, cross-origin frames and `pointer-events` all come out right;
and the highlight is drawn by the overlay layer rather than appended to the
page, so nothing is injected into untrusted content and there is no second
marker attribute to hold in step with the snapshot filter and its sweep.

A pick is a human gesture, so it deliberately does not join BROWSER_HOST_OPS.
Every op on that bridge is something an agent asked realm-server for, and
"consume the user's next click" is not a capability that should sit one
allowlist entry from a tool call. It rides the pane's own IPC instead, like
`saveDownload`, where a call arriving in main is consent a page cannot forge.

`describeElement` moves out of the host and into the CDP module alongside the
rest of the protocol logic, so a picked element and an acted-on element are
named by the same read.

Leave two things for whoever goes looking

Neither is announced anywhere, neither can be reached by accident, and neither
costs anything to the reader who never finds it.

Holding ⌥ while opening a tool card opens every card in the transcript. It is
Finder's gesture on a disclosure triangle, and ⌥ is already the modifier this
app spells "the other way to do this" on a sidebar row, so the people most
likely to try it are the people it is for. The siblings are driven through
their own rows rather than by lifting `open` into shared state: a long
transcript holds hundreds of cards, and a subscription each would be a standing
cost paid by everyone who never holds the modifier. A synthetic click carries
no `altKey`, so one press cannot cascade into a round of its own, and only the
rows that disagree are pressed — they end up matching the card you opened
rather than each flipping to its own opposite.

Clicking the emphasised word in the hero greeting — your name, or the space's —
makes the line nod. It is the one place the app addresses you directly, so it
is the one place worth answering from. The mark goes on the element and comes
off when the animation ends: no state, no timer, nothing left for a later
assertion to trip over, and the nod is on the ladder like every other piece of
motion here rather than inventing a tempo for itself.

Both sit under §6's reduced-motion kill without a carve-out. With the
preference on, ⌥-click still opens every card — it is a gesture, not an
animation — and the greeting simply does not nod.

Give an icon button one way to change its state

Two of them were already good: the copy tick and the send↔stop morph each keep
both glyphs in the DOM and turn them over with opacity, a scale into the centre
and a 4px blur. They were also two copies of the same eight declarations, and a
third and fourth control needed it — so it is written once now, in the motion
block, with `.icon-swap` as the form anything else reaches for.

Writing it down is most of the point. Settings' and the install card's copy
buttons already carried `.tool-copy`, and so already matched every selector in
that rule, but swapped their glyph with a bare ternary and never set
`data-copied` — the tick hard-cut and the rule sat dead over them, because
there was nothing named to reach for and the working version was buried in the
transcript's stylesheet. Both now stack the pair. The media transport's
play/pause and mute do the same through `.icon-swap`: one control whose glyph
turns over, rather than two elements replacing each other with no transition
available to them at all.

The other half is a state that could not be seen. `.icon-btn[aria-pressed]` had
no pressed treatment anywhere, so Bold, Italic, the three headings and the
terminal drawer's ⌘J looked identical on and off. The fill has to carry it,
since the glyph does not, and it sits one rung past hover so "on" always reads
as more than "under the pointer" — riding the hover transition the button
already has, so turning a toggle on settles rather than snaps.

Nothing else moves. Hover stays colour alone and press stays the .97 it was:
the buttons that swap ELEMENTS rather than glyphs — focus/unfocus a pane,
stop/reload a page — are two different verbs with two different names, and
cross-fading them would mean one control whose accessible name changes
underneath a screen reader mid-fade.

icon-state-live.mjs measures what a stylesheet read as text cannot: that the
pressed fill wins the cascade against the hover rule it follows and resolves to
a different colour than it, and that the swap has a middle — both glyphs partly
visible, blur and scale interpolating — which is the one thing separating a
cross-fade from a cut in every other assertion available.

Unfold the archived shelf instead of snapping it open

The shelf was the last disclosure in the app still doing a bare mount: the
caret rotated into place over 140ms and the rows it was describing appeared
underneath it in one frame, which reads as the caret being decorative.

It now shares the tool row's declaration rather than growing a second idea
about how a disclosure opens. grid-template-rows 0fr→1fr is the only technique
that works here — the shelf's height is however many sessions someone has put
away, and max-height would have to guess a number, then ease against a height
the list does not have, snapping a short one and clipping a long one.

The rows have to be in the DOM on both sides of the flip for that to animate,
so they are built on first open and stay built: folding back animates too, and
re-opening is instant. Built on FIRST open rather than always, because a shelf
nobody has asked for should cost nothing; `inert` is what makes keeping them
acceptable, holding a folded row out of the tab order and off the screen reader.

disclosure-live.mjs measures the part jsdom cannot: that folded is genuinely
zero — the sidebar is a flex column, which is exactly where one stray
min-height leaves a shelf permanently open under a caret that says otherwise —
that open is the rows' own height, and that a folded row is neither tabbable
nor hit-testable while still being there to fold back out.

Let popovers leave the way they arrived

Menus and the model picker have had a 140ms entrance since §6 landed and no
exit at all, because React unmounts a `{open && <Menu/>}` child the instant its
parent says so and CSS has nothing left to animate. The delay has to live
somewhere, so it lives in the primitive both surfaces already share: `close()`
marks the surface closing, hands focus back, and tells the parent one
`--dur-press` later.

What makes that safe rather than a leak is the state it holds in between. The
surface goes `inert` and pointer-transparent for the beat it is fading, so the
app behind it is reachable by pointer, keyboard and screen reader as though the
menu had already gone. Placement freezes, because a menu item that closes its
own pane takes the anchor with it and the fallback would fling the surface into
the window corner mid-fade. The next pointerdown or keystroke commits the exit
outright — an exit is a courtesy and stops being one the moment the user does
something else — but never the click that follows a pointerdown, since a parent
told during the click re-opens the very element that is mid-exit and React
reuses it, leaving a menu stuck invisible and inert forever.

Reduced motion skips the hold instead of running it at zero: the global
`animation: none` would otherwise park a fully painted, unusable menu on screen
for exactly as long as the exit nobody asked to see.

Enter and exit are one decision per surface, so this covers the three that
already had an entrance and leaves the @-mention typeahead alone — it opens and
closes between keystrokes, and a ghost trailing the caret is noise, not motion.

The tests that open a menu, pick something and immediately open another now
wait for the first to leave. popover-exit-live.mjs proves the parts jsdom
cannot see: that the fade actually plays, that a click through the middle of it
reaches the app, that a dismissed menu does not move, and that ten cycles
faster than the exit runs leave nothing behind.

State the hues the upstreams publish and let the budget do its job

Six of the nine comment seeds were quietly brightened off their published
values to clear the syntax floor, and only one of those moves was named.
That routes around the mechanism built for exactly this: `lift` corrects a
stated hue along lightness and REFUSES past LIFT_BUDGET, so a seed that
cannot be carried is supposed to fail loudly rather than be edited until
it passes. Hand-brightening clears silently, at whatever distance from the
published colour it took, and the budget never gets to object.

Measured against each theme's own derived surface, every published hue is
reachable: Monokai's #88846f and Gruvbox's #928374 need no correction at
all (3.30:1 and 3.36:1), One Light and Solarized Light need 0.014, Dracula
0.018, Solarized Dark 0.036, One Dark 0.082 — all inside a budget of 0.12.
So all six go back to what their upstreams ship. Solarized Light in
particular no longer needs the deviation it was carrying: base1 lifts by
0.014 where the hand-picked value had moved it far further.

Nord keeps a stated deviation and now describes itself correctly. Its
comment seed WAS #7c8aa5 while the provenance beside it claimed #616e88;
it is #616e88 now, which is the tone Nord's own editor ports adopted and
which needs 0.074. The spec value nord3 needs 0.160 and is refused — a
test pins that, so the one palette in the set whose published tone cannot
be carried stays visible instead of being quietly rescued.

Also: the debounced transparency persist goes through `run` like the
layout persist beside it, since it fires long after its caller's promise
settled and a failed write had nowhere to surface; the live check's
palette assertion compares the palette it asked for and not just the mode,
so a missed menu click fails by name instead of relabelling every later
check; its Realm --canvas expectation was #1c1d20 where tokens.css says
#1c1d1f, which only passed on a tolerance of 2 and now runs at 1; and the
package barrel drops the eleven entries nothing outside it imports.

Make the ramp prove it was measured from the palette it claims

The derivation constants carried a comment saying they were read off the
shipped palette in tokens.css. Two of them were not: the dark ink ramp's
exponents were 0.66 and 0.37 where the palette actually sits at 0.700 and
0.427, which put every dark theme's secondary and hint text a step dimmer
than the ramp they were supposed to reproduce. Correcting them lifts One
Dark's --ink-2 from 3.74:1 to 4.06:1 and Monokai's from 4.70 to 5.15,
against a floor of 3.

A comment cannot hold that line, so the claim is now a test. It reads the
seeds back out of tokens.css, runs them through the same derivation every
theme goes through, and requires the surface ladder, the tooltip chip and
the ink ramp that come back to be tokens.css. Nothing else in the suite
can notice a drifted ramp — the contrast floors are about legibility and a
ramp is about shape, so a theme can stop being the same system as the
palette beside it while clearing every floor. Sourcing the seeds from the
file rather than writing them into the test is what stops the two being
updated to agree with each other.

The tooltip becomes a construction rather than two more rows of the table.
It is the one surface that does not sit on the ladder — recessed below the
page in dark, inverted into a dark chip with light text in light — and as
rows each mode carried two entries the other mode's shape had forced on
it, which the light ramp never read.

Hand the sidebar's transparency to the person looking at it

The sidebar has painted the window ground at exactly 82% since vibrancy
arrived, written as a literal in the one rule that used it and pinned by
a guardrail that asserted the literal back. That number is now the user's:
the stylesheet composes `--sidebar-ground` from a `--ground-alpha` the
renderer writes, the default 82 lives in packages/ui beside the rest of
the theme mechanism, and the guardrail pins the intent instead — that
exactly one surface is translucent, and that the alpha is driven rather
than typed.

No IPC and no setVibrancy(). The material is always on under the window on
macOS; at 100% the sidebar simply covers it, which is visually identical
to never having asked for it. CSS alone was genuinely sufficient, so the
feature adds no main-process surface at all.

The composition deliberately stays in CSS. An inline custom property beats
every stylesheet rule, so composing the ground in applyTheme would put it
out of reach of `prefers-reduced-transparency` — the preference the fade
bands already honour. Written this way the media query wins, the sidebar
goes opaque while it is on, and the user's value is still there when they
turn it off.

The scope is the sidebar and stops there. A pane could be made
translucent, but pane text would then render over whatever is behind the
window, and at any setting where the effect was visible that text falls
below the contrast floor every theme in this branch is held to — so the
range is 55–100, and 55 is where the sidebar's own nav labels stop being
carried by the ground on a bright desktop. That floor came from looking at
a screenshot, because it cannot come from anywhere else: macOS composites
the material below the web contents, so a CDP capture never sees it.
transparency-live.mjs measures what it can — that the slider reaches the
sidebar, that panes stay opaque at every setting, and that Reduce
Transparency overrides both.

Off macOS there is no material to reveal, so the control says so and does
nothing rather than appearing to work. The platform comes from the
preload, and an unknown platform answers "no material" instead of guessing.

Fill out the set, and go and look at it

Dracula, Nord, Solarized and Gruvbox on the same twelve seeds. Two of
them arrive light-and-dark and two dark-only, which is a fact about the
upstreams rather than an omission: Nord is specified as one palette and
the light builds in the wild are community inversions, and Dracula's
light counterpart ships with a paid product that is not ours to vendor.

Two seeds could not be used exactly as published and both are named where
they are written. Solarized's UI ink is base2/base02 rather than the
base0/base00 an editor uses, because primary chrome text is held to a
higher bar than a code buffer's foreground; and Solarized Light's comment
is one step darker than base1, which measures 2.46:1 on base3 and is the
one value in the whole set that would not clear the floor as written.
Nord's comment is the brightened #616e88 its own editor ports moved to
for the same reason.

Colour cannot be checked in jsdom — no cascade, no `var()` resolution
against a real stylesheet, no compositor — so themes-live.mjs boots the
built app and walks all eleven faces through the space menu. It measures
two different things two different ways: the token chain off the real
CSSOM, where every `.hljs-*` rule has to resolve to the theme's own
`--syn-*`, and the composited pane ground off a screenshot, where a
palette that was computed but never applied would leave all eleven faces
the same grey. It also writes a screenshot per face, which is the part
that catches a theme that passes every assertion and looks wrong.

Give the palette its own axis, and One and Monokai to put on it

Light and dark answered "how bright"; nothing answered "which colours".
This adds the second axis rather than folding it into the first, so
"system" keeps meaning what it meant: `ui.theme` still records the mode
the user wants, `ui.themeName` records the palette, and the effective
mode is resolved from both at paint time. A palette with only one face
pins the window while it is chosen and never writes back to the
preference, so trying Monokai for an afternoon leaves "system" where it
was found.

A theme states twelve values and derives the rest. The ground, the ink,
the accent, three semantic hues and seven syntax hues are the anchors; the
surface ladder, the ink ramp, the tints, the tooltip chip and the accent
pair come from ramp constants measured off the palette in tokens.css, so
every theme reproduces a shape that was already validated instead of
inventing one. The border ramp, the shadow stacks and the scrims state
nothing at all, because tembo's overlays are alpha over whatever ground
they land on — that is the property that keeps the seed set to twelve
rather than eighty-five.

Contrast is derived, not hoped for. The ink ramp is placed by the contrast
it has to hold rather than by a lightness fraction, since Realm's own span
is near-white over near-black and copying its fractions onto a lighter
ground collapses the ramp; stated hues are then corrected along lightness
only, within a budget, so a fix can never quietly desaturate a vendored
colour into something else. What survives the derivation is asserted: the
one value nothing can rescue is `--ink`, held to AA on every ground the
stylesheet actually puts it on.

Syntax was the other half. highlight.js was painted straight out of the
chrome palette, which made every theme's keywords Realm blue; it now goes
through ten named roles that mean the same thing on the shipped palette
and are seven seeds away from meaning Monokai. Terminals are deliberately
left out: xterm parses `--rl-terminal-bg` once when a hub is created, so a
themed terminal would be correct only for hubs opened after the switch.

The eight chart series stay put, because their spacing under simulated
protanopia is a guarantee about colour vision and not a mood. What moves
is the ground under them — every dark palette here is lighter than the
#232427 they were validated on, and slot 6 drops under 3:1 on all of them
— so the Usage cards take a chart surface that carries the theme's hue at
a lightness clamped back into the validated band.

Give the delegation dock's list a scrollbar decision

The dock's list is a scroller, and every scroller in the stylesheet has to
have had a deliberate decision made about its bar — thin and trackless like
the rest of the app's lists, or explicitly left alone. It is thin.

The guardrail that requires this landed separately, so the dock arrived
without a verdict and the check named it.

Keep a delegation independent of whoever is watching it

`begin` is on the delegation's happy path and `watch`'s settle runs unobserved
in the background. A listener that threw would abort a real run over a
notification nobody needed, so its failures stop at the engine — the registry
is unaffected either way, and the listener resyncs on its next read.

`end` also reached for the announcement before checking there was anything to
announce. Deleting a session releases its runs whether or not it ever had any,
so clearing out fifty old sessions told every open window fifty times that
nothing had changed.

Refetch the delegation registry when the socket comes back

The dock claimed it leaves when a session's runs do, and it did not. Every
other kind of state the reconnect path repairs is backed by a table the server
can re-read; this one is backed by nothing but the engine's memory. A server
restart is a socket drop and a reconnect, so the registry being mirrored had
already died with the process, no `delegation.changed` was ever coming to say
so, and the dock sat there naming agents that had stopped existing with a
duration ticking up beside them — the exact failure that was the argument for
docking this rather than giving it a pane.

Both key sets are refetched, because a run can have ended under a session
being mirrored and begun under one that was not.

The header said "waiting on" while it was at it. An `agent_start` the parent
deliberately backgrounded is in this list too, and that parent is not blocked
on anything; what every entry does have is an unsettled drain, which is what
"running" means.

Count a sub-agent's calls in the run that spawned them

Nesting took the child's calls out of the top level, and the collapsed ledger
line summarizes the top level, so the counts quietly started under-reporting
the run they claim to describe: three tools and two files where four calls
touched three.

The duration was worse. It spans the run's first stamp to its last, and with
the child lifted out, a Task at the end of a run ended the span at the moment
it was CALLED rather than when its work finished. So the row ticked upward for
five minutes while the sub-agent worked and then froze at "1s" the instant it
settled — the one number that had been right all along collapsing exactly when
it became final.

The span is min→max now rather than first→last, because a sub-agent's calls
run CONCURRENTLY with its parent's and the last call in tree order is not the
last one to happen. Only the end needs looking for: blocks arrive in order and
a child cannot predate the call that spawned it, so the run's first call is
still its earliest.

The builder also carries its nodes through instead of rebuilding them, which
is how a card's nested steps keep the identity the memo compares on, and the
shared empty array is readonly now that it is reachable through a public type.

Resolve a sub-agent's parent only among calls already seen

Building the id map up front made every call in the transcript a candidate
parent, including calls that had not happened yet. Real data cannot express
that — a sub-agent acts after the call that spawned it, never before — but a
malformed pair of ids could, and two calls naming each other would nest into
one another, leave the render entirely, and then recurse until the stack went
while the enter flags were being marked. A white screen is a worse answer than
a flat one.

Resolving against only what has already been seen removes the possibility
rather than checking for it, and collapses the two passes into one on the way.
The self-referential case the explicit guard used to catch now falls out of
the same rule.

Show a session the agents it is waiting on

A delegated child has always been a real session with a pane of its own, but
the session that delegated it said nothing while it worked. The child's report
arrives as one MCP tool result at the very end, so for however long the child
ran — minutes, usually — the parent's pane showed a shimmer and gave no reason
for it. Which children are running, and how far along, is a fact only the
server holds: the delegation engine's registry is in memory and was never
published.

So the engine publishes it, and stays the only copy. It reports which parent
changed and nothing more; `announceDelegation` reads the set back off
`liveRuns` to build the payload, so no listener can be handed a snapshot the
registry has already moved past, and there is one place that decides what
"live" counts as. A run now carries the parent it was begun under, because a
background settle resolves holding only the run and a settle nobody can
attribute to a parent is a settle nobody can be told about. Reviewers the user
starts from a diff pane are begun under a synthetic key with no session behind
them; those are dropped rather than announced to nobody.

The payload is deliberately thin — which sessions, since when, blocking or
not. The child is a real session, so its title, agent and status already reach
the renderer the ordinary way, and a second description of the same thing on
the wire is a second description free to drift.

The pane draws it as a dock between the transcript and the prompter, listing
the children and handing each one to its own pane beside the parent. Docked
rather than a pane kind of its own: a pane is a layout leaf that persists,
while this registry dies with the server process, so a pane would leave an
empty panel behind from a run that finished yesterday. Living inside the
delegating session's pane is also what ties it to that session — it cannot be
dragged away from what it describes, and it leaves when the runs do.

A peer that `agent_ask` put a question to is named apart from the children. It
was doing its own work before the question arrived and goes on doing it after,
and calling it a sub-agent would be wrong in both directions.

Nest a sub-agent's tool calls under the call that spawned them

Claude's mapper has always tagged a sub-agent's tool calls with
`parentToolUseId`, and its header has always said the UI would nest them by
it. The transcript dropped the field on the floor, so a Task call's children
landed flat in the stream, interleaved with the agent's own calls in arrival
order. Reading down the ledger there was no way to tell which of six Reads
belonged to the child, and nothing anywhere said one agent had spawned
another.

`groupTranscript` now builds a tree from those ids before it folds runs.
Ordering cannot do the job — the harness runs parent and child concurrently
and the transcript is one stream — so the ids are the only thing that
separates them. Lifting the child's calls out closes the gaps they left, and
a parent's own calls that were only ever split by its child now read as the
single run they always were. A call naming a parent this transcript does not
hold stays where it is: an id Realm cannot resolve is still work the agent
did, and hiding it would lose the call rather than nest it.

The child's steps then wear the ledger's own treatment one level in, so they
stay open while it is working and fold away once its result lands. Adapters
that report no hierarchy send null forever, nest nothing, and render exactly
as before.

The open-state rules had to narrow to direct children on the way past. They
were written when a tool card could not contain another one; now that it can,
opening a Task would have rotated every chevron beneath it and unfolded every
nested body at once.

Let the model picker be asked who MADE a model

The list can already be asked which harness runs a model twice over — it blocks
the rows by the one each resolved to, and the search matches harness names, so
typing "cursor" answers "what could I get from Cursor". What it could not be
asked is who made the thing. A row reached through the Claude CLI and through
Cursor is one row with two routes and exactly one maker, so "show me Anthropic's"
is a question about the model rather than about the way in, and it had no way to
be put.

So a provider here is the vendor, and the strip under the search is vendors. The
other reading was tempting and would have been a mistake: the detail pane a few
pixels below already carries a horizontal row of harness buttons, and those mean
"run it through this one" — a second horizontal row of the same names meaning
"show me only these" would be two controls that look alike and do different
things, inches apart.

It narrows what the search searches rather than replacing it, which is why it
sits underneath: the two compose, and reading them downwards is the order the
question is asked in. The chips come from the unfiltered rows so the strip never
reflows out from under the pointer, and one the query has emptied dims rather
than vanishing — it stays reachable, and the list then says in words which of the
two constraints emptied it and offers the way back. A model no catalog covers
belongs to no vendor and is hidden by any choice; there is deliberately no
"Other" chip, because a bucket collecting the models Realm happens to have no
maker for would sort by an accident of the catalog. With no catalog at all there
is no axis, and no strip.

The keyboard was the part easiest to get wrong. ←/→ already walk the highlighted
model's routes from the search field, so the strip's own ←/→ live on the strip,
which is a single tab stop in the radio-group way: Tab from the search lands on
the choice in force, the arrows move within it, Tab again leaves for the list.
The route-walk keeps meaning only what it meant.

Let the prompter's row spend its width on the branch name

A branch name is user data and the pane it sits in can be a quarter of the
window, so this row's width depends on two things nobody controls — and it
answered to neither. The name was capped at a flat 160px, which truncated a
thirty-character branch in a thousand-pixel pane with five hundred going spare,
and clipped the entire chip in anything under about 565px of pane: the group is
nowrap with overflow hidden and unshrinkable children, so the branch button was
not truncated there but sliced down the middle, which reads as a rendering fault
rather than as a name that did not fit.

The cap is now whatever the pane has left once everything of fixed width is
paid for, so the name grows and shrinks with the room it actually has. The
reserve is the collapsed row's figure deliberately: sized for the wider
un-collapsed one, panes between the two would fold the permission chip away to
buy the branch pixels it did not need. Below that the row sheds in the order it
can afford to — "N changed" first, since the +/- pair beside it answers the same
question and the file count is already on the button's tip, then the pair, and
last the name itself, which gives way to the mark it was already carrying while
staying legible to a screen reader and one hover away for everyone else.

The chip keeps `flex: none` with the rest of the row throughout, so the measured
collapse still sees a real overflow rather than one this chip quietly absorbed.
The thresholds are the session pane's own width, not the window's, and every one
of them is read off a live sweep rather than guessed: the new script drives the
built app across pane widths with a scratch repo behind the chip and fails on
any control the group has cut. It stops claiming anything below 320px of pane,
where the fixed controls alone no longer fit and the repair is the mode chip
learning the fold the permission chip already knows.

Take the reader to the bottom when they send

The transcript follows the bottom only while `atBottom` says the reader is near
it, and `send()` never touched the scroller. So a reader who had scrolled up to
check something and then typed a reply was shown a "New messages" pill about
their own message, which is the one message they can never need telling about.

The pane counts its own prompter's sends and the transcript pins on that count
changing. It is the pane's count rather than the transcript's own growth because
only the prompter's send carries the intent: ⌘⇧↩ dispatches the draft into a NEW
session and has to leave this scroller exactly where the reader parked it. And
the pin re-arms `atBottom` rather than performing one scroll, because the send is
a round trip — a single scroll would be overtaken by the `user_message` block
coming back and the pill would go up anyway.

jsdom can only see any of this with a scroller geometry staged into it, since
with no layout every element reports a scrollHeight of 0 and looks pinned
already; the live script drives the real window, where the transcript genuinely
overflows and the scripted adapter supplies both the scrollback and the control
case of a block the reader did not send.

Let the scripted agent produce a plan

The fake adapter exists for UI development, and a plan is now drawn by a card of its own — which that
adapter had no way to emit, so the one surface added here was the one surface unreachable offline.
The offline-dev script revises its plan in place rather than sending it once, because a plan that
updates is the behaviour worth looking at.

Add Ask, a read-only mode each backend actually enforces

Ask sits beside Build and Plan: the agent may read and search the repo, and may not edit a file or
run a command. A mode that says read-only and is not is worse than no mode, so every backend refuses
the call itself and none of them is asked nicely.

Claude has no such permission mode, so the adapter denies anything outside an allow-list in
canUseTool, before the tool runs and without putting it to the user — a prompt the user could answer
"allow" to would make the mode advisory. An allow-list rather than a deny-list because the next tool
the CLI ships and every tool of every MCP server a space adds must fail closed. Bash is not on it:
nothing can tell from a command string whether it mutates, and guessing is the lie the mode exists to
avoid. The SDK's own `Options.tools` is not the lever — it restricts built-ins only, so an MCP
server's mutating tool walks past it, and it cannot be changed on a live query, so a session that
started in Ask would be left without its tools until a restart after leaving it.

Codex gets `approvalPolicy: "never"` with `sandbox: "read-only"`, which is genuinely tighter than
Plan rather than a relabelling of it: Plan's `untrusted` policy turns a refused write into an
approval the user can say yes to, and that escalation puts the write through. Codex's own validator
calls this pairing "read-only permissions with approvals disabled", and the sandbox does the refusing
in the kernel. It is fixed at thread start, so a mid-session switch applies next start — the chip
says so rather than implying otherwise.

ACP is the case that validates the shape: Cursor already advertises `ask` as "no edits or command
execution", arrived at independently. Realm resolves it the way it resolves Plan — the agent's own
well-known id, never a name that merely sounds right — and offers nothing where nothing is
advertised.

The `default` permission rung is relabelled "Ask each time". It was called "Ask", and two controls in
one row both offering something called Ask, meaning two unrelated things, is a question the user
cannot answer; the longer label is also the more accurate one, since that rung is about being asked
per action rather than a way of working.

Three modes make the prompter's mode parking wrong in both directions if it stays a Plan/not-Plan
binary, so it is written as what it always meant: park on the way in from Build, restore on the way
out to Build. Plan → Ask now preserves the permission the user chose instead of overwriting it with
"plan", and does not restore it halfway. The places that used Plan as a proxy for read-only ask
`isReadOnlyMode` instead — the browser broker refuses mutations in Ask exactly as it does in Plan —
and delegation ranks the two equal, since neither lets a child change anything and claiming an order
between them would be inventing one. The delegation constraint enum had to learn `ask` too, or the
most restrictive thing a parent can ask for would have been refused outright rather than granted.

Carry the Codex and ACP plans into the transcript too

Codex sends two different plans and Realm dropped both: `toolNameFor` returned null for the `plan`
ThreadItem, and `turn/plan/updated` fell through the notification switch's default. ACP's `plan`
update was parsed and thrown away in the same breath as the advisory notifications, which for a
Cursor or Gemini session means the only plan they ever produce never reached the reader.

The two Codex shapes stay two cards because they are two artifacts, confirmed against the protocol's
own generated bindings: the `plan` item is `{id, text}`, prose, while `turn/plan/updated` is
`{step, status}[]`. Merging them would need one of them invented from the other.

`item/plan/delta` is emitted only as salvage, never live. It is flagged EXPERIMENTAL and its own doc
comment tells clients not to assume the concatenated deltas match the completed item — but an item an
interrupt cut short has no completed content to differ from, and the concatenation is then the only
record there will be. That is the same bargain the reasoning deltas already strike.

Identity is per turn on both sides. Codex re-sends the whole step list every time a step moves and
ACP's spec says its plan is not incremental, so a revision replaces the card already drawn; the next
turn gets a fresh one, because overwriting the last turn's plan would erase what the agent set out to
do. On ACP that reset belongs to the turn boundary and not to `flushRuns`, which every tool call in
between goes through.

Both fixture agents now emit plans, including a Codex item left deliberately unfinished so the
interrupt salvage has something to salvage.

Give a plan its own place in the transcript

Realm throws every plan artifact away. Claude's plan arrives as an ordinary ExitPlanMode tool call,
so it renders as a generic permission card whose one-line summary clips a whole document, and the
plan itself is gone the moment the request is answered — the record of what the agent proposed does
not survive the decision, let alone a relaunch.

A plan is now a session event of its own. It carries prose and a checklist independently because the
protocols genuinely send different artifacts: Claude has only markdown, Codex has both a prose plan
item and a status-bearing step list, ACP has entries. Collapsing the checklist to prose would lose
per-step status and synthesising steps out of Claude's markdown would invent structure it never sent,
so a plan carries whichever it was given and a mapper holding neither emits nothing at all. The event
is keyed, because a revised plan has to land on the card already drawn rather than stack a second one
saying almost the same thing.

The permission ExitPlanMode raises is untouched — answering it is how the session leaves Plan — but
it stops pretending to be a permission. "Allow always" on a plan is a standing grant to leave Plan
unasked, which is not a thing a user can mean, so the plan is a block and this is only the answer to
it. Approving it also settles Realm's own mode row: the agent acts on the approval at once, and
without this the chip went on claiming Plan over a session that was building while the permission
mode Plan had parked stayed stranded.

The prompter's "the plan is ready" guess becomes a fact for the same reason. It fired on any finished
assistant message in Plan, so an agent that asked a clarifying question and stopped was answered with
an offer to implement a plan nobody had written.

Make the forbidden-app check prove something

The absence assertion cannot prove itself. `listApps` filters the forbidden
set before returning, so deriving "which forbidden apps are running" from its
own output is empty by construction no matter what the helper does — the line
reported "this run proves nothing" honestly, but it could never report
anything else.

The refusal is what can be tested directly, and it does not depend on the
machine happening to be running a terminal: ask for one by name and require
the refusal. Snapshot refusals throw where computerAct returns
`{ok:false, refused}`, so the check has to catch rather than inspect a return
value — a version that only read the result would take the throw for a pass.

Verified with the Accessibility grant in place: Terminal, Ghostty and System
Settings are each refused by name.

Refuse the terminals people actually run, not just Apple's and iTerm's

A terminal is a shell, so driving one is arbitrary code execution outside
every sandbox, permission card and mode Realm has — the agent ends up typing
past its own approval gate instead of through it. That reasoning already put
Terminal.app and iTerm on the helper's refusal list, but it stopped there,
and the terminal most likely to be running on a developer's Mac today is
Ghostty, kitty, WezTerm or Alacritty. Every one of them was driveable.

The live check did not catch it because it named the two entries instead of
the rule: asserting Terminal.app and iTerm are absent from a machine running
neither passes without testing anything. It now checks the whole list and
reports how many forbidden apps were actually running, so a run that proved
nothing says so rather than reading as a pass.

The list has to be enforced in Swift, in the last process before an event is
posted, where the suite cannot reach it. So it also lives in the contract,
and a test reads the helper's source and fails when the two drift.

The set is a floor rather than a boundary — a bundle-id denylist cannot name
every terminal that will exist — and the per-app permission card is what
bounds the ones it misses.

fix(desktop): make the Accessibility button work on a build with no helper

The row claimed Electron could raise that prompt without the Swift helper, and the copy said so,
but the request path went through the helper unconditionally and swallowed the rejection — so on
a helperless build the button rendered and did nothing. Main now falls back to Electron's own
prompting query for that one grant, which is what the row always promised. Screen Recording has
no such API, so its row keeps offering System Settings alone.

Alongside it, a pass over the rest. Typed text is chunked in UTF-16 units rather than Characters,
because that is what the event API counts: one emoji is a single Character and two units, so the
old bound put twice the intended payload in an event for exactly the text most likely to overflow
it. Chunks still break on Character boundaries, so a surrogate pair is never split into two
replacement characters.

The helper's screenshot default said true while every other layer says false. Keychain Access was
listed under two spellings, hedging a bundle id that has one. The scroll description asserted a
direction nothing exercises, so it no longer claims one. Argument validation was byte-identical in
both gateway providers and moves next to ok/err/clip; the modifier list is a contract and is no
longer re-typed beside it.

test(desktop): drive the computer-use stack against real macOS

A live check over the real helper client, the real op executor and the real compiled Swift
binary. It runs in two tiers because one of them needs a grant a given machine may not have:
what works ungranted is asserted always, and the end-to-end drive of Calculator — snapshot it,
press a digit by index, read the result back out of the tree — is skipped loudly rather than
silently when Accessibility is missing. Calculator because it has no documents, so nothing of
the user's can be edited or saved.

It immediately earned itself. Excluding "the app that hosts this helper" turned out not to
exclude Realm: the ancestry walk stops at whatever app is really hosting the process, which
under a dev build or this script is Electron, so a separately running Realm.app was listed as
driveable. Any Realm window is a window permission cards appear in, whoever drew it, so the
identity that matters is the product's rather than this process tree's — Realm is now named
statically as well as derived, and the check asserts the exclusion instead of assuming it.

feat(desktop): let Settings ask for the two grants computer control needs

The Permissions tab could report Accessibility and Screen Recording but never request either,
so Realm had no way to obtain a grant it now genuinely needs. These rows can ask.

Asking lives in its own module rather than in tcc.ts, whose governing rule is that no probe
may ever trigger a prompt — a rule that is relied on, since the tab probes on every visit.
Checking and asking are different acts, so they are different files rather than one file with
a flag that weakens the invariant. The rows still read their state through the same
prompt-free queries.

The button says "Ask macOS" rather than "Grant" because that is all it can do. macOS has no
API that grants Accessibility: the dialog's only button opens System Settings, and nothing
changes until the user flips the switch there. A button that promised more would make the page
look broken when the row stayed red, so the copy and the tests both pin that asking is not
granting.

Screen Recording has no request API at all beyond the one in the native helper, so on a build
compiled without it that row offers System Settings alone instead of a button that cannot work.

feat(server): the realm-computer tools, off until a space asks for them

Agents get three tools over the Mac's own applications: list what is running, read an app's
accessibility tree as indexed elements, act on one of them. The shape is the browser's on
purpose — snapshot, address by index, act, with the index re-resolved at act time — because it
is the same problem, and an agent that can drive a page should not have to learn a second
idiom to drive an app.

Two things about the permission model are deliberately unlike everything else here.

This provider is off until a space turns it on, inverting the default the others get. Every
other provider acts inside Realm, so shipping it is the opt-in; this one reaches applications
the user has never mentioned to Realm, and a capability like that should be something a space
was given rather than something it woke up holding.

And bypassPermissions does not skip the card. That mode means "stop asking me about ordinary
actions", and it earns that meaning from the blast radius being a page in a pane Realm owns.
Driving the whole machine has no such bound, so the gate grows an option: ask once, then honour
allow_always. The grant is keyed on the bundle id, because approving TextEdit must not license
Mail, and the difference between those two is not one a mode set for coding agents can express.

A session may only act on a snapshot it took. That is what lets the card name the app, and it
means an id from a transcript or a guess drives nothing.

Snapshots carry no image unless one is asked for: the tree is the addressable surface, and a
read tool an agent calls every turn should not cost a screenshot every turn.

feat(desktop): carry computer-use ops over the main-server bridge

The executor half of computer use, shaped like the browser's: the server names an op, main
runs it, and everything native sits behind one injected seam so the decisions worth testing —
how a tree renders, how an action translates, which failures become which refusal — are
testable without a Mac or a grant.

The ops ride the existing main-server socket rather than a second one. There is one
connection and one registered executor, so a parallel bridge would duplicate the reconnect,
timeout and supersede handling to no end; the two op families are still named separately
because they answer to different hosts and share nothing else.

The helper client is written here rather than reusing the adapters' JSON-RPC client, which is
not a dependency of the desktop app and would pull the agent SDK into the Electron main
bundle. Its bidirectional half — a peer that raises requests of its own — is also exactly what
this protocol does not have.

Typing into a password field is refused in the helper, at act time, against the live role
rather than the snapshot's, because the sign-in sheet that replaced the form since the
snapshot is the case worth catching. Clicking one is still allowed: that is how the user gets
focus to type it themselves.

feat(desktop): a Swift accessibility helper that can read and drive other apps

Realm can already drive a web page: snapshot it, address elements by a stable ref, and
re-resolve that ref to a point at act time. This is the same shape for the rest of the Mac,
over the accessibility APIs rather than CDP.

The helper is a long-lived child speaking newline-delimited JSON rather than a CLI invoked
per operation, and that is forced rather than chosen. An AXUIElement is a live, process-local
handle with no serialisable address, so an element index can only keep meaning while the
process that walked the tree still holds the handle. A one-shot CLI would re-walk and
renumber between the snapshot and the click, which is precisely the failure indexing exists
to prevent.

Two independent checks stand between a tool call and a click landing somewhere unintended.
The target app must actually come to the front when asked, and the point must really belong
to it at the instant of the click. The second needs a layer filter that is not obvious:
Notification Center keeps a full-screen, fully-opaque window at layer 21 at all times, so a
naive front-to-back hit test names it the owner of every pixel on the display and refuses
every click on the machine. Windows above the normal layer are skipped unless they belong to
the target, which leaves its own menus clickable.

Realm refuses to drive itself, System Settings, the password prompt and the terminals. The
self-check reads the process ancestry rather than an argument, because a value arriving over
the same pipe as the commands is one the caller controls; and it walks up rather than reading
the immediate parent, which under a shell is not an app at all.

The tool surface follows open-codex-computer-use (MIT); the code and safety model are ours.

Give light mode the colours the ramps could not reach

--grid-line and --shadow-glass-inset go. Both were referenced nowhere,
and both were declared in the dark block alone — which is worse than
unused, because the first thing to reach for one would have carried a
dark value into light mode with nothing anywhere reporting it.

The real problem was a layer below the ramps. tokens.css flips correctly
and then styles.css writes a literal underneath it that never changes.
The three scrims were the genuine offenders: a veil subtracts from what is
behind it, so 45% black over a near-white window is a far heavier dim than
the same veil over a dark one, and the command palette had to shout
through it. They become --scrim and --scrim-soft, lighter in light mode,
and the two levels stay two levels — a sheet covers the window on purpose
and ⌘K does not.

The rest of the literals turn out to be correct, and the fix for them is a
name rather than an override. The terminal hint's white ink sits on the
terminal's own interior, which is dark in both modes for the same reason
--rl-terminal-bg is; it is now --rl-terminal-ink beside it, because a bare
rgba(255,255,255,.55) in a stylesheet reads as a light-mode bug to anyone
sweeping for one, and has already been mistaken for one. The attachment
badge and its remove button sit on a picture the user attached, which is
the same picture in both modes — the same argument the media transport
already rests on — so their ink becomes --rl-on-media and their veils stay.
The browser pane's white is matching the native view's own ground so a
resize cannot flash the panel tone through the gap.

The white top edge on filled controls also stays one value, and that is a
judgement rather than an omission: the fill under it is a saturated accent
or red in both modes and the light still comes from above. What was wrong
with it was being written out three times, so it is --fill-bevel now, next
to --shadow-bevel, which is the other case — a bevel for a surface, which
does flip, because a white edge on a white card is nothing. Checked on
screen in both modes: the highlight reads as a highlight on either fill.

A check now fails on any raw black or white a rule writes without the mode
being able to reach it, with the handful that are deliberate listed
alongside the reason each one is not the theme's to flip.

Stop ruling lists that already separate themselves

Six lists drew a hairline between every pair of rows, and in five of them
the rows were already separated by something else. Checkpoints, activity
entries and engines are rounded rows that light up under the pointer — a
rule between two of them states the boundary a second time, and the pill
and the line disagree about where it is. Settings rows and checkouts have
no fill to trade on, so those pay for the line in space instead: eight
pixels of padding becomes ten, which reads as a twenty-pixel gap and lets
the name/description luminance step do the separating.

The diff list keeps a seam, but only under an open file, where the patch
panel really would run into the next filename. Between two collapsed rows
it was decoration, and thirty-pixel rows with a hover fill separate
themselves the way the sidebar's list already does.

The question card's options lose their inset rule and take the one-pixel
gap the permission card's options have always used. The two are the same
card asking a different question and there was no reason for one of them
to be ruled.

Everything that survives is a seam content actually passes under: the pane
bar, the sticky diff and file heads, a code panel's language header, the
search field above a popover's list, the footers that hold their place
while a body scrolls behind them, the sidebar's column edge, and table
rules, which are structure rather than chrome.

A check now fails on any new rule drawn between adjacent rows, while
leaving the conditional form the diff list uses available for the cases
where a seam is genuinely load-bearing.

Hide every scrollbar track, not the nine that were listed

Nine containers had been styled by hand; every scroller added since — the
model picker's list and its detail pane, the skill picker, the spaces
overview, the notifications columns, the page body, the checkpoint and
activity lists, the documents surfaces, most of what the transcript draws
inside itself — shipped with the default bar and a visible track.

A longer list would have the same failure built into it, so the track is
hidden by inheritance instead. `scrollbar-color` inherits, so stating it
once on the root covers every scroller in the app including ones written
after this, and the transparent second value is the track going away.
Verified in the running app: a scroller created at runtime and named
nowhere resolves to a transparent track. `scrollbar-width` does not
inherit, so the scrollers that should be thin rather than default-width
are still named — but that list is now a refinement rather than the thing
correctness depends on.

The thumb is quiet at rest and steps up under the pointer. `:hover` is
bare on purpose: hover matches up the ancestor chain, so a scroller
brightens its own thumb with no second copy of the list. `:focus-within`
cannot join it — it would match <body> whenever anything had focus.

The four `::-webkit-scrollbar` rules go. They had been dead since Chromium
121, which ignores those pseudo-elements outright once either standard
property is set, and every selector they targeted also set
`scrollbar-width`. Measured here: a scroller with only the pseudo-element
rules reserves the 24px they ask for, one with both reserves the 11px the
standard property asks for. The width, the thumb colour and the transparent
track were all coming from the line above them already.

Left alone deliberately. The terminal viewport keeps an explicit rule
rather than inheriting: xterm measures that element to decide the
terminal's column count, and its interior is dark in both app modes, so
its bar should answer to the terminal rather than to whatever the app-wide
rule becomes next. The horizontal strips — the space rail, the group tabs,
the page rail, the narrow settings tabs — keep `scrollbar-width: none`,
