because a bar under a 30px row is the tallest thing in it and the space
rail already announces its overflow with an edge fade. The prompter's
textarea keeps its own `none` for the reason written above it: a classic
bar takes width from the textarea's text box and not from the highlight
mirror's, which would slide every wrapped line off the caret. The document
preview iframe is its own document and out of reach from here.

A new check fails on any scroller that has not had one of those decisions
made about it, which is how the nine became nine.

Put every timing on one motion ladder

The four duration tokens described a system the stylesheet was not on.
Only four of forty-one `transition:` declarations reached for one, and
--dur-press and --dur-slow had no users anywhere — every other timing was
a literal, eleven distinct numbers written out at the call site. A ladder
nobody stands on is documentation, and the next few workstreams are about
to build animations on top of it.

So the ladder grows to the durations §6 already assigns, one rung per kind
of change: the drop target, the hover fill, the press, the popover, the
quiet fade, the glyph swap, the item arriving, the box resizing, the
stagger, the surface arriving, the thing travelling across the pane.

No rendered timing moves. The two rungs that shift value — press from
140ms to the 120ms every press in the app actually uses, slow from an
unused 300ms to the 240ms the sheets enter on — had no users to disturb,
and naming them after what the app does beats naming them after what was
imported. The single exception is the terminal hint's fade, which was
250ms and is now 240: it was the last orphan in the file and ten
milliseconds off the nearest rung, on an opacity fade nothing pins.

Loop periods stay literals on purpose. The pulses, the shimmer, the orb
and the generating canvas are tempos rather than the duration of a change,
and the 40ms stagger is a delay between siblings; filing either on the
ladder would invite someone picking one for a transition.

§6's table is now pinned through the ladder instead of against literals,
so each timing is two independent facts: the rule reaches for the right
rung, and that rung still resolves to the millisecond value the spec gave.
A new check fails on any bare duration that creeps back in, which is the
regression that produced this state in the first place.

Draw the prompter's squircle instead of asking for it

`corner-shape: squircle` has been sitting on the composer, the drop hint,
the install card and the commit dock doing nothing. It lands in Chromium
139 and Electron 37.10.3 ships 138, where the property is not even
recognised — so the corners have been plain circular arcs the whole time,
one radius step wider to disguise it.

The shape now comes from a paint worklet, which is the only technique that
survives what these cards need. A mask or a clip-path would have taken the
box-shadow with it, and the prompter's lift and its focus ring are not
decoration. So the painter draws the fill and the edge, and box-shadow
keeps the lift alone: a ring has to trace the same curve as the fill or it
crosses a corner the superellipse has already bulged past, while the lift
is blurred several times wider than the two curves ever diverge. That
split is why --shadow-card is now composed from --card-ring and
--shadow-card-lift rather than written out.

Focus and the drop target become a change of the painter's ring colour and
width, so both follow the curve for free.

The worklet is a `public/` file rather than a module because the renderer's
CSP is `script-src 'self'` and rejects a worklet fetched from blob: or
data:. It is switched on by a root mark set only after the module resolves:
`paint()` with no painter registered resolves to nothing, and a card that
opted in early would render as an invisible box. Everything outside that
mark is the old rounded-rect fallback, and `corner-shape` stays alongside
for the runtime that will honour it.

The under-strip carrying the machine and workspace chips gets the same
treatment on its bottom corners, which is where it was asked for.

scripts/squircle-live.mjs proves it on composited pixels, because jsdom
cannot tell paint() from border-radius. It counts the fraction of a
corner's R×R square the card fills: a circular arc gives pi/4, the
superellipse gives 0.874. The prompter measures 0.885, and with the gate
stripped the same measurement falls to 0.752. It also mutates the shadow
away to show the lift is real, and re-measures the corner while focused to
show the ring did not square it off.

Read the icon-ladder scan's sources through Vite rather than off disk

The scan walked up from process.cwd() to find its own directory, because
vitest can be invoked from the repo root or from apps/desktop and
import.meta.url is rewritten to a non-file scheme under jsdom. That is a
real constraint, but styles.test.ts already carries a copy of the same
walk-up, and a second one is how two copies become three.

import.meta.glob resolves against this module at transform time, so the
question never arises: no cwd, no import.meta.url, and no filesystem. It
also gains a floor on the number of files found — a glob that matches
nothing would have made the scan pass while checking nothing at all.

Sit the traffic lights inline with the panes instead of on a rail

Collapsing the sidebar bought back 280px of width and then spent 38px of
window height buying it back again: a full-width strip above every pane
whose only content was one button, standing there so the macOS traffic
lights would not land on pane chrome. That is a permanent piece of chrome
across the whole window in exchange for a corner.

The lights land on pane chrome now, deliberately. The corner that holds
the toggle is an overlay — absolutely positioned, no height of its own —
and the strip beneath the lights reserves their width instead. Whichever
strip is first in the main column is the one under them, so each
candidate claims the reservation with :first-child and the three stay
mutually exclusive: an error bar pushes the others down, and only the one
actually under the lights should be indented. The pane host starts at
y=0, measured, so collapsing costs nothing now.

Which pane is under them is a fact about where a pane sits, not about the
markup around it, so PaneHost marks the leaf at the host's top-left and
CSS reads that rather than trying to walk a first-child chain through
react-resizable-panels' wrappers.

The lights themselves never move, which is the part worth keeping in
sync: y:14 centres them in a 40px strip, and .sb-head, .panel-bar and the
group bar in this one state are all 40px, so a single placement in main
serves both states and setWindowButtonPosition is not needed at runtime.
Shorten any of those three and the lights go off-centre in that state
alone — both ends of that now say so.

The corner renders after main and carries a z-index because panes are
positioned elements and DOM order alone would let the first pane's bar
paint over it, which would leave the toggle visible and unclickable.

Dissolve the bottom of the sidebar list instead of cutting it off

The list ended at the scroller's edge, which slices the last visible row
through the middle of its glyphs. The transcript and the changes list
already solved this with a two-layer progressive blur sitting as a
sibling of the scroller — a light band over the whole ramp, a heavier one
lower down, each behind a mask that starts further down so the blur ramps
instead of stepping — and this is that, not a second invention.

One deliberate difference: no colour wash. The transcript washes to
--rl-panel because it docks the composer at its bottom and the gap above
that card has to be solid pane. Nothing docks here, and this column is
macOS vibrancy rather than an opaque surface, so a ramp to any fixed tone
would paint a stripe the material shows straight through. The blur alone
is the dissolve. Measured on screen over empty gutter it moves the
column's luminance by a third of one level out of 255, so there is no
seam where there is nothing to dissolve.

The scroller gains a full band of bottom padding, not a fraction of one,
for the reason the changes list needed the same: these are 32px rows of
dense text, and a row ending inside the ramp is a session someone
scrolled down to read and then cannot. Scrolled to the end the last row
sits clear of the band with the blur over empty gutter beneath it.

Reduced transparency is where the two fades have to part company again.
The transcript can drop its blur and keep its wash; this one has no wash
to fall back on, so dropping the blur alone would hand back the hard cut.
It changes medium instead — and that preference is the single condition
where a ramp to a fixed tone composites cleanly here, because macOS
renders the material opaque under it.

Make the split glyph draw the split it is describing

The mark is worth keeping. It appears only when there IS a split, and in
a split two open rows are otherwise identical — it is the one thing in
the sidebar that answers "which of these panes am I looking at". But a
fixed 2x2 grid can only depict halves and quarters, and the layouts
gridPreset builds are not all halves and quarters. Under a three-column
layout the old code fell back to depth-first leaf index modulo 4, so the
pane at the far right of a single row lit the bottom-left quadrant of a
grid with no bottom row. That is not an approximation, it is a wrong
answer, and it is read by exactly the person who cannot otherwise tell
two rows apart — so it sends them to the wrong pane.

Now the glyph draws one bar per slot of the top-level split, along that
split's own axis, with this row's slot lit: two bars for a two-way split,
three for a three-way one, and nothing at all once the root has more
slots than fit legibly, because a row with no mark is better than a
smudge that looks like a reading. Only the top level, deliberately —
twelve pixels cannot hold a tree, and "which half am I in" is the
question actually being asked, which is why a two-way root still answers
by subtree rather than by leaf order.

Dropping the second axis buys the legibility back: two slots are 5.5px
bars here against 4.5px cells before. The blanket 70% opacity goes too —
the contrast between a lit bar and an unlit one is the entire message,
and dimming the whole mark flattened it.

Separately, the row now has one elastic column. The dot and the glyph
both carried margin-left:auto, and two auto margins in a flex row share
the free space, so the dot was pushed into the middle of whatever the
title left over while the glyph carried on to the end — measured live at
54px apart, and the distance moved with the title's length, so no two
rows agreed where the dot sat. Same fix the page rows already use.

Give a running session a ring that survives having its motion taken away

The green dot throbbed between full and 55% opacity, which is not much of
a signal: at 6px a third of a brightness step is not something an eye
finds unless it already knows where to look, and under
prefers-reduced-motion — where the stylesheet strips every animation
globally — it was simply an ordinary dot in a slightly different colour.
An indicator whose whole content is its motion says nothing to the people
most likely to have that motion switched off.

So the mark carries the state in its SHAPE now: a solid core inside a
ring that pings outward from it. The ring is authored at full strength
with no transform, which is the load-bearing part — its un-animated form
is a steady halo rather than a half-scaled ghost, so a running session
still reads as hotter than an idle one when the ping is gone. Only the
ring moves; the core is untouched, so the row's trailing column cannot
jitter.

The three states that mean something is in flight share the idiom and are
told apart by colour and rate together, never by rate alone — 1.8s
against 0.9s of the same motion is not a distinction anyone makes at a
glance. waiting_permission is the one that needs a human, so it stays the
loudest in both modes: fastest ping with motion, warning tone against
success without it. A tripped MCP breaker keeps the old blink, because a
fault that is persisting is not an act in progress.

The space strip's badge deliberately does not join them. It is a rollup
for a space nobody is looking at, where the only answer that asks you to
go there is "waiting on you", and a ring expanding from a badge notched
into a 30px square's corner would cross into its neighbour.

The reduced-motion carve-out has to name these pseudo-elements by hand:
the global rule uses `*`, which does not match a ::after, so without it
the ping would be the one animation on the page that ignores the
preference.

Put the sidebar's icons on a ladder with five rungs

Twenty-one call sites had drifted to nine different sizes, and the drift
was not saying anything: search was 14 in the sidebar's field and 15 in
the overview's, add was 12, 13 and 16 in three places that are all the
same kind of control, and the row's hover cluster ran an archive glyph at
13 beside a close glyph at 12 inside two identically sized 22px boxes.

The rungs are 2px apart because 1px apart is not a difference anyone can
see — it reads as a mistake, not as a distinction — and each one is keyed
to the glyph's ROLE rather than to the type beside it, which is why the
overview's 15px filter field and the sidebar's 13px search field both
take the 14 rung: in both the glyph is the affordance, not the content.
The tile and card rungs survive because there the glyph IS the subject.

The ladder lives on Icon's own definition, where a caller reaching for a
number will actually read it, and the scan test pins it: size is a plain
number, so nothing in a type or a render can notice a call site quietly
picking 15 again.

fix(notifications): land a toast click on the notification, not just the app

Clicking a toast raised the window and, only when the row named a session,
opened that session's pane. A row with no session — an MCP server that fell
over, a probe that stopped answering, a budget ceiling — went nowhere at
all: the window came forward showing whatever it was already showing, and
nothing said which of them the user had just been told about.

A row that names a session still lands on its pane, and a permission row
goes through jumpToPermission, whose focus move is the thing that pops the
card open — that action now takes the session the row names instead of
choosing one, since a row whose question was answered in another window
belongs on its own pane rather than on whichever session happens to be
waiting. Every other row lands on the feed page with the row selected,
through the same selectNotification the in-page click uses, so the landing
is a stop the arrows can retrace rather than a jump they cannot see.

revealSession now reports whether it found a pane, which gives the same
feed landing to a session whose item is gone: the space switch has already
happened by then, and leaving the user somewhere new with nothing opened
was the one outcome worse than not moving.

feat(panes): let a destination page open in the pane you are looking at

One page per space means a second activation of Library, Connections,
Notifications or Settings homes to whichever pane already holds it —
switching pane groups to get there if it has to. That is right when you
meant "take me to it" and wrong when you meant "put it in front of me",
and until now the only way to say the second was to drag the pane.

openDestinationPage takes a placement. The plain click keeps homing;
⌥-click, and the row menu's new Open here, name the focused leaf instead,
which is what turns openItem's homing into a move. The two only differ
once the page is open somewhere else — a page that does not exist yet is
created in the focused pane either way — so both surfaces gate the extra
affordance on that, rather than advertising a choice with one outcome.

The palette carries the same pair for the same reason: the two surfaces
would otherwise disagree about what activating a destination can mean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(delegation): run agents in parallel, and let delegation nest

agent_run was strictly sequential: one blocking run per parent, enforced by
the engine's one-entry-per-parent registry. Fanning out N tasks meant N
round-trips. And a delegated child could never delegate at all — depth-1,
a flat wall.

Both were the same constraint wearing two hats. Depth-1 was never really
about depth; it was the only bound available once concurrency was capped at
one. Put the bound where it belongs — on concurrency — and depth becomes a
budget instead.

- The engine's registry holds a LIST per parent, capped per-parent (4) and
  machine-wide (12). `hasRun` still means "blocked inside a delegation call"
  and ignores detached runs, so the browser agent's, the reviewer's and
  ask's refusals are unchanged.
- `agent_start` spawns and returns a handle (the child's session id);
  `agent_wait` collects, `agent_status` lists. `agent_run` is now literally
  start-plus-await of the same background drain, so there is one settle path.
- A wait timeout gives up on LISTENING; children keep running under their own
  budgets, which is why the watcher starts at spawn and not at wait.
- Depth budget (MAX_DELEGATION_DEPTH=2) replaces the flat rule for agent_run
  children. Browser-agent and reviewer children stay depth-1 — a reviewer that
  can spawn workers is not read-only. A budgeted child sees the agent_run
  family and nothing else.
- The bypass cap applies at every level, so the budget cannot launder access
  down the tree.

feat: session interjection — one session asks another, mid-turn

agent_ask / agent_answer / agent_peers on the existing realm-agent provider.
Session A asks B a question, blocks, and B carries on with its own work.

This is agent_run's SIBLING, not a variant: same engine, same one-run-per-session
registry, same fenced-output posture — but it targets an EXISTING peer, so it must
never do the two things agent_run does to its target. It may not create it (every
guard runs before any side effect), and it may not kill it: not on timeout, not
when the asker is interrupted. A peer was doing its own work before the question
arrived and is still doing it, and the only thing this service may stop is its own
waiting. That is `engine.begin(..., { interruptOnCancel: false })`.

"B resumes its own way" is honest per kind, via AGENT_MIDTURN_DELIVERY read off
the three adapters. Codex alone is literal — turn/steer injects without stopping
anything. Claude and every ACP kind end the turn and are re-prompted; they keep
full context (that is the provider's conversation, not something Realm rebuilds),
but the in-flight tool call is aborted. So a peer sitting on a permission prompt
is refused outright rather than having that prompt denied on the user's behalf.

Cycles are impossible by construction, not by detection. The engine allows one
in-flight run per session, so the wait-for graph has out-degree <= 1; the edge
that would close any cycle necessarily points at a node that already has one,
which the guard refuses. That same guard stops a session mid-agent_run being
asked — interrupting a delegating parent would kill its child as a side effect.

A bug the suite found, not review: awaitAnswer's prose fallback fired on the
peer's PRE-EXISTING output. Interrupting a busy peer ends its turn, so an idle
arrives carrying assistant text from before the question — the act of asking was
read as an answer, handing the asker a fragment of unrelated work. Fixed with a
turn-boundary rule in the engine's scan, and pinned by direct engine unit tests
because the integration test could not: through the real app the peer's next turn
starts microseconds later, so the mutant survived there. It dies here.

Delivery is deliberately not SessionService.send: no checkpoint (send captures
one, which mid-edit records a tree that never existed), no auto-title, and the
user_message carries `from` so the pane labels it. Rendering another agent's
words as the user's would be a lie the user acts on.

Durable runs: a goal that owns a session across attempts

A run is a supervisor, not a delegation. `DelegationEngine` keeps its registry
in memory on purpose — an in-flight MCP tool call cannot outlive the process —
but nobody is blocked on a run, so it is a row and every transition is a write.

Sessions were already durable (`markStaleOnBoot` + `resume: providerSessionId`);
what was missing was something to own the goal across attempts and decide what
happens when a session settles.

Server:
- migration v17 — `runs` + `run_attempts`. The partial unique index over the
  three LIVE states is the load-bearing line: a poller can call `runs.create`
  naively and get one run. No `lease_until` — one process means every `running`
  row at boot is unsupervised by definition.
- `RunService` settles off the SessionService event hook the notifications feed
  already rides. No drain loop, no timer; `structure.test.ts` pins the absence.
- a restart does not spend the attempt budget — `recoverOnBoot` re-queues and
  widens `maxAttempts`, or `maxAttempts: 1` would make "durable" a lie.
- `blocked` is the human gate. `bypassPermissions` is not in a run's vocabulary
  at all: unattended work cannot even ask for it.
- the dispatch recipe (agent kind / skills / environment) is extracted to
  `delegation/dispatch.ts` rather than forked out of `agent_run`.

Renderer:
- the Tasks tab becomes list-beside-panel. Runs are first-class rows; sessions
  dispatched BY a run are excluded, since they are already on screen as the run.
- the detail panel carries what a row cannot: the goal, the result, the attempt
  log, and the actions — Approve/Decline on a blocked run above all, guarded by
  the same rules the server enforces.
- a minimal "New run" affordance, goal only. Scheduling knobs belong to whatever
  fires runs on a schedule, not to a form opened to type one sentence.

Also fixes a PRE-EXISTING pane bug this work exposed: `.page` is a flex item
with no `min-width: 0`, so its min-content floored it and a page whose content
did not fit grew past its slot and was painted over by the neighbouring pane —
with the covered strip unclickable. The Sessions tab was overflowing by 179px
before this branch touched anything. Found by driving the real app with three
panes open; jsdom has no layout, so `styles.test.ts` is the only guard.

Verified end to end against a scratch REALM_HOME with the real claude CLI:
create → run → finish, and NEEDS-HUMAN → approve with a reply → resume on the
same session → finish at attempt 2/2.

Three defects the feature only showed against real data, all found by
importing 290 candidates into the actual database and reading the result
back rather than trusting the run's own summary.

**Codex writes one file per resume, not one per conversation.** 241
rollout files on this machine are 71 threads; 158 of them replay a single
Stora conversation under one session_id. The provider-id dedup already
refused the extras, but it kept whichever copy was scanned first — a

offers conversations rather than files and says so in the source report.

gone imports with providerSessionId null, so it cannot advertise a resume
it could not perform — which also left nothing tying the row back to its
file. Those re-imported on every run: 31 duplicate sessions on the second
pass. Imported source keys are now recorded in settings, the same
install-once posture skills.bundledInstalled takes.

**EVENTS_MAX was measured wrong.** At 4,000 it truncated a real
15,479-event thread to a quarter of itself, and — because `messages` is
what the replay comparison reads — made the fullest copy of that thread
look like the smallest. Across all 392 transcripts here exactly two
exceed 4,000 and none exceed 20,000, so the cap is now a runaway guard
rather than a routine clip.

`scripts/undo-import.ts` is the safety net this needed: an imported

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

docs: plan 21 — visual editor, mobile half (Flutter, Compose, SwiftUI)

Ranks the three platforms by acquisition mechanism, not by preference, because
they do not differ by degree:

- Flutter hands you a source-located widget tree for FREE over the VM service,
  with no code added to the user's app. Build it first.
- Compose emits source locations into the binary already (the Compose compiler's
  sourceInformation strings, readable via ui-tooling-data behind one reflective
  flag flip). UTF-16 offsets, so it is the easiest write-back target.
- SwiftUI hands you NOTHING. Verified on this machine: a VStack renders as flat
  unnamed CALayers, hitTest returns nil, _ViewDebug has no source-location case
  and never has, and @attached(body) is rejected by the compiler on `var body`.
  No shipping tool does this — not Reveal, Lookin, Introspect, FLEX. So SwiftUI
  is opt-in `#realm` instrumentation per view, with zero coverage on anything
  the developer did not annotate, and the product must say so.

Also: React Native is deferred for the same reason plan 17 found for the web —
React 19 deleted _debugSource with no replacement.

The write-back invariant across all platforms: the parser only ever returns
offsets; Node does the splice; nothing outside the range can change, by
construction. Never run a formatter afterward. The refusal list is longer than
the edit list and that is correct.

feat: import sessions, memory and skills from the agent CLIs

Settings → Import reads what Claude Code, Codex and Cursor already have on
disk and brings it into Realm: transcripts as real sessions, the Claude
memory tool's per-project fact folders, and user-level skills.

Two invariants hold the feature up. The agents' directories are opened
read-only and never written, moved or cleaned up — everything produced
lands in Realm's database or under ~/Realm. And `import.scan` writes
nothing at all: it opens files, matches candidates to spaces and answers,
so the preview the user approves is exactly the work `import.apply` does.

Per-source parsers translate each CLI's own store into Realm's event
vocabulary. Codex is the interesting one: its rollout log carries the
conversation twice, and speech is read from the `event_msg` register the
user actually saw rather than the `response_item` wire register, whose
"user messages" include kilobytes of injected plugin advertisements.
Cursor's SQLite blob store is followed through the protobuf root blob's
ordered chain rather than scanned, so messages come back in order and
superseded revisions stay out.

Space matching is most-specific-location-wins over the cwd and its parent.
An earlier version ordered the rules without ordering the paths, and a
stale project row registering ~/Desktop/Home filed 255 of 290 real
transcripts under one space; MATCH_MAX_HOPS and the ancestor walk are that
regression's fix, with a test built from it. Unmatched rows fall to a
profile's Imported space and every row shows the rule that placed it.

Imported sessions keep their provider session id when the recorded cwd
still exists, so they resume the real CLI conversation on the next
message; where the directory is gone the link is left off rather than
advertised and then broken. Memory folders are copied to
~/Realm/memory/imported/ with a marker-fenced index in the space doc —
the largest folder is 712k characters against a 100k doc cap, so inlining
would have dropped 85% of it and called that an import.

fix(desktop): never apply a stale items reconcile or persist a mount-time resize echo

Live verification of the Plan 4 layout migration traced the observed

  scheduled a debounced persist during boot with zero user action —
  cementing whatever transient state the layout was in. resizeSplit now
  applies sizes locally but only persists once the space's items have
  loaded and reconciled; a legacy-shaped DB layout stays untouched until
  the user actually acts, and is then rewritten faithfully.

feat(desktop): native trackpad phases for the space swipe (macOS Spaces feel)

DOM wheel events carry no gesture phase, so 'fingers resting' and 'fingers
lifted' were indistinguishable and the swiper had to guess with a timer —
springing back mid-hold. A tiny Swift helper (native/ScrollPhase.swift,
global scroll-wheel monitor; deltas/phases only) streams NSEvent
phase/momentumPhase as JSON lines; main forwards them to the renderer over
IPC (preload onScrollPhase). The gesture tracker now holds wherever you
rest, decides commit-vs-settle exactly on lift (distance or release
velocity), and ignores momentum deltas. Timer heuristics remain as the
fallback when the helper is unavailable. Built by scripts/build-native.mjs
on predev/build (skips without swiftc / off macOS).
